#3605. Johnny Depp on Honoring Hunter S. Thompson’s Final Wish With a “Death Cannon” That Stood “Taller Than the Statue of Liberty”

He couldn’t remember if it was day or night when he found it, in the place where “one never quite knew or cared for time,” Johnny Depp wrote. He remembered the year—1997—and that he was with Hunter S. Thompson in his basement War Room at Owl Farm. It was just across the hall from Depp’s bedroom, with that old keg of dynamite serving as his bedside table.

Rummaging through beaten-up boxes that comprised Thompson’s archive, Depp unearthed something that would turn out to be equally explosive. “A battered typescript,” he called it. Abandoned among the detritus of Thompson’s renegade life, it was “bound together by rubber bands.” On its cover, “in Hunter’s own hand,” Depp noted, were the words THE RUM DIARY.

“He wrote the book in his early twenties,” Depp wrote. “And then stuffed it away.”

Side by side on the floor of the War Room, Depp and Thompson began “reading it to one another.” And when they were done, Depp had made a decision: “The Rum Diary was simply too good to remain lost.”

Thompson wasn’t able to find a publisher for The Rum Diary when it was written, but now he was, well, Hunter S. Thompson. With Depp as his advocate, The Rum Diary was published in 1998. “Almost immediately, the subject of a film was broached,” Depp wrote in a foreword to the screenplay, recalling Thompson saying, “‘Hot damn . . . yessir, let’s you and I produce this caper together, Colonel! We’ll have Hollywood groveling at our feet! They will crawl over a road of bones to get to us! Yessir!’”

A movie didn’t happen “as easily as we had hoped,” Depp continued in his foreword. “Fiery hoops of all dimensions, covert bear traps, woefully obstinate billfolds” arose in their path, “which neither Hunter or I were remotely experienced in battling . . . But we weren’t giving up.”

Hunter S. Thompson at his ranch in Colorado, 1990.

As the years wore on, Thompson grew increasingly inflamed over the development hell of Hollywood, writing producer Holly Sorensen a fiery missive in January 2001: “Dear Holly, Okay, you lazy bitch, I’m getting tired of this waterhead fuckaround that you’re doing with The Rum Diary. We are not even spinning our wheels aggressively. It’s like the whole Project got turned over to Zombies who live in cardboard boxes under the Hollywood Freeway. I seem to be the only person who’s doing anything about getting this movie Made. I have rounded up Depp, Benicio del Toro, Brad Pitt, Nick Nolte and a fine screenwriter from England named Michael Thomas.”

The eventual screenwriter for The Rum Diary turned out to be Bruce Robinson, the British director of the twisted 1987 cult classic Withnail and I, which both Depp and Thompson were “mutually obsessed with.” Depp had originally asked Robinson to direct the film adaptation of Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas—but by then, Robinson had quit directing, wrung out by the Hollywood system that had subjected him to making the Uma Thurman–led thriller Jennifer 8 for Paramount. He was content to spend the rest of his life writing screenplays and books and had vowed to never direct a movie again.

In 2005, Johnny tracked Robinson down while he was on vacation in Spain. “Have you read The Rum Diary?” Depp asked. Bruce hadn’t. The next day there was a knock on Robinson’s hotel room door, along with “the book The Rum Diary that Johnny had sent,” said Robinson.

“I wasn’t impressed by the book,” he continued. Neither were most critics: “For someone who gets to drink rum all day and have sex on the beach (the real thing, not the cocktail) all night, Kemp is pretty morose,” wrote one reviewer of the Thompson character. Despite some early incantations of the hellish voice that Thompson used with such tremendous force later in his career, it had many of the problems that plague early attempts at fiction. But because it was Johnny Depp, Robinson said he would try his hand at writing the screenplay.

Once back in Herefordshire, however, he found he could not write. Not a single word. “Nothing, nothing, nothing,” he said.

He knew the problem: abstinence. “I think it’s called alcoholism, probably,” he said of his tolerance for red wine. He had been sober for six and a half years, before which he had been “literally drinking wine all day while I worked. I’d finally gotten to the point where I was tired of doing that every day, seven days a week, so I cut the booze out of my life completely.”

Now he was stuck. Without the wine, which he said unleashed him from the gridlock of his superego, he was blocked. “You know I’m just going to have to drink some wine for this,” he finally confided to his wife. With her blessings, he opened a bottle of red, and then another and another, “one bottle of red wine a day—every day—for the three months it took me to write the story,” he said.

Then, as he was almost done with the screenplay (along with the Bordeaux), he drove into town to get the Sunday papers. The news was all over his radio: the American writer and journalist Hunter S. Thompson had killed himself.

“Oh, my God,” Robinson thought. “That’s the end of the movie.”

Hunter S. Thompson takes on his ranch in Colorado, 1976

Sunday, February 20, 2005. A heavy rainstorm lashed the streets of Los Angeles. Mist clung to the palms and a sense of gloom fell over the city, as it always does when it rains in L.A. Christi Dembrowski turned off Sunset and drove up the winding road to her brother’s home, bearing news that she knew would break Johnny’s heart: Hunter S. Thompson had died that afternoon of a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head.

“My sister Christi turned up at the house in a pouring rainstorm,” Depp said. “She’d received a phone call two hours after it had happened and didn’t want me to see it on CNN. She told me Hunter had gone. But as much of a shock as it was, as much horror as I felt when you receive such blunt, bad news, I also knew Hunter was never going to be the guy who was going to collapse in a bowl of soup.”

After the shock—along with the eulogies for the fallen writer dominating airwaves, telephone lines, and barrooms worldwide—came what Depp called the “devastation.”

“Tragic,” he told Tom Thurman in the 2006 documentary Buy the Ticket, Take the Ride: Hunter S. Thompson on Film. “Shocked but not shocked. Angry but understanding. A zillion different emotions flying around all the time. It was like somebody had removed something from your body. It was a heavy hit.”

Mourning the loss of his brother, mentor, hero, and friend, Johnny’s mind flashed back to the 1978 BBC documentary Fear and Loathing in Gonzovision, in which Thompson described in minute detail how he would like to be sent off from this world into the next: he wanted his remains cremated and shot from a cannon on his land in Woody Creek, Colorado.

“When I got the news that Hunter had made his exit, obviously I was devastated,” Depp said. “I remember thinking almost immediately, ‘The cannon. We’ve got to do the cannon.’”

For Depp, this wasn’t a writer’s fantasy; it was Thompson’s final command. “That bastard,” Depp said. “I know somewhere in his crooked mind . . . he knew that I was the only one perhaps loyal enough, perhaps insane enough, to attempt it.”

Over the years, Thompson had spoken about what would be called “the death cannon,” Depp said. “You know, he brought it up every now and again; ‘Oh, yeah, I’ve got to have—I need the cannon, you know. . . . I may have even said, ‘I’ll send you off.’”

Thompson’s son, Juan, was determined to make it happen, too. Only Juan envisioned a twelve-foot cannon, costing a couple of hundred dollars. Johnny wanted something bigger, grander. “A few days later, Doug Brinkley, Hunter’s good friend and editor of his letters books, came over to our cabin and said Johnny Depp had called and said he wanted to pay for the construction of the cannon,” Juan wrote in his 2016 memoir Stories I Tell Myself: Growing Up with Hunter S. Thompson. “We were astonished . . . it is one thing to be a friend; it’s another thing to volunteer to build a friend’s death cannon.

An initial commemoration of Thompson’s life was held at the Hotel Jerome in Aspen on March 5, 2005. It was “essentially a party with music, photos and videos, interspersed with testimonials from friends and family,” Juan wrote. Depp flew to Aspen with Benicio del Toro and John Cusack to attend it. During the event, one of Depp’s assistants found Juan in the crowd “and asked me to come with him to Johnny’s room,” Juan wrote.

The assistant “slowly opened the door. And I entered the dark room and looked around, and in the center of the bed was a sculpture, lit from within. A giant boom box was playing Norman Greenbaum’s “Spirit in the Sky,” with its lyrics, “When I lay me down to die / Goin’ up to the spirit in the sky.”

“The sculpture was a tapering silver tower made of aluminum, about three feet high, topped by a blood-red fist,” Juan remembered. “The two-thumbed fist. The peyote button glowed from within with shifting colors. There was a small hole in the top of the fist where the projectile would exit.”

It was a magnificent miniature model that exceeded even Hunter Thompson’s wildest dreams. The full version, as envisioned by Johnny, would be “153 feet tall, 15 stories, taller even than what Hunter imagined,” wrote Juan. “Taller than the Statue of Liberty.”

The cannon would be fabricated in Los Angeles and hauled in pieces to Owl Farm on flatbed trucks. “It has to be perfect,” Depp told his long-time contractor, Steve Cohn, who coordinated the event over three months in Aspen (residing in three suites in three different Aspen hotels; at one of them, the Sky Hotel, Cohn allegedly set the record on room service booze and “incidentals,” spending more than $100,000). No expense was spared for what would become a monumental undertaking, requiring six months of massive set designing, and construction and engineering crews “numbering at least a hundred” from Hollywood and beyond, said Cohn.

On August 20, 2005, a crowd of 250, including Jack Nicholson, Sean Penn, Bill Murray, and Senators George McGovern and John Kerry, assembled on the meadow behind Thompson’s home. After the toasts and speeches (“Hunter, this is for you,” said Depp), a video clip of Thompson discussing his funeral cannon in his 1978 BBC interview was played on a giant screen. A Japanese drum ensemble began performing. Glasses of champagne were passed around. Then all eyes were on the massive cannon, its red fabric curtains unfurling to reveal the gonzo logo—the two-thumbed fist and the pulsating green peyote button—at the top of the 153-foot tower. “Spirit in the Sky” blasted from the speakers. “Then, at 8:46 p.m., more than thirty fireworks rocketed high above Owl Farm . . .” Doug Brinkley wrote in Rolling Stone. “The cannon atop the tower fired, and Hunter’s ashes fell over the assembled guests like gray snow. ‘Mr. Tambourine Man’ blaring from the sound system on cue. Hunter was literally all around us now. . . . ‘I have never seen an event like this,’ whispered the actor Harry Dean Stanton. ‘And I’m old. Very old.’”

“Everybody was speechless,” said Cohn. “Johnny and I were sitting together when it went off. He looked at me, smiled, and said, ‘That was awesome.’”

With Thompson’s ashes in the air, the party began in a massive tent decorated to look like Hunter’s kitchen and living room.

Bruce Robinson’s initial thought was that the death of Hunter Thompson would mean the death of The Rum Diary. But he was wrong about that.

“I had lost my dear friend and co-conspirator,” Depp wrote. “Sure as fuck wasn’t going to give up now.”

#3604. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input

90 Day: Hunt For Love surprised me when two cast members decided to give dating a serious go, but I'm not expecting it to last. Sorry to Jamal Menzies and Emma Perry, but I'm already seeing all the red flags that this trial-run relationship could be over by the time we reach the Season 2 tell-all.

Emma continues to be the best part of Season 2 as episodes continue to air as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Her continued feud with Chloe Fabiano and relationship with Jamal have carried this season, but I don't know if there's more to the latter than just providing 90 Day Fiancé fans with some quality entertainment.

From storming off in the middle of arguments to sitting down for therapy sessions, it feels like Emma and Jamal are already preparing for an appearance on 90 Day: The Last Resort. These are the arguments I'd expect from a couple who were married and on the verge of splitting, not a couple who only just decided to start dating.

Emma insisted the drama in the latest episode was tied to her ongoing feud with Chloe, and that outside of the show, she and Jamal wouldn't have as many problems. Based on both of their past storylines, I'm more apt to believe they're just very quick to feel deep emotions, which can be a volatile combo when two people are in a relationship.

Imagine my surprise when I saw an update from 90 Day Fiancé insider Shabooty suggesting Jamal and Emma are still together. A photo apparently taken earlier this year is making the rounds online, and it shows them vacationing together in Aruba.

90 Day: Hunt For Love Has Me Wondering If Brittany Intentionally Sabotaged Michael's Love Life

All this to say, neither is posting clues that they're still together as of writing. It's possible the trip to Aruba was something for them to see if they wanted to keep dating after Hunt For Love and that we'll see that unfold in a future spinoff.

If Jamal and Emma are together, I'd genuinely be curious to see how it's going. On the off chance they are going strong, they may just turn into one of the all-star couples of 90 Day Fiancé. I'm rooting for this franchise to have a new star couple, so that would be an upside of these two getting together.

We'll get some updates when the tell-all hits, but until then, we'll just have to keep watching 90 Day: Hunt For Love. Season 2 is so much better than the previous season so far, so here's hoping a potential third season is even better.

#3602. How To Watch Brad Pitt's Heart Of The Beast At Home

David Ayer's "Heart of the Beast" wasn't really a sleeper hit, given that it stars Brad Pitt, but the harrowing survival film turned out to be a surprisingly leggy box office performer thanks to solid word of mouth. Now it's about to find a wider audience as it moves to streaming on November 10 (as the opening of Pitt's kinda-sorta anticipated "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" nears).

The film caught on with moviegoers due to its deeply affecting narrative about a retired Army veteran (Pitt) and his combat dog struggling to survive in the Alaskan wilderness after their seaplane crashes. The crash is caused by Pitt's character having a heart attack, but he's not down for the count — not yet. He and his dog are uniquely equipped to hoof it 58 miles back to civilization, but this terrain is every bit as treacherous as a battle zone. Along the way, they encounter wolves (dredging up memories of Joe Carnahan's "The Grey"), a grizzly bear and other obstacles that test their resolve. Each challenge leaves them a little (or a lot) worse for the wear, but they are determined to emerge from this ordeal as they've done so often in their war-torn past.

Again, "Heart of the Beast" will begin streaming via Premium VOD on November 10, and consumers will get a few extras to go along with their purchase.

According to a press release issued by Paramount today, the PVOD "Heart of the Beast" will include a behind-the-scenes featurette titled "One Last Mission," which is said to be a "love letter to the land, the people, and most of all the dogs who made this film shine." (Their names are Uber, Seeka and Ryker.) Because you can never get enough good-dog footage, there's also "Uber & Brad: A Soulful Bond." Not sure why Seeka and Ryker were denied a mention here, but I guess I'll find out when I watch it. Finally, there are deleted scenes that promise to "play tug of war with your heart strings," so get ready to weep some more once you've finished the film (and you will weep).

While it would've been nice if this visually stunning film remained in theaters for a little while longer, it was clear from jump that its destiny was to become a dad movie classic. It'll be streaming for years and years to come, forcing grown men to complain about their dusty living rooms/man caves. And if you're one of those people who needs to know the fate of the pooch ahead of time, /Film's got you covered.

#3601. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

#3600. Dolly Parton Is Gone, But Dollywood Will Always Love Her

“RIP Dolly Smoky Mountain Angel” was one of the first signs we saw as we pulled up on the side of a motel in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee. Just down the same road was another memorial to her on a Burger King sign. This was in early October. Dolly Parton, the country singer and actor, widely considered a Great American Who Everyone Loves, had died, at the age of 80, in late August. I am not the kind of person who cries over celebrity deaths, but after I heard that she died, I went to my closet to find a Dolly Parton T-shirt I had bought the one time I saw her live, at a concert of mostly acoustic songs in Queens in 2016. I couldn’t find it. I blamed my brief flirtation with the Marie Kondo method, but there was no way that T-shirt hadn’t sparked joy.

Early October in Sevier County, in far eastern Tennessee, where Parton was born, is full of cabins on some parcels of land that dot the ancient Appalachians. But among the rolling green expanses are Mexican supermarkets, coffee shops, apple orchards, and pumpkin patches. This is where she opened the amusement park Dollywood in 1986. The Great Smoky Mountains National Park draws masses about 13 miles from Dollywood. The fancier of my friends identified the area as where the Blackberry Farm resort is. But Pigeon Forge has a feeling of a Jersey Shore boardwalk in Appalachia, with a strip of businesses that sell vapes and ATV rides and Moon Pies a block from a Margaritaville hotel.

Parton opened Dollywood in 1986 at the foothills of the Great Smoky Mountains. Today, it draws in millions of people annually—loving fans who don her iconic pink cowboy hat or accessories honoring the park's famous Grist Mill Cinnamon Bread (a cult favorite).

Locals heap the kind of praise on Parton that we’ve come to expect knowing her reputation as a goddess among mortals. “People don’t understand what she did for this place and meant to this place. She threw lots of money at it and went out of her way to take care of this place,” an Uber driver named Eric told me as we exited the highway into Dollywood, with its script logo and “love every moment” greeting signs. “I got to meet her three times at the park because she would just show up and stand there with a crowd of people. For someone who’s been famous as long as she’s been famous you’d expect a certain air of haughtiness,” he says. “But I was stunned at how kind she was.”

Parton’s job title at the park was dreamer-in-chief, and part of Dollywood’s allure is that it’s a shrine to her life and career. There’s a replica of the two-room wood cabin where she grew up a sharecropper’s daughter, in close quarters alongside her parents and 10 siblings. Her home, not even 500 square feet, had no electricity nor running water. (The original home still stands about 10 miles away but isn’t open to the public.)

Parton wrote the country ballad “I Will Always Love You” in 1973 as a heartfelt farewell to her longtime business partner Porter Wagoner. Now, fans honoring Dolly's memory have used the slogan for the park's new annual festival, which opens in March 2027.

That modest beginning is plenty known, but Dollywood also celebrates Parton as she became a household name and wildly rich. The Dolly Parton Experience is a museum devoted to her trajectory, from Nashville ingenue to a celebrity among celebrities (photos show her with Mick Jagger in the ’60s and Whitney Houston in the ’90s). It has a gallery devoted to her Imagination Library, which has donated more than 300 million books to children around the world. Another building across a landscaped path celebrates her role in the workplace revenge comedy 9 to 5 (September 25 has now been christened a holiday in Sevier County) and houses a half dozen of her wigs, sorted by decade, all platinum, all voluminous. A plaque commemorates her wig stylists, starting with her Aunt Colleen. Parton’s costumes are scattered around the tributes, including a black flared jumpsuit with a hot pink shirt and neck ruffle so intense it looks Elizabethan. One wall features one of Parton’s famously self-effacing quotes: “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap.”

In her mobile home, which guests line up around to take a tour, she has a closet with a hanging yellow diamanté dress, a full-size bathtub because she preferred baths to showers, mirrored ceilings because she was claustrophobic, and cheeky digital clocks that display her most hallowed time zones: Dollywood (5:53 p.m. ET) and Nashville (4:53 p.m. CT). I ask our tour guide, a woman in a sparkly vest, how she and the park employees have fared without Parton. “Today is the first day I haven’t cried,” she admits.

Dollywood is more than a museum—it's an amusement park. The 165-acre Pigeon Forge carnival features over 50 rides and Dollywood's Splash Country, a 35-acre water park.

But more than a museum, Dollywood is an amusement park, and a much bigger one than I had realized. It’s a place where you can stand in line for 45 minutes to buy a corn dog while listening to a four-person singing-and-dancing group in the vein of the Mickey Mouse Club does peppy but half-assed covers of Fleetwood Mac and Van Halen. Looping rollercoasters and water tube rides leave families soaking wet in matching T-shirts commemorating their vacations. Dondre, my colleague and our photographer for this journey, waits probably a full hour to squeeze into a vintage muscle car with me so I can simulate steering around a track. It wasn’t until deep into our wait time that we realize this is a children’s ride. At this point, the two of us notice that, in the sea of people, we are the only ones who are childless, wearing dark colors, and audibly bemoaning that Dollywood is dry. (Parton was not a strict teetotaler, but the park bills itself as assertively family-friendly. “Weapons and alcoholic beverages are not permitted on Dollywood Property” is the only explanation given on its website.) No one else seems to care. The ride is quick, but we are ecstatic, high on refillable Diet Cokes, kettle corn, and driving a car, which neither one of us knows how to do in real life.

Some park employees have not fared well without Parton. One tour guide admits: “Today is the first day I haven’t cried." Parton passed away on August 25 at the age of 80 after a battle with cancer.

We don’t want real life at Dollywood. We want the dreamer-in-chief’s dreams. For dinner, we hit the 8:30 show of Dolly Parton’s Stampede in Pigeon Forge, an equestrian version of dinner theater where guests are served a whole chicken, pulled pork, corn, greens, a biscuit, pie, and unlimited soda, all to be eaten by hand while the not so vague perfume of manure wafts through the air. Horses with cowboys and cowgirls astride them jump through rings of fire, someone does wire work while dangling from the ceiling, and American flags fly in abundance. We catch a pig race. Sooo-ey! At another point, a volunteer from the audience disappears from a barrel before our eyes. The whole thing feels psychedelic, and we peak when performers in butterfly wings ride around to Parton’s song “Love Is Like a Butterfly.” I squeal as a few actual buffalo take the arena. After the show, I ask a cowboy how the majestic creatures are as animal coworkers, and he shakes his head. “There’s a reason I stick to horses.”

Even in the perfect bubble of Dollywood, in the wake of her death, Parton’s spirit has already faded into the nostalgia.

There isn’t enough acknowledgement of Parton’s death at the park for my taste; no candlelit vigil or impersonators we can hug. By the second day, my mania has subsided, giving way to contemplation. I ask fellow parkgoers if they have come to pay respects. Every single one replies that their trip has been planned long before. My attempts to make small talk with strangers doesn’t result in the fantasy of one collective mourning. Families in seasonal T-shirts seem shy and uninterested in chatting with me, a strangely inquisitive middle-aged woman who wants to ask them if they’ve heard the rumor that Dolly Parton was secretly covered in tattoos. (They haven’t.) A friend group of two lesbian couples from Pennsylvania brushes off my line of questioning around whether Parton might have been more than just queer-friendly (rainbow Dollywood shirts and backpacks and trucker caps are for sale). Too soon, they say, and shake their heads—too salacious to be airing gossip. I ask other strangers if they have heard the family drama over Parton’s estate. Most dismiss me, but another Uber driver, this one named Austin, says, “She has a huge estate and a big family, and it was always going to happen. We’ll see how it plays out.” (In November, the lawsuit was dropped, and Parton’s nephew said he was happy to put the issue behind him.)

The butterfly is a key part of Dollywood's logo, representing Parton's personal emblem. As a little girl growing up in the Smoky Mountains, she was fascinated by butterflies and related to their gentle grace. She cemented the motif into her career in 1974 with the hit song, “Love is Like a Butterfly.”

Maybe, I say to Dondre, no one will talk to me because I, unlike about 50% of the people there, am not wearing a T-shirt emblazoned with a Bible verse, a military slogan, or a celebration of America’s 250 years. I keep pointing out paintings of crosses and eagles and American flags—often all combined on one canvas together—for sale. Dondre says, in a kind way, that nothing is more cliché than hearing someone from New York talk about other parts of the country. Maybe what made Dolly Parton so winning—her apparent lack of judgment—is not something I inherently have. It can’t hurt to try to be a little more like Parton in our own daily lives.

Maybe she had an optimism no one can ever replace. And that’s ultimately okay because you can try to channel that anywhere. Even in the perfect bubble of Dollywood, in the wake of her death, Parton’s spirit has already faded into the nostalgia, a curio like Graceland, but with a vintage steam train ride.

I succumb and buy a Christmas ornament with Parton dressed as Santa and eat a chicken salad sandwich served on a butterfly-logo-shaped pretzel. I guess I enjoy Dollywood the way I enjoy going dancing in Berlin gay clubs or karaoke birthday parties: It is an experience, and a fun one, but not what I would choose. I will never, in the vein of a Disney Adult, be a Dolly Adult. More power to those who cherish their season passes. But Parton doesn’t even have to be core to your identity for you to enjoy an intricately branded amusement park. Its unchanging presence is a comfort. If you need to commune with her earthly treasures, there is always Dollywood. May her costumes and wigs remain.

Dollywood will always be a place for fans and dreamers alike to marvel in the wonder of the country icon’s extraordinary career and charming home.

#3599. Warhammer Survivors Isn’t Good Enough to Be a Vampire Survivors Replacement

Good clones are the sincerest form of flattery

Vampire Survivors and its plethora of clones are always more fun in hour ten than hour one. The passive nature of the auto-attack gameplay means this style of experience lives or dies by how fun and visually over-the-top the action can get once you upgrade your character, gain access to more weapons, and manage to survive long enough to level up or evolve your weapons.

I did eventually hit that point of satisfaction with Warhammer Survivors, which was developed by Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 studio Auroch Digital with help from Vampire Survivors creator Poncle. When I got to the point where I could rip and tear through enemies with a Typhoon Crossbow as followers with upgraded weapons of their own fired at enemies around it, the game offered spectacle worthy of the Warhammer and Survivors names. But getting there doesn’t feel quite as good as its inspiration.

Warhammer Survivors doesn’t contain any sort of important lore to speak of; it’s more of a hodgepodge of various recognizable Warhammer characters (like Boltgun’s Malum Caedo) fighting against waves of unrelenting creatures from both eras of the franchise. Warhammer Survivors is essentially two games in one, with one half based on the sci-fi Warhammer 40,000 and the other on the more fantasy-like Warhammer: Age of Sigmar.

Each half of Warhammer Survivors has unique characters, weapons, enhancements, and objectives to unlock, but the core gameplay loop of each is the same. As a player, all you have to do is walk around levels as your character automatically attacks. Enemies drop experience when they die most of the time, and you collect that to level up and upgrade all of the weapons that you have equipped. Considering Poncle was directly involved with this game, it’s not surprising that Warhammer Survivors does not do much to hide its inspiration or reinvent the formula.

The most unique gimmick here is a follower feature, which solves for the fact that Warhammer Survivors’ characters are connected to factions that only let them use specific weapons. Rather than one character wielding every weapon and upgrading at once, sometimes you can save or summon another character that uses a different weapon to fight alongside you. This feels fitting for the large-scale battles Warhammer is known for. Yet in practice, all it really does is add an additional layer to a choice you were already going to make regardless.

It shouldn’t be too surprising that what you’re getting with this game is Vampire Survivors with a Warhammer coat of paint, even if it does go a bit deeper than Vampire Survivors’ typical crossover DLC. Vampire Survivors is a great game, and Warhammer Survivors is a good one too. That said, I won’t herald Warhammer Survivors as some amazing replacement for that indie classic, because there are some things it doesn’t do quite as well as the original.

Survivors games are all about snowballing power, building up to a chaotic storm of attacks. In Vampire Survivors, almost every weapon has auto aim and will hit something in range when used. But that’s not the case for certain early-game weapons in Warhammer Survivors that shoot the direction the player is facing, like the Boltgun. Those simply don’t mesh well with the auto-attacking gameplay.

The lack of auto-aim on these weapons meant that, as I moved to avoid enemies, I would shoot away from the horde, toward nothing. Eventually, I was able to unlock better weapons that would actually hit the enemies approaching me, but the fact that the earliest weapons are some of the worst means it takes a bit too long to find the fun.

By hour 10 with Vampire Survivors, I had found the characters and weapons I enjoyed using the most. They tended to be the ones that would allow me to exponentially increase in power most smoothly and actually felt like I could survive 20+ minutes and 40+ levels into a single run. From that point onwards, Warhammer Survivors is as good as Vampire Survivorsor any other game of its ilk. It’s just not quite as instantly captivating and rewarding.

Diehard Warhammer fans who haven’t played Vampire Survivors or any of the games it inspired will have a fantastic time with this, but there’s not much reason to abandon the original Vampire Survivors for this official clone. Warhammer Survivors certainly won’t usurp its direct inspiration as my go-to game of this style because it forgets to emulate some of what made Vampire Survivors near-perfect. Still, it confidently delivers exactly what the title promises.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

#3598. Christopher Nolan's Batman Begins Borrowed Part Of Its Plot From A Beloved Animated Series Episode

In each of the three "Dark Knight" trilogy films, the villains make an attempt to destroy Gotham City from within. In "Batman Begins," one of those villains is Doctor Jonathan Crane/The Scarecrow (Cillian Murphy). The head of Gotham's Arkham Asylum, Crane is obsessed with fear. With ingredients provided by the League of Shadows, he's manufactured a "fear toxin" that can drive anyone exposed to it to terror. Using Arkham inmates, Crane has been dumping the toxin into Gotham's water supply via the asylum's pipe systems.

"Scarecrow tries to infect Gotham City with fear toxin" has become a stock "Batman" plot, like in the 2015 video game "Batman: Arkham Knight" or the 2021 comic crossover "Fear State." Look back, though, and you'll find it before "Batman Begins" — specifically, in "Batman: The Animated Series" episode "Dreams in Darkness," written by Judith and Garfield Reeves-Stevens. Batman, exposed to the Scarecrow's fear toxin and suffering hallucinations, is judged insane and locked inside Arkham as a patient.

Under his doctors' noses, Scarecrow plots to dump his toxin into an underground river that flows into Gotham's reservoirs, infecting the city and sparking a mass frenzy of fear. Crane isn't doing it for ransom or a statement; a former academic, he's running a mass experiment in studying the psychological effects of fear.

Still, it's hard to write off the similarities between "Dreams in Darkness" and "Batman Begins" as coincidental. The scene of Batman (Christian Bale) defeating Crane is even taken from a different "Batman: The Animated Series" episode: Scarecrow's debut, "Nothing to Fear." Batman poisons Scarecrow with "his own medicine," causing Crane to hallucinate Batman as not merely a man in a bat costume but a demonic, man-sized bat creature.

Whereas in "Dreams in Darkness" Crane is moving in and out of his cell, "Batman Begins" put him in control of Arkham (reimagining Crane's original backstory as a college professor). "Dark Knight" trilogy co-writer David S. Goyer has said he convinced Christopher Nolan that Scarecrow needed to wear his mask, and they devised a practical reason: The mask is a gas mask that keeps Crane from ingesting his fear toxin and scaring his victims who do. That is not the case in "Dreams in Darkness," where Crane is exposed to the toxin while in costume and ends the episode back in his cell as a hysterical mess.

Goyer has said the selection of Scarecrow as the villain of "Batman Begins" came out of the movie's theme of confronting fear. If you're going to steal, steal from the best, because "Dreams in Darkness" is a masterclass at showing Scarecrow getting under Batman's skin. It's the most frightening Scarecrow episode of "Batman: The Animated Series" and the only one that actually comes close to being a horror story, thanks to Batman's repeated and menacing hallucinations.

The first fright is a jump scare; Batman sees the Joker walking towards him reflected on the Batcomputer's screen, only to turn around and find it was Alfred. The terror doesn't let up, and once Batman makes it to Arkham, there's also the dash of psychological horror. Batman is locked in the same asylum as his greatest foes, where no one believes his pleas, and their doubt could cost a city's worth of lives. Granted, the doctors' refusal to believe Batman does border on incompetence. Scarecrow wanting to poison the city is just another night in Gotham, but Arkham's staff treat Batman like he's raving mad.

Many of the best "Batman: The Animated Series" episodes feel like 22-minute film noirs, and "Dreams in Darkness" is no exception. The episode begins in media res at Arkham, with the opening twist that the "new patient" the doctors are talking about is Batman. Batman gets a voiceover narration — a noir staple — as flashbacks explain how he ended up in a straitjacket.

The hallucinations get worse before they get better. Batman's cell door swings wide open, bathing him in a hellish red light. His parents walk into a dark tunnel, disappearing as that tunnel becomes the barrel of a giant handgun. Once Batman escapes and makes it to the caverns where Scarecrow dwells, he imagines a rat taking on the Joker's face. Imagined villains then keep gruesomely metamorphosing into others. As Batman imagines himself falling into an abyss, the darkness becomes a spiral shape with Scarecrow's face in the center.

It's beautifully animated and genuinely creepy stuff; the central image of Batman falling looks right out of Alfred Hitchcock's "Vertigo."

As for the straw-man of the hour, Scarecrow doesn't appear much. He only shows up onscreen halfway through and spends his time waiting on a countdown for his experiment. But "Dreams in Darkness" is Scarecrow voice actor Henry Polic II's best, and most subtle, performance in the role. His baritone is soft, almost mellifluous, which only makes moments like Scarecrow's cruel snicker at how he's left Batman "much, much worse" off than death more unnerving. Polic's time as Scarecrow can be overshadowed by Jeffrey Combs' later, superior performance on "The New Batman Adventures," but "Dreams in Darkness" shows he could be as great a Scarecrow as Combs — or, indeed, Cillian Murphy.

#3597. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

If Parks and Recreation and The Office have one thing in common, it's that both series took a little while to find their footing. Of course, these two comedies have more than one thing in common -- both aired on NBC around the same time, both were created (or co-created in Parks & Rec's case, alongside Michael Schur) by Greg Daniels, and both debuted with big expectations from fans of an existing series. It's no surprise that Amy Poehler would find some very common ground with Steve Carell when talking about their experiences on their respective shows.

Not all of the best sitcoms of all time got off to an amazing start. The Office and Parks and Recreation are two perfect examples of shows that needed more than a few episodes to find their groove. In March, back when Steve Carell's new HBO series Rooster was just getting started, the Office star sat down with Amy Poehler on her Good Hang podcast. Among the topics that came up was how poorly their earlier sitcoms were initially received by viewers.

As Poehler tells it, there are two people that she's been told she's a "poor man's version of," and Carell is one of them. She went on to laugh about how terribly the debut of Parks and Recreation went, saying:

Parks and Rec had the worst launch ever. Everyone was like, 'This is not The Office, we don't like this.' I just remembered we're like -- 'You're not Steve and you're not -- we don't like it!' And I think I just dissociated and was like, 'well.'"

That viewers might have been looking for more of what they'd come to know and love from The Office -- and Carell's character, Michael Scott -- is not that surprising, given its creators and the fact that it was another single-camera mockumentary-style workplace comedy. In the case of Parks and Rec, the focus was on the office workers at the Parks and Recreation department of a small town in Indiana. That included Poehler's optimistic and determined Leslie Knope.

When Greg Daniels and Michael Schur's new series debuted in spring of 2009, it was around the same time that The Office was wrapping up its fifth season. Months prior to Parks and Rec's debut, The Office had its post-Super Bowl double episode, "Stress Relief," which was watched by millions (and is remembered as one of the best episodes of the series). The Office was firmly established with its fanbase, while Parks and Rec was just getting warmed up.

It's almost easy to forget that The Office had faced a similar challenge years earlier, as Carell noted in his conversation with Poehler:

Our pilot was the lowest casting pilot in the history, I think, of NBC. People really hated it ... They actively hated this show, and I don't quite know how it got legs after that.

Lest we not forget, The Office didn't debut to universal praise and sky-high ratings when it arrived in 2005, and it was nearly cancelled after its first season. The show arrived on the heels of the success of the 2001 Ricky Gervais sitcom that started it all, and to say that the U.S. version of the beloved UK comedy had big shoes to fill would be an understatement.

Personally, I didn't hate the first season of the U.S. version of The Office when it aired, but I also wouldn't argue with many of the criticisms of the show's first six episodes. That's a whole other conversation though. Getting back to the topic at hand, in his conversation with Amy Poehler, Carell called himself out as "a poor man's Ricky Gervais."

I don't think anyone would say that about Carell today, but he certainly had a high bar to meet when leading the U.S. version of The Office. And from what he said, he intentionally didn't watch more than a minute of Gervais in Office:

I watched like a minute of him, and he was so good, and so specific, and so funny, I thought, if I watch a second more, I'm just going to go on an audition with that. I won't be able to even imagine it a different way.

There really is only one David Brent, so it's understandable that Carell wouldn't want to try to recreate that character in Michael Scott. Ultimately, Carell's character became iconic in his own right, thanks in large part to the actor's comedic brilliance. Several seasons after he made his debut as Michael Scott, Carell had a say in how his character would exit the series.

All of this to say, I can see why Carell and Poehler would connect on this particular topic, as both of them saw success in their respective roles and shows, but it wasn't instant and both had to find their way out from under the shadow of other performances. Each show had to find their own way to success, and it's just really fortunate that both were given time and seasons to do so. I can't imagine a TV world without Michael Scott or Leslie Knope!

You can watch Parks and Recreation and The Office streaming with a Peacock subscription.

#3595. Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries Face Democratic Leadership Revolt After Midterms

The latest conflict brewing in the Democratic Party’s cold war between the blue dogs and the insurgent progressive wing is the fight over its next congressional leaders. But with no alternate candidates stepping up to run, it’s hard to determine how real the threats to replace Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries actually are.

At least six incoming Democratic senators—including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, South Carolina’s Annie Andrews, Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan, Illinois’s Juliana Stratton, Kansas’s Adam Hamilton, and Maine’s Troy Jackson—have said they won’t support Schumer for majority leader. Michigan senator Elissa Slotkin has called for a “a new generation of leadership.” Even Cory Booker, who praised Schumer for helping engineer last week’s blue wave, stopped short of saying whether he would support him. On Monday, Richard Blumenthal did the same, but walked by his comments later in day, saying he would support Schumer. And Jon Stewart said that the senator “does not understand the urgency of the moment and what the future demands.” Regardless, Schumer is confident. His aides say he has enough votes to become the next majority leader.

In the House, several incoming Democrats—including Claire Valdez, Angela Gonzalez-Torres, Darializa Avila Chevalier, Melat Kiros, Adam Hamawy, Chris Rabb, and Donavan McKinney—have been noncommittal with their support for Jeffries, while Ohio democrat Don Leonard has threatened to seek alternative leadership unless Jeffries changes his position on Israel.

There’s an online effort to prevent Jeffries from becoming Speaker of the House. A change.org petition demanding that House Democrats reject Jeffries as their next Speaker has attracted more than 1 million signatures as of Sunday, with actor Mark Ruffalo among those encouraging people to sign. But scroll to the bottom of the petition, and you’ll find a disclosure: Its creator, Nicole Whitted, is a paid “Change Ambassador” who receives compensation from change.org in connection with the signatures. “Thousands of organizations and brands worldwide run similar programs and in the social-cause space specifically, it’s a way to encourage people with reach and influence to use their voice for causes they care about,” Whitted told Vanity Fair in a statement.

Whitted also said she was traveling to Washington, DC next week to urge congresspeople to vote against Jeffries, and to meet with Representative Ayanna Pressley, whom Whitted told VF she’ll be supporting for Speaker. Pressley’s team did not respond to Vanity Fair’s request for comment sent on Sunday. Neither did her closest congressional allies, Rashida Tlaib, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, or Ilhan Omar.

Reports indicate that some congresspeople have been flooded with calls from constituents urging them to find new party leadership. But one Democratic aide told Vanity Fair that they’ve noticed what they claim is a coordinated effort to undermine Jeffries on social media, including AI-generated videos attacking Jeffries that have gotten tens of thousands of engagements.

The Brooklyn congressman does have good relationships with members of both the moderate “blue dogs” and the party’s progressive flank. Ocasio-Cortez has already backed him, and last month, Representative Ro Khanna declared that “Hakeem Jeffries is going to be Speaker.” “Don’t believe what you’re seeing on the internet,” the aide said. “It’s not reality.”

Schumer’s allies, meanwhile, have been reminding skeptics of the work he did to deliver the Democratic majority. The New York senator helped recruit candidates including Roy Cooper and Sherrod Brown, while the Democratic political operation supporting Senate candidates spent lavishly on competitive races. According to final figures provided to Vanity Fair, Senate Majority PAC and its affiliates spent nearly $407 million across races in eight states, including $150 million in Ohio, $67 million apiece in Iowa and Michigan, $65 million in Maine, and $40 million in Texas, all of which flipped. Another $14 million went toward Kansas, with smaller investments in Mississippi and South Carolina—$2.2 million and $750,000 respectively. Some of that money helped elect candidates who are now skeptical about whether Schumer should stay in charge.

In the House, each party will choose its leadership this month, but in order to become Speaker, a candidate still needs to get a majority of the entire chamber, usually 218 members, to vote for them when the new Congress convenes in January. It’s a little easier in the Senate, where the Democrat will only need to win a simple majority of their own caucus in an anonymous early December vote to become majority leader.

El-Sayed has suggested Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen, although a source close to Van Hollen told Vanity Fair that he isn’t planning to run, instead setting his sights on a potential presidential campaign in 2028. “Prior to selecting a majority leader, Senator Van Hollen believes the caucus needs to have an honest and open conversation about how we move an agenda forward that reflects the will of the American people,” says a Democratic aide familiar with the senator’s thinking. “He’s made clear that Democrats need to use their power to immediately end the illegal war with Iran, advance a robust pro-worker kitchen table agenda, and fight political corruption.”

Another name circulating among Democratic aides is Hawaii senator Brian Schatz, a relatively young progressive who has developed relationships across the party’s ideological factions and is already pursuing the number-two leadership position being vacated by retiring senator Dick Durbin.

“He’s the heir apparent,” one Democratic aide told Vanity Fair, describing Schatz as someone who could appeal to both progressives and moderates. Asked about speculation surrounding his leadership ambitions, Schatz’s spokesperson offered a noncommittal response: “I don’t have anything new to share on this but will keep you posted if that changes.”

Some Democrats are also hesitant to replace their experienced leaders after they’ve been given this narrow opportunity to get stuff done with control of both chambers of Congress. “I don’t think you’d want somebody new who’s, like, learning the ropes while we have the opportunity to really get meaningful legislation passed for the American people,” another Democratic aide said.

Still, the fighting online and on cable news exposes a tension within the Democratic Party. Moderates see the blue wave as vindication of the party’s disciplined, affordability-focused strategy. Progressives see it as a mandate for a more ambitious agenda—and a rejection of the establishment’s familiar faces.

Both factions are claiming the election as their own victory. But before they can fight over what to do with their new power, they’ll have to decide who’s going to lead them.

#3594. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

#3593. This Classic Marvel Villain Could Reshape The MCU — And Introduce Nova

With heavy-hitting villains like Loki, Thanos, the Red Skull, Galactus, and now Doctor Doom already featured — and in most cases, thoroughly defeated — in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, it's easy to wonder who might be next in line to pose a threat to the Avengers. It is, after all, pretty difficult to raise the stakes higher than the death and resurrection of half the universe in "Infinity War" and "Endgame," even when there's an entire multiverse out there just waiting to be put in danger. There is, however, one major Marvel Comics villain who has yet to step into the spotlight in the movies, with a track record as one of the deadliest enemies not just to a single team of heroes, but to the entire cosmos.

Annihilus, the insectoid ruler of the Negative Zone, has over 60 years of comics history and has proven himself to be every bit as deadly as Thanos, but without the veneer of nobility that came with the goal of seeking some kind of cosmic balance. Annihilus has no noble goals or grand designs, just a massive army of mindless drones hellbent on consuming everything in its path, and if he's introduced into the MCU, he has the potential to not only wreak havoc across the entire universe, but also pave the way to finally introduce the fan-favorite hero Nova to the big screen.

Originally introduced in 1968's "Fantastic Four Annual" #6 with the ominously over-the-top nickname of "The Living Death That Walks," Annihilus was at one point considered by director James Gunn to be the villain of "Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3," and with good reason. While he's been a perennial foe for the Fantastic Four, Annihilus' most prominent and destructive moments came in the 2006 crossover "Annihilation," which saw him unleash billions of locust-like drones across the galaxy in an "Annihilation Wave" that toppled long-established star-spanning empires and still has lasting effects on the Marvel Universe two real-time decades later.

Perhaps most importantly, "Annihilation" paved the way for the introduction of the modern Guardians of the Galaxy. Rather than the original Guardians concept of a team of sci-fi heroes in the distant future of the 30th century, Annihilation and its sequel, "Annihilation Conquest," rebooted them as space-faring hard-luck heroes led by Star-Lord, which led directly to the version that made it to the MCU. As a result, Annihilus is a natural fit to face off against the Guardians in some form, so it makes sense that he'd be considered for the third film, even if the decision was ultimately made to focus more on Rocket's origin and pit the heroes against the High Evolutionary instead.

Despite not making it into "Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3," Annihilus remains one of the biggest comic book supervillains who hasn't been tapped for a role in the movies, providing the MCU with an opportunity — although not necessarily one that fans might expect. After "Annihilation," Annihilus wasn't just tied to the Fantastic Four, but found a new arch-enemy: Nova.

The Nova Corps were introduced to the MCU back in the first "Guardians" movie as an organization of galactic peacekeepers, but Earth's representative, Richard Rider, has been floating around for years as a potential addition to the franchise. We haven't seen him yet, but if the films continue to draw on the events of "Annihilation," the fact that the Corps is already established makes it possible for the films to recreate one of the comic's biggest moments. As the opening shot in his war against the rest of the galaxy, Annihilus, well, annihilates the Nova Corps on the planet Xandar, leaving Rider as the sole survivor. Rich does eventually get his revenge, literally punching down Annihilus' throat and tearing out his guts in one of the most truly badass moments in Marvel Comics history, and one that plenty of fans would love to see recreated in the films.

Of course, insectoid space dictators and comic books being what they are, Annihilus did eventually make his way back from the dead, but that could be very beneficial considering that unlike the comics, the movies have a tendency to kill off their villains. Giving them the ability to return and rise again allows their characters to develop over time alongside the heroes, even if some of them definitely deserve their fate.

Nebula is one of my favorite MCU character.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Marvel Cinematic Universe is nearing its 20-year anniversary, and many fans have been watching the Marvel movies in order since Day 1. The shared universe (which is streaming with a Disney+ subscription) has a few fan favorite franchises, chief among them being James Gunn's Guardians of the Galaxy. I've been missing Nebula and the rest of the team, but Karen Gillan recently gave me some hope about their return.

The end of Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 saw the team splitting up and going their separate ways. The final title card confirmed that Chris Pratt's Star-Lord would return to the MCU eventually, which put doubt into whether or not we'd ever see everyone else. In an interview with The Direct, Gillan was asked if there's a chance we'll see Nebula back in upcoming Marvel movies, with the actress responding with:

Maybe... You know I can't tell you that [laughs]. I have Marvel snipers on me. I have definitely spoken to them. Whether or not that was about making another appearance or not is a different story. Okay, waffle without saying anything at all. I'm still going. Basically, no spoilers over here.

Honestly, I'll take it. This isn't a confirmation about if/when we'll see the Blue Meanie back in the shared universe, but the fact that Karen Gillan is in contact with the powers that be at Marvel is a hopeful message. Nebula is one of my favorite characters in the entire MCU, and I'd love any opportunity to catch up with her sometime in the future.

When we last saw Nebula, she and Drax were committed to staying on Knowhere and raising the children that they saved from the villainous High Evolutionary. I'd love to se how this was going, as well as how Karen Gillan's character stands with her the revived Gamora. There are certainly narrative threads to pull from, so let's hope that the studio moves forward with a project that includes Nebula.

James Gunn is departing as co-CEO of DC Studios, which might offer some hope for Guardians of the Galaxy fans who want to see more from the cosmic team of heroes. Now that his schedule is freed up, perhaps he'll be inspired enough to explore what happened after Vol. 3. After all, Marvel fans adore the Guardians.

For now fans can re-watch Karen Gillan's tenure as Nebula on Disney+. That includes the three Guardians movies, the Holiday Special, as well as appearances in Avengers: Infinity War, Endgame, and Thor: Love and Thunder.

The next MCU movie hitting theaters is Avengers: Doomsday on December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. We'll just have to see if the Guardians of the Galaxy end up popping up in that movie or its sequel Secret Wars.

#3591. Elon Musk’s Cybertruck Is Dumb, Ugly, and Mercifully Dead

In March 2024, a Tesla Cybertruck speeding down Sunset Boulevard slammed head-on into the Beverly Hills Hotel’s iconic entrance sign just before midnight. Passersby winding through the Flats slowed down to watch as Elon Musk’s statue to his own insecurities—the stainless steel embodiment of nuance-free American ego—demolished in front of Hollywood’s unofficial canteen.

Every decade gets the iconography it deserves. At just about the midpoint of the 2020s, ours had arrived, fully formed.

And now the Cybertruck is dead, which is wonderful news. Musk, who’s having a historically bad November, announced late last week that Tesla will be “winding down” production of the Cybertruck around mid-2027, putting an end to the most hated car in America. I was going to call it the most polarizing car in America, but honestly, no one likes this thing. And it’s not entirely due to anti-Elon sentiment: Tesla’s general sales have been relatively steady, going down a bit as Musk went full DOGE mode in 2025 before rebounding in 2026. People like Elon’s cars. They just do not like the Cybertruck.

True, its death has been mourned by some—especially the self-selecting devotees who installed bulletproof glass in their Cybertrucks before shooting them with rifles. These people exist. But mostly, the news has been greeted with a rush of enthusiasm, relief, and, more than anything else, blue-pilled schadenfreude.

Now would be the right moment in the news cycle for an art writer such as myself to make a contrarian argument: that the Cybertruck was secretly a design masterpiece—some kind of neo-Donald Judd breakthrough unleashed ahead of its time.

I am not going to make that argument, because that is not true. Not even close. No one in the future will look back on the Cybertruck as an unheralded art object. It’s The Jetsons for meatheads, a Batmobile for people who secretly root for the Joker. It looks like a birdhouse designed by Zaha Hadid, which I would love to have as a vessel for feeding hungry birds at my (sadly hypothetical) Zaha Hadid house. But I would not want it as a vehicle to park in a driveway. It is a bad car.

And yet, that crashed Cybertruck in front of the Beverly Hills Hotel is seared into my brain, playing on repeat like the most un-subtle Lana Del Rey song ever written. Even beyond that crash, the Cybertruck is the ultimate symbol of this surreal and cruel decade, one that started with a global pandemic and a government suggesting the possibility of a bleach injection as treatment. It’s a decade that wound through four years of a former president denying the lawful election of a current president, only to see that former president return to power. Through it all, we’ve sunk deeper into our collective psychosis—one that’s forced us into rooms with our devices, addicted to social media and artificial intelligence, consuming half-real information and spewing it back out into the world.

It’s a perfect world for the Tesla Cybertruck to define.

The Cybertruck arrived right at the dawn of the decade, in what we can now see as a completely different timeline.

Musk unveiled the car in November 2019 at Tesla’s design studio. Head designer Franz von Holzhausen attempted to demonstrate the vehicle’s shatterproof glass by hurtling a metal ball at a window at full speed. The window shattered. Great omen! It was also pretty weird that Musk was introduced by a hologram of someone called “Cybergirl,” who people speculated was actually a hologram of Grimes, the pop star Musk was dating at the time.

Plenty of design press fawned over the shiny new thing—“Long live the Cybertruck. See you in the Thunderdome,” wrote Dwell. But Wired wisely asked the opinion of an actual expert: Raphael Zammit, who chairs automobile design at Motor City’s own College for Creative Studies.

“I was like, ‘Oh my goodness! What did Tesla do? What did they do?” he said. “It literally breaks every rule we tell to our students. It’s what we tell them not to do.”

Regardless, the Cybertruck started to infiltrate the cultural atmosphere. It was lampooned on The Simpsons. There were countless memes. It was embraced, very early, by rappers. Weeks after the unveiling, Travis Scott used his personal connections to the Tesla CEO (they did Christmas together with the Kardashian-Jenners) to snag a Cybertruck for his video for “Gang Gang,” a posse cut with the Cactus Jack crew.

Three years later, Pharrell Williams, 21 Savage, and Tyler, the Creator featured the Cybertruck in their video for “Cash In, Cash Out”—rendered in Claymation. Offset’s video for “Swing My Way” has Anok Yai sitting atop a Cybertruck. Bad Bunny said, “Me monté en la Cybertruck y me acordé de la Montero de los viejos tiempo.” Meek Mill said, “They was doing cyber attacks, so I bought a Cybertruck.”

The cars fascinated artists too. Julia Wachtel’s CyberChrist, on view at Todd Von Ammon’s DC gallery, von ammon co, earlier this year, pictures Jesus Christ pulling an elongated Cybertruck behind him. I recall with great happiness the perverse thrill of Frieda Toranzo Jaeger’s Cybertruck, a painting in her 2022 show at MoMA PS1. These artists were certainly taking a critical eye toward the Cybertruck, but for some art collectors, there was nothing ironic about it. At least, a specific kind of collector. When I arrived at the convention center for Art Basel Miami Beach in 2024, the first full year of Cybertruck distribution, there was a line of Cybertrucks wrapped around the block.

But that’s the thing about the Cybertruck: There was always more supply than demand. Musk initially hoped to sell 250,000 units per year. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, Tesla moved nearly 39,000 of them in 2024, a decent start. In 2025, sales dropped, then dropped again in 2026.

Perhaps the Cybertruck could have endured the ridicule of design experts, car enthusiasts, and aesthetes with even just a whiff of good taste if it weren’t for the massive backlash that accompanied Musk’s move into radical right-wing politics, and his full-throated support of Donald Trump. After his efforts at DOGE resulted in the gutting of USAID and other agencies, along with unprecedented and remorseless mass firings, Cybertrucks started getting vandalized around the country. Some owners tried to protect their weird boxy investments with mea culpa stickers—“I bought this before Elon went crazy,” etc.—but no one believed that, or really cared. The cars got defaced. No one stepped in to intervene. The Cybertrucks deserved it.

There was also a bleaker incident that parallels the Cybertruck at the Beverly Hills Hotel: the dystopian hellscape of the Cybertruck that exploded on the Las Vegas Strip, in front of the Trump International Hotel & Casino. The man responsible for that explosion served in the US Army, and authorities believe he suffered a self-inflicted gunshot wound just before the vehicle detonated. The Beverly Hills crash was an accident in which no one was harmed—but the charred, deadly remains of the truck in Las Vegas seemed downright terrifying, a vision of American capitalism and greed that had met its grisly moment.

Perhaps now, with a new era of Washington poised to define the final years of this most delirious of decades, we’ll eventually look back at the Cybertruck with at least some nostalgia for its silliness, its boxy stupidity, its pop culture ubiquity. If it does linger in the annals of history, maybe we’ll think of the Cybertruck as a roadbound folly of the world’s first trillionaire, and a footnote in Musk’s legacy, for better or for worse.

Put it this way: By the time Hollywood studio heads arrived at the Polo Lounge for their Monday power lunches, the mess of the Cybertruck that had crashed at the Beverly Hills Hotel the night before was gone. Almost as if it never happened at all.
