#3574. Exclusive: ‘Breaking Bad’ Star RJ Mitte, in His Own Words

For those of us who managed to land a role on Breaking Bad, the show is a formative part of our lives. It represented a chance to work on what is now considered one of the best shows TV has ever seen, and the cast and crew forged an unbreakable bond. RJ Mitte was part of the show’s heartbeat. When I spoke to him for this book, we reflected on our days shooting in New Mexico fondly.

I’ll always remember him as a young kid—bright, talented, and a real sweetheart—who was so thrilled to be on set with us that it reminded us how lucky we all were. We'll all miss him dearly. Rest in peace, RJ. —Dean Norris

The last person to join the White family was RJ Mitte, cast in the role of Walt Jr., aka “Flynn.” RJ, who was only fourteen years old at the time, joined the project after we had already begun filming the pilot, following multiple rounds of auditions stretching out over several months. You might wonder why casting Walt Jr., a comparatively minor character among the core cast, took so long. Well, it was about verisimilitude. As written, Walt Jr. had cerebral palsy, albeit a relatively minor case. It was a fundamental part of the character, and Vince was adamant that the role not be played by a nondisabled actor.

VINCE GILLIGAN, creator: I was worried at the beginning that people wouldn’t connect with Walt. They’d say, Why is this guy doing this terrible thing? And so I kind of loaded him up for bear in terms of, you know, he had a son with cerebral palsy. You felt bad for him. People bullied him.

SHARON BIALY, casting director: We had a lot of autonomy with casting, once we knew what Vince was looking for, once we all agreed that, aesthetically, we were talking about the same type of actor. A case in point is RJ Mitte’s role. Vince only wanted actors who had CP. So, we conducted a nationwide search.

RJ MITTE, Walt Jr.: Walt Jr. is actually based on a real person, a friend of Vince’s from college who had cerebral palsy. So, Vince was really particular about the role of Walt Jr. and who was going to play him.

Experienced actors who also have mild CP is not the deepest pool, of course, but there are more candidates than you might expect. And RJ Mitte’s casting has to be considered something of a surprise, given his relative lack of experience and a variety of other challenges he faced while growing up.

RJ MITTE: We were living in Houston when my sister got discovered at a water park, and that’s what brought us to LA. My sister got booked on a job at Universal Studios for an ad campaign. She was one and a half at the time. We really didn’t have a lot going on. Things were tough. My mom was a single mom, and she had recently been partially paralyzed in a car accident, and my grandparents, who I was very close to, were both sick and dying, so when we got this offer to go to LA, we took it. It was a paid trip. They put us up in a motel in Hollywood—there was a strip club on one side, and a Ralphs and a library on the other side. That’s LA.

Everything was covered for six months, so I just started acting to meet kids my own age and have a little extra cash while we were there. And it ended up turning into a career for me. I started working at a young age, not in the acting industry, but with my uncle and family jobs and stuff to make money as a young kid. I would like to think I grew up with a strong work ethic. So, when we got to LA, I hit the ground running. Within the first six months, I was on shows like Hannah Montana, Everybody Hates Chris, Weeds, Seventh Heaven, Drillbit Taylor, Epic Movie—­ all as an extra. I think that really helped prepare me for Breaking Bad, just with the quality of work and the type of professionalism that the set had. I’m very grateful, because if I did not get Breaking Bad, I wouldn’t have an acting career.

At any number of points along the journey, RJ’s dream could have died. It’s hard enough for a known actor to land a role in a show of this quality, but for a newcomer, it must have been daunting, although you never would have known it by the way he carried himself on set.

RJ MITTE: Funny story: My very first audition ever in my career was an anti­ meth campaign for the state of California. It was a wild PSA, and I ended up not getting it. A year or so later, I started auditioning for Breaking Bad. The description of the role literally said, “dark hair, big eyebrows, and mild cerebral palsy.” And I was like, that’s me!

Sharon Bialy called me in, and I already had been on quite a few auditions by that point, and I didn’t book any of them, so I knew what rejection felt like. I had a sense of, Don’t hold your breath. But I’m a firm believer that you go in owning it and when you walk out, don’t look back. Every callback was a little more like, Wait, I’m actually still in the running.

Walt Jr. had a somewhat more severe case of CP than RJ, who did not use assistive devices for mobility in real life.

RJ MITTE: When I went in for my first audition, Sharon was there, and she had hurt her foot. So, she actually handed me her crutches that she was using for the audition. Six months went by, four callbacks, four auditions, and in that final one, they’re like, Okay, we’re sending you. You’re going to New Mexico. The next day I was on a 6 a.m. flight to audition for Vince and the team. Then he excused me for a moment and brought me back in to do my test screening with Anna and Bryan.

Think about that. RJ was fourteen years old and trying to land a job that would change his life, a job that would help him support his entire family. Talk about pressure.

RJ MITTE: I think in life I’ve always had pressure. It really didn’t stand out to me too much. I can only do what I can do. And so as long as I’m doing my best, that’s what matters. But it always kind of felt like I was part of the team to some degree, even when I wasn’t. And so when it came to doing the scene with Anna and Bryan, it really felt like a family. It was like, Oh, yeah, this feels right. Apparently, they must have had the same feeling because they hired me.

Like everyone else, RJ made the most of his opportunity and crafted a fully formed portrait of an adolescent at the center of a family storm; one whose disability may have helped shape him but did not define who he was.

RJ MITTE: This was the first time I think people really saw a character with a disability who wasn’t disabled. There’s nothing he couldn’t do that other kids were doing. It wasn’t about the disability, and that’s something that I think Vince really stressed: it’s not about his disability; it’s about being a part of the family and living with it.

Six seasons in, Breaking Bad reached its apotheosis with the monumental episode “Ozymandias,” in which Walter White’s house of cards comes crashing down. It’s also the episode where Flynn learns the truth about his father’s double life, and that Walt has led my character—his brother-in-law, Hank—to his death. The episode builds to a climactic moment where Flynn’s mother, Skyler, grabs a knife and brandishes it at her husband.

RIAN JOHNSON, director, “Ozymandias”: The actual fight itself, I remember being surprisingly fun to shoot—­just making sure to give Anna and Bryan the space that they needed to find it. I think RJ also did a terrific job in that moment—­ he’s kind of the linchpin of the whole thing.

It is indeed Flynn who rises to the occasion. When Walt wrestles the knife away from Skyler, his son jumps on top of him and throws him across the room. He’s a big kid, strong enough to handle Walt despite his disability; strong enough to protect his mother.

RJ MITTE: It was very intense to shoot. At the same time, we’re professionals. Everything was very choreographed. There was one moment when we first started, I got so heated, and so into it, that I kind of accidentally grabbed Bryan the wrong way and kind of like tossed him . . . wrong. And everyone was like, “Whoa, RJ! You can’t throw him like that.” And I was like, “Oh, I’m so sorry. I just got caught up in the moment.”

RIAN JOHNSON: When you see Walt Jr. turn, then you know it’s truly over. And Bryan’s reaction to that just breaks my heart every time I see it.

In the series’s penultimate episode, Walt clandestinely calls Flynn at school. A package is on its way, he says, to be delivered to the home of one of Flynn’s friends. The package contains money, one hundred thousand dollars—­the most he could stuff into one box. “I wanted to give you so much more, but this is all I could do,” Walt explains, leaning into the pay phone as Flynn listens, wordlessly, on the other end.

RJ MITTE: I remember at the time we were shooting that scene it was in this school-slash-doctor’s-office that we were using. Bryan was in the room with me when we did this part. It definitely was heartbreaking to have to feel that way about someone that I admire. And I think that’s what Junior felt as well. I’m a believer that in life, there’s always a moment where you have to choose to either be an adult or to stay a child. This moment comes in many different forms, but it comes down to that moment where you say, Am I going to accept this and give them what they want and be submissive, and still have that child aspect of who I am? Or am I going to take charge and become the person that I need to be—­ the man, the adult?

RJ does some terrific wordless acting in this scene, wrestling with this decision. Then he speaks: “Just shut up! Just stop it. Stop it. I don’t want anything from you.”

“You need this money,” Walt says. “Your mother needs this money. It can’t all be for nothing.”

Yes, it can, as Flynn makes abundantly clear.

RJ MITTE: A lot of the decisions I made for Junior were based on my own experiences as a young adult. At the time I was still a child, but I utilized those moments from my own life of having to stand my ground and make that decision—­ realizing who I am and what I need to do to take care and provide for my family. In the show, Walt was no longer doing that. He was actually creating more danger for his family.

I think it’s very powerful that Walt Jr. had the ability to stand his ground, and to put those boundaries in place: “You’re out. This is my family now, and you’re not a part of it.” I find a lot of young men and women have to take that stance at some point, especially with parents or family figures that live in a volatile world, a world that is corrupt.

Later, in the series finale, Walt is standing over a crib, caressing the hair of baby Holly as she naps. He leaves and then watches from a distance as Flynn gets off a school bus and walks into the apartment.

VINCE GILLIGAN: With Walt, you want him to have a goodbye scene with his wife. We were sad we couldn’t have a goodbye scene with his son, Walt Jr., because RJ is a wonderful actor. We just didn’t have the room.

For those of us who were fortunate enough to be a part of it, Breaking Bad remains a seminal event in our lives, both personally and professionally—­ an opportunity to work on one of the greatest television shows in history, alongside people who became lifelong friends.

BRYAN CRANSTON: I knew when it ended that this was the role of my life.

AARON PAUL: I think I can speak for everyone involved in the show: It changed all of our lives.

RJ MITTE: I will be eighty years old in a nursing home and there will probably be someone looking at me through a window, saying, “There’s Walt Jr.” And I’m okay with that.

Excerpted from the book DO WHAT YOU’RE GONNA DO: The Definitive Oral History of Breaking Bad by Dean Norris with Joe Layden. Copyright © 2026 by Dean Norris. From William Morrow, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Reprinted by permission.

#3573. These Surprisingly Powerful Soundcore Earbuds Are Under $35 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The Soundcore P31i earbuds are down to $32.99 (originally $59.99), which is as low as they’ve been, according to price trackers. At this price, most earbuds stick to the basics, so it’s unusual to see features like active noise cancellation and LDAC included here. That doesn’t mean they compete with premium pairs, but they do give you more to work with than you’d expect for under $35.

These earbuds are light, they fit well, and they don’t get uncomfortable after an hour or two, which isn’t always the case with cheaper earbuds. Battery life, too, holds up through a full day of use, with a little over seven hours on a single charge and extra top-ups from the case. The sound quality is better than expected for the price, though it leans toward bass-heavy tuning out of the box (you can tweak it in the app, but the app itself is not the most intuitive and takes some getting used to, notes this ZDNET review), and if you’re using a compatible device, LDAC support gives you the option for better audio quality.

There are also a few extras tucked in, like HearID for tuning the sound to your ears and an AI translation feature, though features like that feel more like a bonus than something you will use every day. As for its noise cancellation, it works, but expectations need to stay in check—it reduces steady background noise like engines and traffic, but it won’t match the isolation you get from more expensive earbuds. That lines up with its overall build, as well, which feels a bit basic compared to more expensive options.

#3572. GTA 6 Presales Are 'Running Far in Excess of Our Expectations,' Take-Two Interactive CEO Says

GTA 6 is so hot, it's hurting Take-Two's other games

Grand Theft Auto 6 is one of the most anticipated releases of this decade, so it's no surprise that it's selling like hotcakes before it's even out. In this fiscal quarter's earnings presentation, the CEO of developer Take-Two Interactive revealed that pre-orders "are tracking far above initial expectations". However, GTA 6's success might also be the reason Take-Two's other game series failed to meet target sales.

For many, the world will stop on Nov. 19 as gamers enter Leonida for the first time. Players across the globe are preparing to use vacation days for the launch of GTA 6. Some companies are closing stores so their employees can play. Even the United States Army is granting soldiers four days of leave to experience this one-of-a-kind release. The hype around the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 is unprecedented.

Pre-sales for GTA 6 went live on Jun. 25, giving players nearly five months to pre-order the game, and it's going even better than anticipated. Take-Two Interactive's CEO, Strauss Zelnick, told Variety that pre-sales are "running far in excess of [company] expectations." While Rockstar Games has yet to confirm these numbers, reports from earlier this month indicated that Grand Theft Auto 6 had sold 8 million copies ahead of launch.

In the fiscal report, Zelnick stated that with pre-orders continuing to "reach unprecedented levels," Take-Two expects to deliver "a historic year." Despite this, the release of GTA 6 might have hindered other Take-Two releases. It's no secret that many publishers deliberately avoided launching their games in November this year, as they knew most eyes would be on GTA 6. That is why so many games came out in September, and as a result, Take-Two's NBA 2K27, which launched on Sept. 9, fell through the cracks and failed to meet sales expectations.

While Zelnick hoped for better results from NBA 2K27, he told Bloomberg that "if your lunch is going to be eaten, I'd rather be the one eating it," fully aware that this is a case of "suffering from success." Even though the sales numbers were below company expectations, it was still the second-biggest launch for Take-Two's basketball game.

Rockstar's new Grand Theft Auto game is on pace to make up to $5.2 billion at launch

#3571. Robert Pattinson's James Bond Comments Resurface 14 Years Later Amid Casting Rumors

Fresh off his electric performance in the dark, unsettling media satire "Primetime," Robert Pattinson is said to be in contention for the role of James Bond. According to The Hollywood Reporter, Pattinson screen tested for the part in Denis Villeneuve's upcoming Bond reboot movie for Amazon MGM Studios, which puts him in the running alongside several other well-known contenders. For the actor, it has been a long time coming. It seems that, 14 years ago, Pattinson envisioned stepping into the 007 role at a later point in his career.

In a 2012 interview with The Sun (via NDTV), the British star said he'd "definitely like to go for Bond" but wanted to wait another 20 years. "There'd be nothing worse than, like, 'Let's get a fresh-faced Bond!'" he added. "That would be the worst idea in the world. It would be ridiculous to reinvent it as some young posh kid." At the time, he was just starting to make his transition from teen heartthrob to chameleonic leading man, and was promoting what has since become known as one of Pattinson's best movies, David Cronenberg's "Cosmopolis." Since then, much has changed, and while it hasn't quite been two decades, it seems the actor wasn't kidding when he said he'd one day like to play 007.

Back in October 2026, it was reported that Josh O'Connor was one of the Bond finalists, alongside "Fantastic Beasts" actor Callum Turner, and "Slow Horses" star Jack Lowden. Since then, reports have claimed that Nicholas Hoult and Pattinson are also in the final group, which means five actors are now vying for the role of England's greatest spy. If Pattinson does land the role, it will be yet another major success for the actor and, given his prior comments, a particularly satisfying one.

In his interview with The Sun, Robert Pattinson seemed entirely opposed to the idea of a young James Bond. "After Daniel Craig you have to have some baggage," he said of the erstwhile Bond actor, who reinvented the spy for a new generation with the unbeatable "Casino Royale" in 2006. "I'd have to be tortured in the first few scenes. I'd have to do the first film with one arm or something." It's unclear just how serious Pattinson was at the time, but he seemed to have an awareness of just how tortured a version of Bond Craig portrayed during his tenure in the tux.

With that in mind, it will be interesting to see, if Pattinson does land the part, whether he doubles down on the haunted loner version of 007 he mentioned in his 2012 comments. The best Bonds have all had an edge to them, but it might be that Denis Villeneuve and Amazon MGM want to go in a different direction after the diminishing returns of the Craig era Bond films.

As it stands, nobody knows for sure who will play the lead role in Villeneuve's upcoming film. Based on the finalists, one thing we do know is that Amazon won't be going the "young posh kid" route, to use Pattinson's phrasing. All the contenders are 36 years old, except for Pattinson who at 40 is the oldest of the bunch. With final screen tests said to have already taken place, it won't be long before we get an official announcement, and if Pattinson does land the role we at least know he's been mentally preparing for 14 years.

#3570. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

#3569. 22 Years Later, The Polar Express' Best Line Is Still One Of The Best Christmas Movie Quotes

Published in 1985, Chris Van Allsburg's picture book "The Polar Express" is a staple of children's Christmas literature. Filmmaker Robert Zemeckis brought its yuletide magic to the silver screen in 2004 with an animated film. Zemeckis had once blended live-action and animation in "Who Framed Roger Rabbit" by sticking Bob Hoskins next to cartoon characters, and with "Polar Express," he aimed to achieve an even deeper fusing of mediums with motion capture.

"Polar Express" didn't open to the smoothest ride. With an exorbitant $170 million budget, the movie was greeted by some as a failure for grossing only $286 million. The use of motion capture animation made the whole thing look uncanny (and became a "30 Rock" punchline), which is the last thing you want for what's meant to be a heartwarming family movie. Not that this stopped Zemeckis from using the same "Polar Express" style in 2007's "Beowulf" and 2009's "A Christmas Carol" (featuring Jim Carrey as Scrooge). "The Polar Express" divided critics in its day, as seen by its 55% Rotten Tomatoes score. Roger Ebert gave it a perfect four stars rating, but others couldn't get over the creepy animation.

But any kids movie seen by enough kids of its generation usually transforms into a classic with time. The movie is also often re-released in theaters during the holiday season. There have been events like branded Polar Express train trips or "Polar Express in Concert," too. Many see "The Polar Express" as a ride they like to take again and again, and, as of 2024, a sequel was in very early development. Let's take a look at one of the film's most memorable quotes.

"One thing about trains: it doesn't matter where they're going. What matters is deciding to get on."

The Conductor (Tom Hanks) tells this to the Hero Boy (Daryl Sabara, with some motion capture work from Josh Hutcherson) at the end of the latter's adventure. The boy is departing the Polar Express and returning home, never to doubt the existence of Santa Claus again. It's a clear rewording of the "it's the journey, not the destination, that matters" aphorism, but tweaked in a way to fit the story's themes of faith and belief.

Note that, in the film, we see the Conductor makes the kids choose to get onboard. The train shows up in front of their house, he tells them they're going to the North Pole, and if they refuse, he shrugs and says "suit yourself." The Hero Boy only jumps on when the train starts pulling out of his yard, seizing his moment and making his leap of faith at the last chance.

Faith is only faith if you believe without having true proof that the object of your belief is real. Even for something as harmless as choosing to believe in Santa Claus, making a choice of what to do with your life requires faith. Note also the other name for a train: a locomotive, a name all about movement. What matters is deciding to get on the train, the Conductor says, because choosing to not get on means standing in place and surrendering to fear of change. It's a good message to have in mind during Christmas, as one year closes out and a fresh one is about to blow in like a winter storm — or, indeed, a train arriving at a station.

#3567. How Nicolas Cage Really Feels About Ryan Gosling Playing Ghost Rider

In September 2026, Nicholas Cage slammed the Marvel Cinematic Universe for becoming a "glorified WWE." But that doesn't mean he's displeased about Ryan Gosling preparing to take on a role that he previously played — Johnny Blaze, aka Ghost Rider — in Marvel Studios' upcoming movie "Ghost Rider."

Cage's "Ghost Rider" ended up flopping its way to a franchise back in 2007, with the actor returning for the 2012 sequel "Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance." Despite seeing sort of okay returns at the box office, neither film was a hit with critics, and after "Spirit of Vengeance," Johnny Blaze was relegated to cinematic history as Marvel Studios pushed ahead with the MCU. But at San Diego Comic-Con 2026, the studio announced that Gosling is set to star in a new Ghost Rider film, with "Deadpool & Wolverine" director Shawn Levy overseeing the project. Meanwhile, Cage has nothing but nice things to say about that.

The actor spoke to The Hollywood Reporter at the premiere of his new sports biopic "Madden" (the trailer for which left us wondering how David O. Russell is still making movies). "Ryan's going to do his thing with it, and I'm looking forward to seeing it," Cage told the outlet. "Ryan knows how I feel about him as an actor. We've had nice conversations, and we stay in touch. I was happy for him and wished him best of luck on his adventures, and I look forward to seeing the movie."

2007's "Ghost Rider" was written and directed by Mark Steven Johnson and saw Nicholas Cage in the title role, a motorcycle stuntman who sells his soul and transforms into a flaming emissary of Hell. Peter Fonda played the villain Mephistopheles, Ryan Gosling's wife Eva Mendes was Cage's love interest Roxanne Simpson, and Sam Elliot played mentor Carter Slade/The Caretaker. Sadly, despite a decent cast, the film received pretty terrible reviews. It did, however, make $228.7 million at the box office on a $110 million budget, which was evidently enough for Sony Pictures to make a sequel. But 2012's "Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance" was met with even more scathing reviews, and despite bringing in a reasonable $132.5 million in theaters on a $57 million budget, the film marked the end of Cage's run as the hero.

Now, Gosling is set to take on Ghost Rider for the character's MCU debut, and it remains to be seen what direction the movie will take. Cage previously told JoBlo that Johnson's film "should've been an R-rated movie," adding that David S. Goyer's original script was "still a movie that should be made." Obviously, Marvel Studios won't be using Goyer's screenplay, but fans have yet to get a truly dark Ghost Rider film, and Gosling's outing as the character could — and, if you ask Cage, should — be it.

For now, THR claims "Heated Rivalry" star Connor Storrie is in talks to play the film's villain. Rosamund Pike was also previously reported to be a top pick for the love interest in Gosling's "Ghost Rider," but for now, we'll have to wait for official news.

Marvel Studios' "Ghost Rider" hits theaters on July 28, 2028.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

#3561. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3560. Cinematographers’ Favorite Festival Is All About AI This Year — but Artists Still Hate the Tech

During the opening ceremony of the 34th ToruńCAMERIMAGE International Film Festival on Saturday, November 7, audience members saw a human replaced by a machine right in front of their eyes. The festival’s founder and artistic director Marek Żydowicz was invited to the stage, only for a robot to walk out in his place and begin addressing the audience and thanking sponsors.

Żydowicz took the stage a few moments later and joked that none of us are immune to the threat of AI and robots coming for our jobs. (The machine was Edward Warchocki, a humanoid robot “influencer” who has gone viral in Poland for videos in which it chases wild boars around Warsaw.) The stunt set a fitting tone for a festival that has devoted this edition to covering the film industry’s most controversial topic. Warchocki remained on stage for much of the opening ceremony, later joined by an actor in an “Inland Empire” rabbit costume who helped tee up an AI-generated video in which the rabbit symbolically opened the festival gates to the new technology. Anyone hoping for a boring, consensus-driven film festival immediately had their expectations adjusted. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It?

A festival devoted to the technological craft of filmmaking is a fitting place for these discussions. ToruńCAMERIMAGE (formerly known as Camerimage before changing its name to include its Polish host city) is an annual homecoming for cinematographers. Directors of photography are treated like rockstars at the festival, and the entire profession makes an effort to descend upon Toruń each November to discuss their craft and party late into the night. The main competition screenings are crucial to the Best Cinematography Oscar race, with so much of the voting branch in one room. Panels and Q&As often focus on the specific technical details that the overwhelmingly below-the-line audience wouldn’t hear at other festivals. The job of a cinematographer is uniquely positioned at the intersection of art and technology, and the festival was right to assume that its audience would have a lot of thoughts about the topic.

ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 is taking a pluralistic approach to the subject by giving AI advocates and opponents equal time, and the programming appears more interested in stirring the pot and sparking discussion than taking a firm position. The festival gave an honorary award to Darren Aronofsky, who has founded an AI studio that works with Google DeepMind, yet also programmed Luca Guadagnino’s biting Sam Altman satire “Artificial” as its opening night film. The opening ceremony was interspersed with video clips featuring the likes of Aronofsky, Steven Spielberg, Gal Gadot, and Ben Affleck sharing views on AI that ranged from optimistic to paranoid. The message was clear: All opinions are welcome, but we can’t put off talking about AI.

Broadly speaking, directors have been more open to the technology than cinematographers — before “Artificial” screened, Guadagnino stressed that his film was driven more by opposition to the consolidation of wealth and power in a few individuals than AI itself. He explained that he simply sees AI as a neutral tool, though he described its current filmmaking applications as a “cheap” trend that he expects to fade with time in the same way that 3D did. And while Aronofsky avoided the topic in his award acceptance speech, a video message from him played during the opening ceremony saw him repeating his mantra that film has always been a technology-driven medium and AI is simply the latest tech innovation that storytellers need to embrace.

But the cinematographers in attendance have not shied away from the bleak reality that the technology is creating. The term “we’re fucked” has been thrown around a lot, and audience questions have been fiery. The program is filled with panels about AI’s influence on cinematography, many of which focus on the rise of “greybox” filmmaking. The technique, notably employed on Doug Liman’s upcoming “Bitcoin” movie and rapidly popping up on other projects, involves filming actors on a neutral background before using AI to add all the production design and lighting during post.

Nobody is denying the practicality of the rapidly improving technology, which eliminates logistical problems relating to weather and locations that have plagued filmmakers for as long as the art form has existed. But it fundamentally alters the role of a cinematographer, whose job has always been to use light and composition techniques to create images in camera. Cinematographers speak about directors asking them for the softest, most generic lighting on set — not because it looks the best, but because it provides the blankest canvas for changing things in post. Even if you’re still booking gigs as a cinematographer, are you even doing the same job if you’re no longer lighting each image?

Cinematography has always been an art form that’s easy to recognize but hard to describe. Countless moviegoers have walked out of theaters praising a film’s cinematography while having no idea what a director of photography actually does on set and how that job overlaps with other positions. A cinematographer’s job is to make images beautiful (or ugly, when the script calls for it) with their knowledge of light and camera equipment. But directors can theoretically frame their own shots, gaffers can light them, and colorists play an increasingly large role in shaping the final look of each image. A recurring topic at the festival has been the fear that new technologies could freeze cinematographers out of the process altogether.

At a debate titled “State of the Image,” Polish cinematographer Bartosz Nalazek was initially presented as the most pro-AI voice on the panel. He explained how he recently wrapped a major TV show that used greybox techniques for 40 percent of its scenes. His message was that cinematographers have to embrace and adapt to the technology in order to keep working. After he finished his opening statement, fellow cinematographer Arthur Reinhart, a two-time recipient of the festival’s Golden Frog award, asked a simple question: “Are you enjoying the work?”

Nalazek did not hesitate to respond. “Totally not,” he said. “It’s horrible, I’m brain-dead.” He went on to explain that while hybrid production is technically easier for cinematographers, moving so much of the artistry to post-production means that “an elevated camera operator could do it.”

The topic represents a seismic change to a constant that cinematographers could always take for granted: their status as the most technologically savvy person on set. Even as filmmaking tools shifted from film stock to digital cameras, DPs stayed employed and respected because they knew how to use those tools better than anyone else. Now, for the first time in history, technology threatens to be the force that pushes them out of the decision-making process.

“I think what made cinematographers become who we are is the leverage over technology and the creative input. When we were shooting on film, that leverage was tremendous because nobody knew how to do it except the cinematographers,” Nalazek said. “What worries me is that we have this feeling that our position is undoubtable and unchangeable. We have this feeling that the director should respect us, the producer should respect us. I think running on that thought is pretty dangerous. We’re kind of in a time where we have to prove our worth. And that’s sad.”

One advantage of having these conversations at such a technically-oriented festival is that the cinematographers are also honest about what AI isn’t doing. Criticisms are often preempted with the caveat that AI is a broad, loaded term — anyone who edits in DaVinci or uses biometric functions on cameras has technically been using AI tools for years. Cinematographers who have worked on greybox sets make it clear that hybrid AI films are not made by one guy typing prompts in a room by himself. It can be true that AI has shrunk crew sizes enough for the community to feel strained while still acknowledging that these projects often employ hundreds of traditional film workers. And speakers have at times pushed back against audience questions that blame all AI adoption on strawman arguments about greedy producers and execs who could afford to pay artists but simply don’t want to. But nuance doesn’t make the problem any less existential.

Nobody knows where things are going next, but there’s a deep sense that every option and idea should be on the table right now. Some cinematographers are making peace with the notion that traditional filmmaking will become a specialized niche product, akin to artisanal pottery or handmade furniture, rather than the norm for everyday entertainment. We’ll be making a luxury product for a smaller audience willing to pay for it, and we’ll have to charge them accordingly, the thinking goes. Others have floated the idea that the on-set cinematography work of setting up shots will become a lower-level, commoditized job. Directors will still need masterful artists like Roger Deakins to advise them on lighting and image composition, but that high-level work could become more of a post-production role.

The only idea that nobody is taking seriously is that there’s anything cinematographers can do to put the AI genie back in the bottle.

“Camerimage is a place where all the cinematographers from around the world are coming,” Reinhart said. “If we had a voice, then it should be coming from here, and I hope it will. But I am not very optimistic it will change anything.”

#3559. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3557. 'Avatar' Officially Unveils a Very Different Version of Zuko in New Book

A bold hairstyle experiment almost changed the Zuko we know and love

2026 has been a fantastic year to be a fan of the Avatar franchise — the elemental fantasy saga, not the blue alien sci-fi movies. The animated sequel series Avatar: Seven Havens has been phenomenally successful, with a second season already confirmed, and Paramount Studios even has an Avatar fighting game that actually feels great to play. However, arguably the biggest win for Avatar fans this year was Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender. Set 12 years after Avatar: The Last Airbender ended, the movie reunited the gang for a new adventure. And even though it didn't get a theatrical release as originally promised, it was still a win for Team Avatar.

Now, Abrams Books is releasing a new art book with that reveals fresh details about Avatar: Aang: The Last Airbender.

Featuring insights from co-creators Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko, director Lauren Montgomery, and the extended animation team, this art book offers a behind-the-scenes look at what it took to bring the next chapter to life.

Thanks to Abrams Books, Polygon has an exclusive preview of the art book. Take a look at these two eye-opening pages below.

While every member of Team Avatar had a serious glow-up by the time of the movie, we felt one member got the biggest: Fire Lord Zuko, Aang’s former nemesis and later close friend and firebending mentor.

As she followed Aang and his friends into their 20s, character designer Christie Tseng wanted to explore how varied the returning main cast could be.

“Considering how often his hairstyle changed in the show, [Zuko] certainly earned the biggest hair silhouette update out of the main cast!” Tseng shares in the art book. “We explored many different hairstyles for him, including shoulder-length to long, flowing manes, worn in styles ranging from low buns to high ponytails.”

Throughout the animated series, Zuko’s hairstyle often reflected his role in the story. In season 1, he wore a top knot, in keeping with typical Fire Nation style. In season 2, Zuko and his uncle Iroh cut their hair to symbolize leaving behind their status and going on the run, leaving Zuko looking rather scruffy. Zuko returns to the top knot in season 3 and wears it for the last time in the series finale, after becoming Fire Lord.

In Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender, Zuko’s still got that traditional top knot. However, animator Ki Hyun Ryu says the team considered many different versions of Zuko’s look, including one that would have fit right in at a concert hall as he sang in front of millions of fans.

“Early versions of Zuko leaned a bit too much toward a ‘pretty boy’ look, but I strongly felt he needed to appear the most mature among Team Avatar, as he is the ruler of the Fire Nation,” Ryu explains in the art book. “I focused on adding stronger angles to his face and shifting away from a K-pop-idol vibe toward a more grounded, masculine presence that reflects a true imperial leader.”

It’s true that Zuko is gorgeous, and a more K-pop-inspired look may have been appealing — just look at the popularity of KPop Demon Hunters. But one of the highlights of Avatar: The Last Airbender was seeing how wonderfully mature the characters had become over the years. It’s notable to see that maturity reflected in the team’s desire to tell a serious, meaningful story, right down to the small character details.

Fans can now see even more of how Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender came together, with Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender: Art of the Movie now available for purchase.

#3556. Russell Crowe’s Fan-Favorite 116-Minute Mystery Moves to a New Streaming Platform

Known for his big-budget epics and hard-hitting crime movies, Russell Crowe is a powerhouse in the entertainment industry. It is his work in comedy, however, that makes him a true gem. Now streaming on Apple TV, viewers can relive the tragically underrated mystery from Shane Black, The Nice Guys. Also starring Ryan Gosling, the film was criminally under-watched at the theater, a phenomenon that Gosling blames on the success of Angry Birds at the box office.

True or not, the fact remains that The Nice Guys has gone on to be a cult classic due to the undeniable chemistry between the movie’s leads. Crowe plays against type as Jack Healy, one half of the humorous P.I. set looking to solve a mystery of widespread corruption. While on the hunt for a missing girl, he runs into a concurrent case investigated by the hilariously inept Holland March (Gosling). The two make up a team impossible not to root for in the jungle of 1970s Los Angeles.

It can be easy to get sucked into the comic stylings of Ryan Gosling, who, in the latter half of his career, has come out as one of the great comedy actors. After grim roles like in Drive and The Place Beyond the Pines, he threw audiences for a loop in the 2016 movie about bumbling private detectives who get drawn into a life-or-death case. Gosling steals the show as March, a PI who is as good a detective as he is a father.

During a case, he runs into Jack Healy, more of an enforcer type, who warns him to stop looking for Healy’s client, Amelia (Margaret Qualley). It turns out that both their cases are connected, and they are forced to work together, resulting in one of the most hilarious duos put on screen. Russell Crowe is the straight man to Gosling’s ridiculous portrayal, but The Nice Guys is nothing without their team-up. Together they make up a somewhat decent detective duo who learn how important Amelia actually is.

March and Healy uncover a government conspiracy way above their pay grade, but it opens the door to more implied adventures as they create their own detective agency. Tragically, this would never be seen again. A decade after the release of The Nice Guys in theaters, Shane Black confirms that a sequel is unlikely. This is largely due to the dismal box office returns when it was initially released.

2026 is a different era, however, and the time has never been better for a resurgence of The Nice Guys. Not only is Gosling more popular than ever thanks to Barbie, Project Hail Mary, and his upcoming Ghost Rider endeavor, but Angourie Rice is also a hot ticket commodity. 10 years ago, she played March’s precocious teenage daughter, Holly, and she has only gotten bigger since then. The Nice Guys continues to be a favorite touchstone of many and deserves a second chance.

#3555. ‘Half Nelson’ at 20: How a $700,000 Indie Addiction Drama Earned Ryan Gosling His First Oscar Nod

“He said it felt like we were the kind of people who talked about the script like we were plotting to build a bomb,” laughed Ryan Fleck, remembering how he and his longtime filmmaker partner, Anna Boden, convinced Ryan Gosling to star in their feature debut, “Half Nelson.” “It was probably a little bit true though,” adds Boden. “We hadn’t done much except try to make this movie for a long time, and maybe that came off the page. Maybe he was like, ‘Let’s just throw them a bone!’”

It was the right choice. “Half Nelson” arrived in 2006, an era when introspective indies still had time to flourish theatrically and find their crowd — and that’s exactly what happened. Filmed for just $700,000, Fleck and Boden’s first film turned a limited theatrical run into a $4.9 million global box office haul, while earning their leading man his first Best Actor Oscar nod. Looking back, it’s undoubtedly a success story — but far from a predictable one. Related Stories King Ghidorah Is Ready for Its Close-Up: How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Cracked the Legendary Monster’s Next Evolution Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore Nailed ‘The Debut’ by Singing, Styling Her Hair Like Liza Minnelli, and Avoiding Playing ‘Some Suffering Mom’

“The thing about not yet being a professional filmmaker is you’ve got time until someone greenlights your movie, so there was lots of time,” said Fleck, recalling the movie’s long road to production. The pair met on a summer filmmaking course at NYU in the early aughts and quickly realized they wanted to work together. “We were always big movie fans, and the ones that moved me the most were films like ‘Midnight Cowboy’ and ‘Harold and Maude.’ They all had flawed people at their core. We started there and began digging into things we knew a little about.”

Together, they spliced their own flawed character with themes of isolation and addiction, and before long they had someone they felt they could form a feature around. Their idea centered on Dan Dunne (Gosling), a twenty-something middle-school teacher and struggling creative balancing full-time work with a freebasing addiction, and Drey (Shareeka Epps), the young student who stumbles on his secret. That was their starting point, but over time, it evolved.

“When we first started writing in 2002 or 2003, it felt like a lot of young people had all this energy but didn’t know how to affect change in the world around them,” said Boden, explaining how external conflicts like America’s involvement with the Afghanistan war impacted the story they wanted to tell. “We were finding this character that was going through that too, in his own way.”

Fleck unpacked this disconnect further: “[Dan] understands how history, politics and change work outside of himself but he can’t quite get it under control within himself.”

Despite having a finished screenplay, securing a green light proved elusive. However, instead of feeling dejected, the pair got to work. “We had this script but literally didn’t have anybody to give it to, so we made a short because that was something we did know how to do. We focused on the young student character, changing her from male to female and casting somebody from a local middle school,” said Boden, of Epps’ entry into the project. In fact, all the actors in their short “Gowanus, Brooklyn” were nonprofessionals. “It was a great way of working through the ideas, emotions and feelings we were trying to get across. Going back to the script after that deepened it a lot.”

Being proactive paid off. After a successful Sundance screening, “Gowanus, Brooklyn” bagged 2004’s Grand Jury Prize, paving the way for the feature they’d initially dreamed of — or so they thought. “I remember coming off stage and whispering to Anna, ‘I think this means we’re going to get to make our feature,’” said Fleck, laughing at his naivety. “It didn’t make it easy, but it certainly made it a more clear path.”

The win secured the duo an agent and key industry connections, through which their feature script reached their would-be leading man. Looking back, it’s easy to see someone as multi-faceted as Gosling deliver on the many faces this role required. Dan’s someone who’s simultaneously dejected, drug-addled and lost — but also inspirational, trusted and boasting a strong moral compass. Easy for someone with Gosling’s skillset, right? Fleck and Boden weren’t convinced right away.

“It had been written for someone a little bit older than him,” revealed Boden, describing the struggle of seeing the world-weary Dan in 24-year-old Gosling. “I remember when he met us, he’d grown his chin hairs out and looked a little older.” Fleck has similar memories: “It wasn’t immediate. We thought of somebody who had more life experience. He didn’t have the body of work he has now, but he just had this old-soul quality to him. He didn’t seem 24.”

Gosling threw himself into the role. “We introduced him to a public school teacher who was about his age so he could shadow him,” explained Boden. “Ryan picked up all these subtle little things from him, like wearing rubber bands around his wrists. The guy ended up looking so much like him that we cast him as Dan’s brother.” His ability to keep things loose lent itself to the pair’s fly-on-the-wall style, too. “Some of those classroom scenes have a very spontaneous feel,” she added, confirming that the students often didn’t know what Gosling was going to ask. “Some of their lines were scripted, some weren’t. They were reacting in real-time.”

Then there was the heavy stuff, like Drey unceremoniously discovering Dan’s freebasing habit in the school bathroom. As an inner-city teen, she’s caught in her own internal battle between a life of honest education and the quick wins of neighborhood crime, tempted by toxic family friend Frank (Anthony Mackie). It’s a challenging role for any actor, let alone someone making their feature debut.

“The other big thing [Ryan] brought was stripping away the dialogue. The scene where Drey is taking care of him after his overdose felt so much more visceral without any lines. You could hear a pin drop,” said Boden.

“I think Shareeka was genuinely frightened,” recalled Fleck. “There’s such an intensity… I think she was genuinely concerned for him — and I was concerned for her watching it. I was just blown away, like ‘Wow. These people are really good.’”

Meanwhile, low-level dealer Frank offers Drey his own guidance in a morally blurry role that’s part friend, part corruptor. “[Anthony] immediately got what we were going for,” said Boden. “Frank isn’t a cartel guy or a big kingpin. He’s your working-class drug dealer making just enough to live on. It’s something that should feel relatable, even though he’s doing something illegal. Anthony and Shareeka immediately clicked. You can feel it on screen.”

To score their first film, the duo drew inspiration from one of their favorites, Hal Ashby’s “Harold and Maude,” a film that dedicates its entire soundtrack to one artist: Cat Stevens. For “Half Nelson,” Fleck and Boden chose Canadian indie-rock collective Broken Social Scene, blending their stark imagery with a dreamy sound that delivered a deftly emotional punch.

“A friend of Anna’s introduced us to their music, and we became obsessed,” said Fleck, explaining the choice. “When you put their music against some of the images we were playing with, it gave us goosebumps.”

There was just one issue: They needed the band’s permission. Luckily, they had a connection to Broken Social Scene lead singer Kevin Drew — but the Canadian musician was a bit suspicious. “He made us watch the film with him in his living room,” laughed Fleck. “Thankfully, he really liked it and said, ‘OK, you can have all of our music.’”

Turns out, it was kismet. “When we played the song ‘Lover’s Spit’ for Ryan, he was like, ‘Oh my God, who’s this band?’” said Boden. “He’d been listening to a burned Broken Social Scene CD in his car for the past two months and didn’t know what it was because it wasn’t labeled. It was meant to be!”

Twenty years on, “Half Nelson” feels like a product of a bygone time, one that benefitted from having the space it needed to find its audience. As the movie prepares for a 2027 dual disc re-release and a return to theatres, its remarkable journey hasn’t gone unappreciated by its creators.

“It wasn’t a huge blockbuster. It played really well in independent cinemas and the people who wanted to see it saw it. I’m not sure it works like that anymore,” said Boden. “So I’m really grateful for the experience we had with ‘Half Nelson.’”

Fleck echoed the sentiment: “It was our first and the one that allowed us to continue doing this. I love everything about the process of making that movie and think back on everything really fondly.”
