#3553. How John Malkovich Nailed the Role of His Career with ‘Wild Horse Nine’

Editor’s Note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Telluride Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures opened “Wild Horse Nine” in select theaters on November 6.

While early “Wild Horse Nine” press screenings in Los Angeles and New York got the ball rolling, the first whiff of a strong public reaction was the Venice Film Festival, where edgy auteur Martin McDonagh, John Malkovich, and Sam Rockwell soaked up sustained applause. Then they were whisked to the Colorado Rockies to screen the movie in Telluride.

Instantly, Malkovich jumped up the Best Actor rankings for what would be his third Oscar nomination. His first two were for Supporting Actor, in 1985 for “Places in the Heart,” and 1993 for “In the Line of Fire.” Now the movie is screening at the Toronto International Film Festival ahead of its November 6 release. Related Stories King Ghidorah Is Ready for Its Close-Up: How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Cracked the Legendary Monster’s Next Evolution Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore Nailed ‘The Debut’ by Singing, Styling Her Hair Like Liza Minnelli, and Avoiding Playing ‘Some Suffering Mom’

I caught up with Malkovich in the back of a large black SUV parked in front of the Herzog Theatre before his first of two Telluride Tributes.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

Anne Thompson: How did you first get to know Martin McDonagh?

John Malkovich: I was offered a couple things of Martin’s over the years. One, “Seven Psychopaths,” one, [the play] “A Behanding in Spokane,” but I couldn’t do it. I was busy. I love the scripts, but I couldn’t do it, and so then this came. I thought the thing was great. Beautiful piece of writing, just a perfect screenplay, and I couldn’t believe I got sent it. I couldn’t believe he asked me to do it.

Yeah. So I said, “Yeah!” with no hesitation at all. I have two little granddaughters. I don’t love being away for two, three months, whatever. But it’s part of the job, so you got to do it. We met in London because I’d never met Martin. We rehearsed five to six days in London with Sam, who I love. I’d worked with him before on “The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy,” not a long gig, but I knew Sam a bit socially. And I’d worked with Buscemi before twice because he was in our film “Ghost World,” and we worked together in “Con Air.” Sam and I hit it off, workwise, very well, very quickly.

You may not agree, but I think Sam receded slightly and supported you in an amazing way. I find it moving, actually, that he did this for you. Do you feel that’s what he did?

Yes and no. I think he played his part. And the part [of Lee] is slightly recessive in that sense. Chris is the older one. He’s the wild card. He’s killed whatever, 168 people, but apparently none while they were eating. And he’s a legend in the CIA. Sam is an exceptionally generous actor, as generous as you could ever find, you couldn’t ask for a better partner in every way.

You’ve been doing this a long time. Your first Oscar nomination was in 1985. That’s over 40 years ago. Both your nominations have been for Supporting Actor. Are you a character actor?

I’ve had leading roles. But people don’t understand what a role is, the general public or anybody except actors. First of all, you can be a terrific actor in anything, but if the film isn’t good, it’s utterly meaningless. You may as well not have bothered. You may as well not have done it. It’s a waste of time. For a good role to be really good, people have to not just like the way you do that, but like what the character is doing, and understand it if they don’t like it, and they have to like the arc of the character. The best performances I gave would have been on stage first of all, but secondly, those in the cinema wouldn’t necessarily be in good movies, ugh. And that, on a certain level, has precious little to do with performance X, Y, Z. That’s just one small part of a movie.

In this case, you’re given an extraordinary amount of verbiage. So you had to make the rhythm of it, the sense of it, the emotion of it. Sometimes it’s hilariously funny, sometimes sad, and you run that gamut.

Yeah, but that’s great writing. This material, I believe, causes a big wave, and you ride that wave where it’s going, through comedy, through drama, through tragedy, even if that’s the nature of a particular text, and that’s what actors do. The collision between the public and the material is caused by a recognition in their lives.

Our CIA agent Chris is messing around with Chile in 1973 as Pinochet waits in the wings.

November 22, 1963 is a trauma, as is September 11, 2001, and 1973 in Chile. For those of us who were alive at that time, it’s immutable. Doesn’t matter your politics then or now, or if you had any. Doesn’t matter anything. I directed Don DeLillo’s great novel “Libra,” adapted it for the stage with Don, and Don referred to it in the book as the seven seconds that broke the back of the American century in Chile and it was not the only place on earth: Chile, Argentina, Brazil, Peru, Ecuador.

And various actors have been bad along with us, and possibly not worse, but the birthday party was spoiled. What’s left, and it caused generations of pain, of nihilism, of loss of innocence, of loss of faith in a political system. People everywhere can understand that, and Martin mines that beautifully. It’s beautifully structured in the writing and modulated in the filmmaking. So the wave is there.

Your character is fun to watch because he’s unfettered, he’s unleashed, he doesn’t give a fuck anymore. He’s just going to say what he wants to say, and he’s going to tell the truth.

And people appreciate that because in this culture, it’s very odd. You say this word or that word, and the anti-social media mob goes berserk. I don’t have social media. I don’t want it designated to me in the slightest. I don’t care what they say. They can say whatever they want, and so can people who offend you. They can say whatever they want, and voila, who cares? And this idea that you can’t say that because it’s offensive to this or that, and covers everything and every topic and every subject and every blah blah blah seems incredibly dumb. It’s a dumb world.

Well, that’s one of the great things about being a certain age, right? You don’t care anymore. He doesn’t, and maybe you don’t.

I stay off [social media] because I don’t see the value. I’m doing things. If people like them, beautiful. If they hate them, beautiful. I do a [stage and short film] piece called “The Music Critic,” which is all the worst reviews of all the most beautiful pieces of classical music in the world. They were all trashed. They were all hated. So what? Get used to it. Grow a thick skin, go on with your life, do what you think is good.

#3552. These Sony ANC Headphones Are on Sale for $128 Right Now

It's hard to convince yourself to spend nearly half a grand on premium headphones, like the Sony WH-1000XM6, even if you consider yourself an audiophile. Not everyone can afford those prices, which is why the budget, mid-tier, and premium tiers exist. While the premium 1000XM6 headphones are over three times the price of the mid-tier Sony WH-CH730N, they're not three times as good. The Sony WH-CH730N are $128 (originally $179) right now, the lowest price they've ever been according to price-tracking tools, and they offer an amazing value for your money.

It's pretty impressive what $128 in headphones gets you in 2026. The CH730N uses the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0. The Adaptive Sound Control feature can detect your activity (walking, sitting down, loud environment, etc.) and automatically switch the level of ANC and transparency to make your experience as comfortable and seamless as possible.

The microphones are decent and use a feature to isolate your voice in noisy environments. I love that there's an AUX connection to give you the option, which seems to be coming back with newer headphones. The design is light and will feel like plastic, but they are comfortable to wear for long sessions. If you're looking to maximize the quality of headphones you can get for your money, the Sony WH-CH730N offer a pretty compelling option at $128.

#3551. How Wyatt Fits Into Sam's NCIS: New York Team Explained By Shane Harper

LL Cool J’s Sam Hanna has returned to the Big Apple for NCIS: New York, and Shane Harper’s Wyatt Sellers is one of his new Naval Criminal Investigative Service colleagues.

Last month, NCIS: New York premiered on CBS, serving as the long-running procedural franchise’s eighth installment. New York arrives nearly 20 years after LL Cool J first started playing Sam in NCIS: Los Angeles, which ended in 2023 after 14 seasons. The actor then reprised Sam in a recurring capacity on NCIS: Hawai’i, as well as made a handful of guest appearances on the main NCIS.

While Sam initially only came back to New York to investigate the murder of a close friend, he decided to stay and lead a new NCIS team alongside his “roguish partner” Scott Caan’s Nick Schaeffer. This quartet of field agents includes Harper’s Wyatt, who’s usually working alongside Jacqueline Byers’ Addy Ross. Early into season 1, Wyatt has already proven himself to be an integral member of this team that also includes Assistant Special Agent-in-Charge of NCIS’s New York office, Robyn Wells (Jennifer Beals), and Technical Operator Sean Sullivan (Devin Druid).

In an interview with ScreenRant’s Adam Holmes, Harper opened up about Wyatt’s role in NCIS: New York beyond apprehending bad guys. One of the few personal details that’s been revealed about the character so far is that his fiancée broke up with him shortly before the series began, and he’s had no luck selling the engagement ring. Harper shared that New York will explore Wyatt’s former engagement in depth later in the season, though unfortunately for him, that ring isn’t going anywhere:

Coming into these embodying these new characters, we're always looking for little pieces to latch onto because we don't know that much about them. So, as an actor, I'm experiencing what the audience is experiencing as well, where it's like, ‘What's going on? I want to know more about this.’ I'm excited to say that… no spoilers, but we are exploring that, and we have been exploring that more in an intimate way to get more of an understanding of him and this ex-fiancée and all of that. So not giving too much away, but we touch on that and a lot more.

I think that's the fun thing about a show like this: we have 20 episodes to slowly unveil more of the personal stuff, which I think the audiences want. They like the procedural, the ‘what's the new case,’ but then slowly peeling back the layers of the characters is certainly really fun for us as actors, and also I think fun for the audience.

It's funny, and I don't think this will spoil anything too much, but the ring is still around. He hasn't sold it yet. I don't know if he's going to sell it or if he's going to maybe find someone new to give it to, but there hasn't been an episode yet where the ring gets sold. So I have to talk to Byron about that, but it's a really funny bit. At least I thought it was really funny.

As far as Wyatt’s partnership with Addy goes, the latter pokes fun at the former quite often, particularly for his failed attempts to sell the ring, as well as how he likes drinking milk. However, it all comes from a good place, and Addy and Wyatt make an effective investigatory duo. Harper said the following regarding what he likes about their dynamic:

I think there's a real yin yang with them. I think Addy has that New York edge and swagger, and Wyatt, it's the opposite of that. But I like the way that they complement each other. It’s interesting to see them play off of each other and continue to learn about each other. I have to take quite a bit of ribbing from Addy, which is okay. I think as the as the story progresses with them, they'll start to pick up things about each other as the friendship builds, and I don't know if there's going to be more than friendship there. You certainly could see something like that happening.

I don't know if it will, but I really like their relationship and the way that they work together on the cases. They ping pong back and forth, and they feel like a kind of classic duo when they're out on the field. I love when we have to do field days together because we'll be out in the city solving the cases being just the two of us, and I have a good time when we're filming that stuff together.

At the end of the episode “Carousel,” Wyatt and Addy’s relationship entered new territory when she agreed to answer 10 of his personal questions about her. However, at the beginning of the following episode, “Homecoming,” it sounded as though the number had been increased back to 20. Harper described the discrepancy thusly:

That's really funny. So yeah, at the beginning of four, this is really great, but Jackie and I did a bit of ad-libbing at the top of four where we're arguing about how many questions we actually did settle on. I don’t know if we had intentionally done that or if we had read the script and been like, ‘We should add this in,’ but that is in there. If you go back … because the director was like, ‘Do some preamble, and so we were like, ‘Well no, I told you it's 10.’ There was a little bit of that: how many questions do we actually get?

So to be honest, I think maybe they're still unclear, although I'm convinced that it is 10. But they have been going back and forth on it quite a bit. I think the fact that the characters are also in their universe, they're also confused about any questions that they're owed, if that does anything for anyone.

ScreenRant: How’s your experience been working with LL Cool J, the guy on the cast who goes back nearly 20 years with the NCIS franchise?

It's a neat experience … The way that he approaches his work after what he did 14 seasons on NCIS: Los Angeles, so much success both in music and in acting, and for someone that's been as famous for as long as he's been, and to act the way that he does is really remarkable. He's so wonderful to work with, and is such a great leader, and really shines a light on everyone, gives everyone their flowers, and is really encouraging.

When he walks on a set, it's like he's walking onto a new show. He has so much enthusiasm. I don't know how he does that, but it's really great to work with him, and I'm learning a lot from his approach to the creative process and the long hours and the commitment to the job. He's all about the audience. He’s all about [how] we’re making something for people to put on at home and relax and have fun and enjoy being entertained by by a show that hopefully gets the job done. He’s all about the audience and working really hard, which I think we're all falling in line with that because we really appreciate it.

You never know [with] these big stars. You never know how they're going to be. Sometimes they can be difficult, and he's the opposite. So I think we're all just enjoying that process.

ScreenRant: You mentioned in a previous interview that there was about 20 minutes cut from the NCIS: New York pilot, including a scene where you ended up drinking 4–5 glasses of milk. What was some of the other material that was cut?

So just for the fans, the milk scene, there was a really great moment with Addy and Wyatt talking about them being great partners, and there was a moment where they were like, ‘We’re great partners.’ Obviously they're very different, but they have this moment where they’re like, ‘We’re a good team,’ and then Wyatt is still focused on the ring, and he's pretty sad.

It's a moment of sadness, which, again, we don't know what's going to make these final cuts. It's interesting because he is going through this heartbreak. That was a closing scene in the pilot, and he's quite sad, and you get to feel that for him, which I really liked. So that was that piece, and that’s the scene where I was drinking the milk, if you can believe it. It was a very sentimental piece, but at the top of the scene, I'm chugging milk. It’s very funny.

But there was another scene that we did at a halal cart that was really fun, a little bit more conversational stuff with Addy and Wyatt. But there was a lot. Just those two scenes for us are off the top of my head, and then for the rest of the characters, there's a bunch of other stuff. There was a lot of material to work with, but I definitely liked the halal cart scene as well. I didn't eat the halal though, because I was worried that … I don't like talking with my mouth full in the scene, so I was acting like I was about to eat it. But then it worked for my character. I was like, he's such an out-of-towner. He's probably never had halal before, so he didn't even know how to eat it.

It was funny. Yesterday, we were filming another scene. I'm filming a scene, and I asked for oat milk instead of whole milk because I just wanted it to be easier on the tummy.

ScreenRant: What characters from other NCIS shows would you like Wyatt to meet?

I'm not sure. I guess that could be fun for him to maybe meet … I know they were talking about [Sam’s] old partner from Los Angeles coming back, [that] could be fun. Anyone that ties into Sam Hanna's world that can give Wyatt more understanding of Sam would be cool. So anyone that [Sam’s] had any kind of meaningful interactions with either on the field or off, I think could be interesting.

I think the fans too are obviously looking forward to potential crossovers, and I think we're in big support of of that because we're all newbies. Anyone that would get the fans excited, that are fan favorites that could maybe pop over for a few episodes, I think would be good. It just always gets everyone jazzed.

ScreenRant: I’d like to get your thoughts about NCIS: New York’s most important star: Duncan, a.k.a. Sid [the dog].

It's funny because our cinematographer is Sid, and I think that's why they named Duncan Sid. So that's a fun tidbit, he’s named after our DP, which is fun. But Duncan is really great. I grew up with two pit bulls myself, and I have a real soft spot for Duncan. I don't interact with him enough, even though Wyatt's definitely an animal person. So I would like to get some more cuddles … Addy’s always playing with the dog at the top of a scene or something, but it’s never me. So I feel like they need to change that because I'm a dog guy. I love dogs, and particularly pit bulls.

But it's funny, because I think there was a post yesterday that went up with Jennifer and Duncan walking around. I don't know if you saw that, it was a BTS video, and it got so many views. Dog videos just get so many views. Everyone loves them. [Duncan's] the star. I just told Jennifer Beals yesterday, the fans are going crazy for her and Duncan. But yeah, Duncan's great, and Sid is a very important character that hopefully will be featured many, many, many more times in the future.

He's so good. He's so well-behaved and so sweet, and he'll just come up to you on a break and just give you a little snuggle, and then go back to his mark. It's wild. He's a very good performer. The other funny thing that we do is there's a big stuffed animal that we'll use when he's not ready to come to set yet. I don't know where he is. I don't know if he's in the hair and makeup chair or something, but Jackie will be rehearsing with this giant stuffed animal, and I get a kick out of that. I think it's really funny.

ScreenRant: What was it that drew you to working on NCIS: New York when you first read the pilot script?

Well, I thought the pilot was incredibly fun and action-packed. [It had] all of the pieces of a great pilot. It was paced really well. The characters were extremely well-defined, and it was just a really perfect pilot. And then when I heard that Byron Belasco was doing it, and he was going to be the showrunner and executive producer. I was really excited about that because I'm a big fan of his, and I really loved Kingdom and the other things that he's worked on.

So that drew me to it. And I'd never done a network show like this in the capacity that I'm doing, and I, to be honest, have always wanted to be a part of a big network show like this. So when I initially read for this, it's one actor in a million. There are difficult roles to get, so I wasn't expecting it to even go my way, but I obviously had my fingers crossed, and here we are.

ScreenRant: How has working on NCIS: New York compared to your time on Power Book IV?

It's different. It's funny, I’ve joked around when people stop me, and they know me from Power, and then they will talk to me about NCIS. The bit that we have is, I'm going from playing a gangster to playing a badge, or a shield as we say, in New York. It's interesting to be on the other side of the law there, and I'm honestly still adjusting to playing like a very wholesome character. I'm still figuring it out.

We're halfway through right now. I'm starting episode 11 tonight. I'm gonna leave for set in a few hours, but it's still an adjustment because that role in Power was, like everything in Power is, so hard edged. I loved the crew and the cast and the producers on Power. I love everyone on this show, and we do also get a lot of that good New York grit in NCIS as well that I know [LL Cool J] certainly is interested in finding all the things that we love about the NCIS world, and also servicing more of a New York edge and flair to it, which has been really fun as well. Two very different projects, but I'm enjoying them equally.

ScreenRant: What’s been your favorite location to film in for NCIS: New York so far?

Well, it's hard to beat Central Park, which was in the pilot. Central Park was pretty extraordinary to be in with a big film crew. That was pretty awesome. Again, the Diamond District was really cool as well. Also, in the pilot, we filmed right here in Williamsburg, near the docks, where [there’s] the beautiful view of the city. I think it’s in Episode 2, there’s a car crash scene down there that we filmed. It's an empty lot, and you get the whole skyline looking over the river. That location's been really fun. We’ve been there a couple times because it's so nice and it looks good. I like it down there a lot.

I'm trying to think if there are any other interesting locations. We're all over the city. We're all over Brooklyn. I think it's a big part of the fun. It’s just getting to be out there amongst it. And the New Yorkers have been nice so far, so hopefully we don't overstay our welcome when we're parking our big trailers out in a city that already doesn't have parking. There's a lot of stuff filming in the city I think is really good for the entertainment community and everything. So yeah, we're happy to be here.

NCIS: New York airs Tuesdays at 9 p.m. ET on CBS's fall 2026 schedule.

#3550. We Need More Games Like Murals

A simple game, straight from the heart of a studio that's been around the block

You don't hear much about game developers like the U.K.'s Dlala Studios: neither a AAA megalith nor a fashionable indie, but a smallish outfit that's been chipping away at the coalface for years, making characterfully animated versions of other people's properties. I suspect there are more of these studios out there than any of us realize, propping up bigger projects with their work-for-hire services in between trying to get their own games off the ground.

You might know Dlala from its 2020 take on Rare's vintage beat-em-up Battletoads, or from its 2023 Mickey Mouse platformer, Disney Illusion Island. Now it's time for the studio's "one for me," in the form of Murals, a combat-heavy isometric action-adventure that looks like Hades but is chasing something much simpler and more nostalgic: a linear cartoon romp full of wit and quirky charm.

I found Dlala in an appealingly scruffy workspace on a small industrial estate in the unremarkable commuter town of Witham in Essex, a 40-minute train ride from London. Founder and local boy Aj Grand-Scrutton (huge, chatty, barrel-chested, with the hair and beard of Gandalf) proudly gave a tour in his slides, apologizing for the absence of his dog and the number of monitors plugged into his PC (seven). He finished with the cinema projection room management had built in secret while the staff was working remotely during COVID.

For a studio like this, it's all about keeping the lights on, but Grand-Scrutton is careful not to disown Battletoads and Illusion Island, which he says the studio was given a lot of freedom on, as mere work-for-hire. He considers both "true Dlala games." Nevertheless, Murals is different. For one thing, Dlala will self-publish it. For another, it is entirely Dlala's own creation, unless you count the classic fairy tales it is extremely loosely based on.

In Dlala's offices, I played the first two chapters, or "murals," of the game, based on Sleeping Beauty and Rapunzel. The player controls The Hero, a sturdy, silent protagonist in baggy overalls who can inline-skate around for a lick of extra speed. The Hero has been transported into this twisted fairy-tale mural by The Creator, a self-aware meta-villain; in the process, The Hero's sidekick Loaf, a chirpy and loquacious slice of bread, has been accidentally brought to life from a sketch in The Hero's pocket.

Grand-Scrutton has a passion for 2D animation (he idolizes 16-bit titles like Cool Spot and Aladdin), and loves to write silly, surreal, pun-riddled scripts. The Hero picks up a sword called Slash Gordon and a medallion called Dragon Thee Dallion. Sleeping Beauty has turned from a soporific damsel into a haughty insomniac called Bri who needs to listen to heavy metal at full volume to sleep. Rapunzel is Harriet, tortured by her own hair, and attended by a surfer-dude prince called Kit who is blinded by "the foreboding weight of my previous self." Grand-Scrutton is extremely proud to have obtained the services of dadaist British comedy legend Bob Mortimer to voice Magic Dave, a vendor of boons. (If you want to laugh until you can't breathe anymore, search for clips of Mortimer's appearances on the panel show Would I Lie to You?)

In other words, we're in Whimsy Town. This will either appeal to you or it won't, but there's no doubt that Dlala is pouring all its personality into the game, as well as its distinctive art and animation style. Grand-Scrutton admits the studio is less sure of itself when it comes to combat, but says the team enjoyed the experience of making Battletoads and wanted to challenge themselves to make a combat-first game. You can tell: to begin with, fighting in Murals feels quite basic, but it quickly builds in confidence without betraying its simplicity. It's frantic and fun.

The twisted fairy-tale skits that make up Murals have been invaded by The Distorted, a breed of paint-themed creatures. (As well as Dlala's own Mickey game, Murals seems influenced by Warren Spector's Epic Mickey.) The Hero has ranged attacks, melee combos, and area-of-effect blasts which are modified by equipment and Eeries, the roguelike-style modifiers sold by Magic Dave. There's room to sculpt your own build here, and Dlala isn't too concerned if it breaks the balance.

But by far the most important button is the dodge button. The Hero's health pool is small, and Murals is much more about dodging attacks than stringing together fancy combos or executing perfect parry timing. It's rhythmic and spatial, predicated on the attack patterns of each enemy type. Murals keeps layering these on: cannon things that launch splats at your location, blobs that breed mini blobs, large cattle things that charge. Just to reinforce the value of dodging, there's a bonus for kill streaks without taking any damage.

I hope Murals works out for Dlala. The game’s combination of simple structure and strong personality aren’t as common as you might think. And while there might be more Dlalas out there than we realize, it’s probably also true that there are fewer of them every day.

#3549. 12 Perfect Christmas Movies Nobody Talks About

Halloween is over, so according to the gods of commerce, it's officially Christmas season. That means many of us will soon begin our seasonal movie watching, returning to a wide variety of X-mas classics that span from It's a Wonderful Life to Die Hard. There are a lot of Christmas movies that are perfect for this time of year, offering moods that make us feel everything from warm and fuzzy to dark and depressed. Beyond all those classics, though, there are a number of equally perfect Christmas movies that haven't dominated the conversation enough.

These lesser-discussed Christmas movies cover the Yuletide spectrum from naughty to nice, full of sugary delights and some harsh spices as well. There are new animated masterpieces, classic Westerns, and neo-noir thrillers. There's something under the tree for any kind of Christmas movie fan, whether you're an optimistic Buddy the Elf or a cynical Grinch. We're making a list, checking it twice, and we're gonna find out what perfect Christmas movies no one is talking about.

The Western genre doesn't exactly lend itself to heartwarming tales of Christmas. The dusty locations don't inspire Yuletide cheer, and even those that are set in snowy locations are more frigid and cold-blooded than festive and warmhearted. That didn't stop John Ford and John Wayne from using the Christmas season for their biblically inspired Western 3 Godfathers. Based on the short story The Three Godfathers by Peter B. Kyne, which had been adapted to film several times before, the movie offers a retelling of the fable of the Three Wise Men that swaps the New Testament for the Old West.

Bob (Wayne), Pete (Pedro Armendariz), and the Abilene Kid (Harry Carey Jr.) are three outlaws who rob a bank and go on the run into the desert. Their escape plans are complicated when they come across a dying woman who gives birth to a child and makes them promise to take care of the baby. A more sentimental Western than fans might expect from the collaboration of Ford and Wayne, 3 Godfathers offers some perfect Holiday counterprogramming for genre fans.

If you need more trios of criminals at Christmastime, then We're No Angels is the perfect stocking stuffer. Based on a Broadway play adapted from a French original, the film was the final collaboration between director Michael Curtiz and Humphrey Bogart, but it hasn't enjoyed the same legacy as their biggest movie together. Co-starring Peter Ustinov and Aldo Ray, it's a darkly comical Christmas movie that taps into the seasonal themes of redemption and goodwill.

Joseph (Bogart), Albert (Ray), and Jules (Ustinov) are three convicts who have escaped from Devil's Island at Christmastime, ending up in a colonial town in French Guiana where they ingratiate themselves with the locals to aid their getaway plans. Over time, the trio comes to care for the residents, who soften their hardened criminal hearts. We're No Angels is the perfect mix of breezy comedy and crime movie elements, with the three leads giving criminally overlooked performances.

Criminals make for seemingly perfect Christmas movie protagonists, as evidenced by the prior two films on this list. Blast of Silence continues that trend but with a far more cynical tone befitting a film noir. Directed by and starring Allen Baron, the film was shot on a low budget in New York City, lending it a gritty authenticity that also makes it a black-and-white Christmas card for the city during the time period. It's a lean, mean little thriller that makes perfect use of the juxtaposition between the bright holiday lights and the dark shadows.

Frankie (Baron) is a mob hitman who has come home for the holidays to carry out a contract. While he bides his time plotting and planning the hit, Frankie also meets up with friends from his past, which brings up all kinds of demons within him. Not all Christmas movies are designed to be uplifting experiences, and Blast of Silence is one of the best at making you feel bad. It's a dark neo-noir thriller that's a great gift for the Christmas cynic in your family.

There have been so many adaptations of Charles Dickens' seminal A Christmas Carol that some were naturally going to be forgotten along the way. Everyone has their personal favorite cinematic interpretation of the tale of Ebenezer Scrooge, from the 1951 classic starring Alistair Sim to George C. Scott's more abrasive take on the character. One that should be at the top of everyone's Christmas list is the Academy Award-winning animated short film directed by Richard Williams. Both Sim and actor Michael Hordern reprise their roles as Scrooge and Marley, respectively, and the film is a properly haunting adaptation.

Running only 25 minutes, the short film manages to hit all the highlights from the Dickens novel, and even includes a few moments often left out of other adaptations. The hand-drawn animation lends itself to the material, evoking 19th-century illustrations and giving the ghost story a proper element of darkness and danger. Williams, who's probably best known as the animation director on Who Framed Roger Rabbit, is a true legend of animation, and his rendition of the quintessential Christmas story should be more renowned.

Every one of these four started as a cast recording people played until the disc wore out, and every one of them eventually turned into a film. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You work like the clock is against you, because in your head it always is. Hamilton is three hours about a man who cannot stop producing, cannot stop arguing and cannot leave a single thing alone, and you recognised yourself in it immediately.

People made up their minds about you early and they were wrong. Wicked takes the most famous villain in American children's fiction and asks what the story looks like from her side, which is a question you have asked about yourself more than once.

You cannot walk past something unfair. Les Mis is a show about a man who spends his entire life trying to make one wrong right, and about everybody around him deciding what they are prepared to lose for other people.

You are not interested in saving it all for later. Rent is a year in the life of people with no money, no plan and a very clear sense that the time they have is the only thing they genuinely own.

One of the most popular adaptations of A Christmas Carol happens to be the one starring a felt frog and a pig. The Muppet Christmas Carol has become a perennial favorite for many, but it's not the first time Jim Henson's beloved characters have tackled the holiday. A Muppet Family Christmas was a television special that featured not only the titular characters, but also members from Sesame Street and Fraggle Rock as well. It's an absolutely charming movie musical which has also unfortunately fallen by the wayside due to its unavailability on streaming and the fact that most physical media releases have had to cut some songs due to rights issues.

The special follows the entire Muppets cast as they head to Fozzie Bear's mom's house for Christmas, turning it into an absolute madhouse. The Swedish Chef tries to cook Big Bird for Christmas dinner, Fozzie tries to form a double act with a talking snowman, and everyone forgets to mind the icy patch in front of the door. A Muppet Family Christmas has everything to satisfy fans of the Muppets and more. It's a sweet, funny, perfect Christmas special.

See if you can guess the Christmas movie from this premise: A young boy is left alone at home during the holiday season and has to defend himself against a home invader through the use of booby traps. If you answered Home Alone, you'd be correct. You'd also be correct if you answered 3615 Père Noël, also known as Deadly Games and Dial Code Santa Claus, the French horror-action-comedy which many have compared to the Macaulay Culkin classic, including director René Manzor, who unsuccessfully tried to pursue legal action against the producers.

There's never been any official confirmation that Home Alone was ripped off from Manzor's film, and the differences in tone and style become quickly apparent when watching them. Thomas (Alain Lalanne) is similarly resourceful as Kevin McCallister, but he's more inspired by Rambo and other action heroes, which serves him well after an attempted phone call to Santa Claus attracts the attention of a deranged man who breaks into Thomas' high-tech home while his mom is at work. As an homage to '80s action movies, 3615 Père Noël brings on the set pieces and violence, but also a surprising amount of holiday spirit. It makes for the perfect Christmas double feature with Home Alone.

Here's another holiday home invasion. This one comes in the form of an acerbic burglar who takes a WASPy couple hostage while on the run from the police. The Ref comes from director Ted Demme and received solid reviews when it was released but was a box office disappointment. It's since gained a minor cult following, but remains far less celebrated in comparison to other Christmas dark comedies. Its only real sin is having Kevin Spacey in its cast, but at the time it was made, that was actually considered a good idea.

Gus (Denis Leary) is a thief on a job in a wealthy neighborhood that goes south, so he takes a rich couple, Lloyd (Spacey) and Caroline (Judy Davis), hostage and forces them to harbor him in their home. Gus doesn't get the silent night he's hoping for since Lloyd and Caroline are having marital issues, and the thief unwittingly serves as counselor between the two of them. The Ref is sharply written and acted, and was a precursor to darker Christmas comedies like Bad Santa.

Inspired by the aforementioned 3 Godfathers, Tokyo Godfathers is an animated masterpiece from acclaimed director Satoshi Kon. It similarly follows three lost souls who find themselves taking care of an infant on Christmas Eve, but this version of the story takes some unexpected detours and finds shining moments of humanity amid its dark odyssey into the night. Gorgeously animated and determinedly unconventional, Tokyo Godfathers is the perfect Christmas movie for those who are sick of the same old holiday lessons.

In Tokyo, the homeless Gin, Hana, and Miyuki find an abandoned baby along with items to help them track down the child's parents. Their adventure takes them across the city and into contact with all sorts of colorful figures. Tokyo Godfathers is less surreal than Kon's other masterworks, Perfect Blue, Millennium Actress, and Paprika, but is no less creative. Its miracles are all the work of real people rather than any magical beings, and the film itself finds magic in found families and the triumph of the human spirit.

If there's any screenwriter most associated with Christmas, it's Shane Black. The writer has infused the holiday into most of his screenplays and films, from Lethal Weapon to Iron Man 3, but none more perfectly than his neo-noir directorial debut Kiss Kiss Bang Bang. As a two-hander between Robert Downey Jr. and Val Kilmer, the film is filled with all the witty banter Black is best known for and similarly offers a pulpy mystery set in the City of Angels during the most wonderful time of the year.

Harry Lockhart (Downey) is a thief who makes his way from New York to Los Angeles by posing as an aspiring actor. While attending parties in the Hollywood Hills and wooing his hometown crush, Harry also gets involved in a murder mystery, causing him to join forces with private investigator Perry van Shrike (Kilmer). Kiss Kiss Bang Bang wasn't the same kind of blockbuster success as the films Black wrote in the '80s and '90s, but it's a perfect gift for fans of his.

Despite the presence of several animated films on this list, none of them feature stop-motion animation, the medium most associated with Christmas thanks to specials like Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer. While there are some underrated stop-motion Christmas movies worth checking out, they can't quite match the perfection of Arthur Christmas, a computer-animated film from Aardman. That studio built itself on stop-motion with characters like Wallace and Gromit, but their first Christmas movie has all the same charm despite being wholly digital.

Arthur (James McAvoy) is the youngest son of Santa (Jim Broadbent). He's clumsy, awkward, and far from the tech-savvy professional his brother Steve (Hugh Laurie) is, but he does have plenty of Christmas spirit. So, when a child is missed on Christmas Eve, Arthur takes it upon himself to get the present delivered, with the help of his elderly Grandsanta (Bill Nighy). Filled with wildly inventive set pieces and indelible characters, Arthur Christmas offers a unique take on the Santa Claus mythos, and it delivers it with a perfect earnestness.

#3548. This Samsung 32-Inch OLED Gaming Monitor Is $300 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3547. From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race

From “Project Hail Mary” to “La Bola Negra” and “You Can See Everything,” this awards season is dominated by director duos.

Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, better known as Los Javis, are seen as locks for “La Bola Negra,” the Netflix-backed gay historical epic, while longtime collaborators Phil Lord and Chris Miller are also firmly in the Oscar conversation for their work on “Project Hail Mary.” Then there’s Emmy nominee Nathan Fielder teaming up with documentary-world wunderkind Lance Oppenheim on “You Can See Everything,” a less conventional contender, but one that could muscle itself into the race thanks to its box office success. Related Stories King Ghidorah Is Ready for Its Close-Up: How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Cracked the Legendary Monster’s Next Evolution Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore Nailed ‘The Debut’ by Singing, Styling Her Hair Like Liza Minnelli, and Avoiding Playing ‘Some Suffering Mom’

Expand the scope further, and there’s recent indie box office success “Wicker” from husband-and-wife filmmaking duo Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson. Plus “Clarissa” from brothers Arie and Chuko Esiri, and “Mouse” from director couple Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson, which picked up a Gotham Best Feature nom.

That’s six different films in this year’s awards conversation, suggesting director duos are becoming more common in filmmaking overall. But in terms of Oscar recognition, only five films across the Academy Awards‘ 98-year history have had their filmmaker duos nominated for Best Director. More than one team nominated for Best Director this season would be a record.

So what makes director duos so rare at the Oscars? Much of it comes down to the Directors Guild of America. Keep in mind, Best Director nominations are determined by the contenders’ peers in the Directors Branch, so even though the DGA is a separate group with its own eligibility rules for the DGA Awards, the guild overlaps enough with the Academy to set the tone. The DGA also has a bylaw that states, “One Director to a Film.” The logic behind the rule, established in 1978, is to prevent anyone, especially producers, from delegating tasks to other members of a director’s team. Director duos can request a waiver, but they must prove they intend to be lifelong collaborators.

The “One Director to a Film” mentality is another major hurdle for “You Can See Everything” directors Fielder and Oppenheim in particular, as both filmmakers had established solo careers before teaming up. Meanwhile, the rest of the class of 2026 director duos have been collaborators from the start of their careers, with Los Javis and Lord and Miller, the two most viable Best Director candidates, even having shorthand nicknames within the industry. “You Can See Everything” has already been deemed ineligible for a Best Director nomination at the DGA Awards, because the category does not include documentaries.

Despite the hurdles they must overcome, director duos often go on to win Oscars if they secure a nomination. That was the case for “West Side Story” directors Robert Wise and Jerome Robbins in 1962, for “No Country for Old Men” directors Joel and Ethan Coen in 2008, and most recently for “Everything Everywhere All at Once” directors Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert (aka Daniels) in 2023.

Of the two director duos that fell short, one was the Coen Brothers again for “True Grit” in 2011, only three years after they won the Best Director Oscar. That makes “Heaven Can Wait” helmers Warren Beatty and Buck Henry the only director duo that didn’t win the Oscar the first time they were nominated as a pair. Henry and Beatty would never direct together again, and Beatty would win the Oscar for directing “Reds” three years after “Heaven Can Wait” came out in 1978.

So while there’s a tremendous barrier for entry, if any of the director duos in the awards mix this year are able to secure a Best Director nomination, history indicates they should probably have an acceptance speech ready.

#3546. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3545. Alan Ritchson’s DC Future Just Got Murkier After James Gunn’s Sudden Exit

Following the announcement of James Gunn and Peter Safran stepping down as co-CEOs of DC Studios, Alan Ritchson's future in the DCU just got murkier. Just weeks ago, Safran confirmed that DC was in talks with Ritchson for multiple projects. Now that DC Studios will be under new leadership from former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham, these recent developments make Ritchson's role in the DCU much less clear. Given Ritchson's interest in joining the modern DCU, this sudden change certainly shakes his candidacy up.

Ritchson has appeared in several previous DCU projects in the past, including his role as Arthur Curry/Aquaman in the hit television series Smallville and Hank Hall/Hawk in the HBO Max series Titans. Ritchson's star power has grown immensely as the titular lead in Prime Video's massively successful Reacher franchise, suggesting that a more significant role would become available to him within Gunn and Safran's DCU. Now that Latcham, who served as a producer on The Avengers, Guardians of the Galaxy, and Spider-Man: Homecoming, is officially in the DCU driver's seat as of December 1, a completely new rollout strategy may be introduced that could exclude Ritchson.

During Gunn and Safran's 4-year run as CEOs and chairmen of DC Studios, they released a Superman reboot that introduced David Corenswet as the latest Man of Steel, as well as Supergirl, which fell far below box office expectations. The duo was expected to retain their executive roles after the historic Paramount/Skydance acquisition of Warner Bros. earlier this year, with their upcoming Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow as well as the long-awaited sequel to Robert Pattinson's Batman slated for release. While these projects remain intact, this leadership update has cast a cloud of uncertainty over the modern DCU, which includes how Ritchson could enter the fold.

Ritchson previously expressed interest in becoming the DCU's new Bruce Wayne/Batman, but talks with Gunn have led the 43-year-old actor to officially shut down that prospect. Instead, Gunn and Safran were searching for a role within their DCU that better fit Ritchson's age range, while also trying to land on a role that would have given Ritchson a more morally complex, less full-blown superhero character to play. It's important to note that Gunn and Safran are staying on at DC Studios to commit full-time to creative projects, suggesting that there is still hope for Ritchson to match their initial vision. If that happens, they'll have to do so under the discretion of Jeremy Latcham​​​​​.

On October 26, 2026, Peter Safran confirmed that DC was still in talks with Ritchson and noted that while interest was there, the right role for him had yet to be ascertained within Gunn's superhero universe. He stated, "We talked about a couple things, but nothing that's come to fruition at this point. I think he's great. Yeah, but he's just good. I also think there's a lot more depth to him than you might have seen. I think there's more that he can do that people haven't seen." These comments suggest that Safran and Gunn saw clear potential in the idea of Ritchson joining their DCU, specifically in finding him an ideal role that would tap into his abilities as both an action star and a performer.

Anthony Mackie faces a career criminal in Apple TV’s new 8-part heist thriller, combining a high-stakes vault robbery with an international chase.

The fact that Safran and Gunn hadn't landed on the right role for Ritchson in their DCU might actually work in Ritchson's favor, as Latcham may potentially be more eager to cash in on Ritchson's immediate draw and emergence as a one-man-army movie star. Ritchson remains one of the most sought-after leads in the action genre, having recently starred in Runner, War Machine, Playdate, and Motor City, all of which were met with mixed, if not poor, reviews. While the new leadership at DC Studios makes Alan Ritchson's DCU future unclear, it could also finally land him the role we've all been waiting for.

#3544. DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn, Peter Safran Stepping Down as Co-CEOs, Marvel Vet Jeremy Latcham Named Chief Creative Officer

James Gunn and Peter Safran are out as heads of DC Studios.

The move comes after Skydance closed its $110 billion deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery in October. Jeremy Latcham, who helped shape the Marvel Cinematic Universe, has been appointed president and chief creative officer, DC Studios, beginning December 1, 2026.

Gunn and Safran joined the company four years ago with the goal of making DC a true challenger to the MCU, but they’ve had mixed success. “Superman,” which Gunn directed, was a hit at the box office, but “Supergirl” bombed and “Clayface,” an R-rated body horror film, has performed modestly. The pair also launched new series based on the comic book company’s characters, including “Peacemaker” and “Lanterns.” Gunn has one more film on the horizon, the “Superman” sequel, “Man of Tomorrow,” which opens next year. Related Stories Our Plea to the New DC Studios Head: No More Shared Universe! James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next

“James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we’re incredibly proud of,” David Ellison, Chairman and CEO, and Ynon Kreiz, Co-CEO, of Skydance said in a statement. “We’re grateful for their passion, contributions, and commitment to this legendary brand. Jeremy has been a longtime creative partner to both, and we have complete confidence that James and Peter will ensure a smooth, collaborative transition and continue this work with care. We look forward to working with Jeremy to build the next generation of DC storytelling and to doubling down on our commitment to fans.”

In a separate statement, Gunn and Safran said, “Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore ‘Superman’ to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with ‘Peacemaker,’ ‘Creature Commandos,’ ‘Lanterns,’ and ‘Clayface.’ We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews, and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter.”

Latcham will lead DC’s film, television, and animation slate. He will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, Co-Chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group.

“Jeremy brings a deep reverence for DC and its passionate fanbase, recognizing that they are the very foundation of this storied, multigenerational brand,” said Goldberg and Greenstein. “Under his leadership, every film and television show will be ushered from start to finish through the prism of the legions of fans who love and champion it. Jeremy’s track record exemplifies the excellence he will bring to building out DC and the many beloved characters within it.”

At Marvel, Latcham produced several of the company’s biggest hits, including “The Avengers,” “Spider-Man: Homecoming,” “Iron Man 2,” and “Guardians of the Galaxy,” which Gunn directed. As an independent producer, his credits include “Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves” and “The Breadwinner.”

Latcham faces a steep challenge. DC has suffered from a lack of consistency in its creative direction. The studio was initially overseen by comic book veterans Geoff Johns and Jon Berg, who were later replaced by veteran producer Walter Hamada, before he too was ousted. Over that time, DC had hits such as “Aquaman” and “Wonder Woman,” but they were outweighed by costly failures like “Justice League” and “The Flash.”

When Discovery bought Warner Bros. in 2022, David Zaslav personally courted Gunn and Safran to turn the ship around. But the timing was tricky. Comic book movies remain popular, at least the ones featuring marquee heroes like Spider-Man or Batman, but audiences have grown more discerning. They are less likely to show up for second- or third-tier characters (see: Supergirl). So it will fall to Latcham to figure out a new strategy to meet the moment, one that either builds on Gunn and Safran’s foundation or takes the studio in yet another direction.

#3543. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

#3542. All 3 ‘NCIS’ Shows Officially Return to CBS Tonight

Although the entire NCIS franchise has been on a roll to start the fall television season, the trio of crime procedurals ran into the one thing that could stop them last week — democracy. Midterm coverage meant Parker, Gibbs, Hanna, and the rest took the night off while the results of House, Senate, and other elections rolled in. It's far from unusual for network programs to be preempted at some point in the fall, especially for those airing on Tuesday nights in an even year, but it nonetheless slowed the series' momentum at a time when the franchise ratings are at a high. Fortunately for fans, their absence on CBS won't last any longer.

All three of NCIS, NCIS: New York, and NCIS: Origins are locked in to return tonight in their usual time slots, starting with the flagship at 8 p.m. ET/PT. Season 24 has been riding a ratings high with the reintroduction of Michael Weatherly's fan-favorite agent Tony DiNozzo as the new director of NCIS in place of the late Leon Vance (Rocky Carroll). As part of a strong CBS premiere week, the series returned with a 20% increase in viewers over the previous season's first episode, drawing in 6.45 million viewers and carrying the momentum in Nielsen's live plus 7 days of multiplatform viewership. Episode 5, "Speechless," will next send the team to take on the case of an eight-year-old girl, played by NCIS star Katrina Law's own daughter, Kinley Andreen, left alone when her Marine mother goes missing. In a race against time to find her parent, they learn the lengths the mom was willing to go to for her family and discover that their shy witness' unexpected skill may be the key to blowing their search open.

The newcomer New York, meanwhile, will continue Sam Hanna's (LL COOL J) homecoming at 9 p.m., with an episode that hits close to home for his new partner, Nick Schaeffer (Scott Caan). The Big Apple's agents are called in to investigate after a naval interrogator is violently murdered in her own home. In the background, however, the corruption investigation into Nick's old partner is still unfolding, and he's unsure how to process it all. Finally, at 10 p.m., Origins will continue where its previous episode left off with "Baila Esta Cumbia," as Gibbs (Mark Harmon) and Bishop (Emily Wickersham) continue their off-the-books mission with an intense interrogation while, in 1993, Franks (Kyle Schmid) leads the team on a murder case involving a con woman that hits Lala (Mariel Molino) especially hard.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

While Weatherly's return as Tony and Harmon's return as Gibbs have both drawn extra attention to NCIS and Origins early on, at least one of them will be gone from the screen once more before the year ends. With the addition of the LL-led New York to the lineup, Origins is one of several series CBS cut down to just ten episodes instead of the 18 its past two runs have clocked in at. The shortened Season 3 means the finale is expected to air in December, leaving room for NCIS: Sydney to return for Season 4 sometime next year. That means only five episodes are left after tonight to wrap up one of the most dangerous and personal cases of Gibbs' career that has tied so deeply into his past at Camp Pendleton.

NCIS, NCIS: New York, and NCIS: Origins air tonight on CBS. Stay tuned here at Collider for more changes in scheduled programming throughout the rest of the year.
