#3541. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

#3540. Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It?

Don’t be surprised if you emerge from Alex Thompson and Kelly O’Sullivan’s piercingly moving coming-of-age grief dramedy “Mouse” in a puddle of tears. Graceful in technique, compassionate in its writing, this movie, one of the year’s best, is a crying machine. But that’s not to say this story of a high school girl’s (Katherine Mallen Kupferer, astonishing) formative first encounter with major loss is any bit manipulative.

As heartbreak ripples through a small town, “Mouse” has the texture and deep feeling of Kenneth Lonergan’s post-9/11 New York City drama “Margaret,” starring Anna Paquin as a precocious teenager in freefall after witnessing a pedestrian’s brutal death. Unlike “Margaret,” “Mouse” didn’t take over half a decade to reach screens after production wrapped, but the road was still paved with rejection (baffling in retrospect) for Chicago directing duo Thompson and O’Sullivan. Related Stories King Ghidorah Is Ready for Its Close-Up: How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Cracked the Legendary Monster’s Next Evolution Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore Nailed ‘The Debut’ by Singing, Styling Her Hair Like Liza Minnelli, and Avoiding Playing ‘Some Suffering Mom’

With “Mouse,” the filmmakers found themselves at the Berlin Film Festival for the first time back in February — even as an American indie set in Arkansas about the challenges of coming of age feels like catnip for a festival like Sundance, where such topics are historically de rigueur. And Thompson and O’Sullivan had been to Sundance before, with their critically championed 2024 comedy-drama “Ghostlight,” about an emotionally ramshackle, rookie community theater production of “Romeo and Juliet.” While placement at the legacy indie festival, headed to Boulder in January, doesn’t always mean you’re grandfathered into the acceptance pipeline for your next movie, it was still a surprise to the directors (who are also life partners with two children) when Sundance turned down “Mouse” not once, but twice.

“To be totally fair, we submitted before we probably should have, with a long cut,” O’Sullivan told IndieWire over Zoom. “Apparently, it didn’t matter,” Thompson added.

“We submitted it again the next year, when it was tighter,” added O’Sullivan, though the filmmakers were dismissed again. “The feedback that we got — and again, this is a game of telephone, so we don’t know — is that it had real champions, but that it also had people who didn’t get it. Yes, it was crushing. It was confusing. More than anything, I was like, ‘Wait, but people did such great work on this movie. The work is incredible.’ And not ours even, but Sophie [Okonedo] and Katherine [Mallen Kupferer], and the crew, I was like, ‘I feel like they deserve a really big stage.’”

Luckily, the Berlin Film Festival stepped in to program “Mouse” in the Panorama section, marking Thompson and O’Sullivan’s first bow at a European fest, where it grabbed strong reviews. And, as the filmmakers point out, that festival turned out to be the proper home. (Berlin, after all, just had its strongest lineup in years, under artistic director Tricia Tuttle’s second festival.)

“It really was hard for a moment, and then we heard back from Berlin, and it kind of felt like a career opportunity that went way beyond Sundance,” Thompson said. “Tapping into the narrative outside of the American indie felt like something we’d always aspired to. And those are the films that I identify with the most, the sort of work that comes out of those great European festivals. The most jealous and childish I am is every year when the Venice reviews start coming out, and it’s like, ‘Ah, well, those all sound great.’ And Cannes and Berlin, and our favorite festivals, we have a relationship with Thessaloniki and American Film Festival in Wrocław, and to have that stage at Berlin, it’s like this sort of historic stage. It’s absolutely mind-blowing. I’ve never been in a theater that big with a movie.”

A Gotham nominee for Best Feature, “Mouse” is now quietly in theaters from Independent Film Company. (A sparsely attended Academy screening also took place in Los Angeles over the weekend.) Film chatterers may deem this a “small” movie in a year of “You Can See Everything” and “La Bola Negra,” it is huge in every way.

The film follows Minnie Dunn (Kupferer), who, just as she’s about to enter her senior year, is dealt a life-altering loss. It’s 2002, Michelle Branch is on the radio, and September 11 is not even a year out of view. Faced with a hole in her life in the shape of her lifelong best friend after a tragic accident, Minnie forms a tight bond with the girl’s British stay-at-home mother, Helen (Sophie Okonedo, luminescent here), mourning on her own. Meanwhile, Minnie’s classmates all but literally compete to see who can grieve the loudest in the form of a talent show. “Mouse” is about the centrifugal force of grief and how life goes on around you, but you’re still stuck in the same place.

Big on emotional generosity and ace turns from the filmmakers’ stable of theater-based Chicago actors — including Kupferer and her real-life mother Tara Mallen, who plays Minnie’s struggling, lower-middle-class mom onscreen — “Mouse” deserves as much attention as any of the year’s best films. The grand ambition of “Mouse” and its emotional dividends and wonderful performances suggest it could’ve cleaned up at Telluride or even Toronto, where, in the latter case, a number of indie films flopped, and even the most acclaimed are still searching for distribution.

“Rejected, rejected,” O’Sullivan laughed, later adding, “We understand how complicated programming a festival is, and we don’t feel entitled to be programmed anywhere. We’re grateful to every festival that’s given us a slot.”

She wrote the script for “Mouse” in 2019, around the time their debut feature as collaborators, “Saint Frances,” opened at SXSW. That microbudget indie, directed by Thompson and starring O’Sullivan as a drifting 34-year-old nanny in Chicago, won the Austin festival’s audience award and later earned a John Cassavetes Spirit Award nomination. “Mouse” was actually meant to be their next feature, with one financier, a cushier budget, and a slightly different cast — until the strikes changed their plans, leading to “Ghostlight” as their Sundance debut on a smaller scale.

Based on O’Sullivan’s own experience with loss as a teen, “Mouse” picked back up in fall 2024, shooting on location in her home state of Arkansas. “We were amazingly able to retain the vision” of “Mouse” from before the strikes, she said. “Nothing got cut for budget.”

Thompson, who produced the film, said, “Knowing the budget so intimately, I guess that’s my superpower on the producing side that most directors don’t have is I just get really intimate with the budget. And it seems really boring, but it’s kind of like a script where if you don’t have the means, if it’s not there in the budget, it’s not going to happen… A lot of directors I talked to have been like, ‘Oh, well, my producer said we couldn’t do a rain tower, or my producers said we couldn’t do this shot because we can’t afford it.’ And it’s like, well, you can pretty much afford anything. You just have to give somewhere else. We tend to make really ambitious one-liners like schedules. We had 30 days on this, but that ended up being a two-hour and 15-minute movie, and we cut 20 minutes.”

When asked about the “Mouse” budget, he said, “I think we can say. We’re already underdogs. We might as well say. It was $3 million.”

And it’s $3 million, well-budgeted and in true indie spirit — like a scene where Minnie and her friends watch “Titanic” in a parent’s basement during one of those classic sleepovers where private confidences spill out, insulated from the adult world upstairs and outside.

“We didn’t even try to get the rights to ‘Titanic,’ but we’re mixing at Skywalker,” Thompson said. “They have the entire effects library for ‘Titanic’ … so we rebuilt the dance scene in ‘Titanic’ and used public-domain Irish music, and then Kelly and [producer] Pierce Cravens do the voices of Leo and Kate off in a room being like, ‘I feel so young,’ or something, whatever that is. If you watch the movie, you think they’re watching ‘Titanic’ in the basement, but it’s a totally constructed thing because we’re like, ‘We can’t get the rights to this.'”

On top of “Mouse” already dwelling on a very specific point of loss from O’Sullivan’s own childhood, the filmmaker’s mother also died in Arkansas toward the end of production. That meant she was actively grieving while also leading a set, alongside her partner.

“It was so bizarre,” O’Sullivan said. “She died when we had a week and a half left to shoot… It was incredibly complicated. I just couldn’t believe the timing of it for so many different reasons. I mean, one of which is just that it took forever to make this movie, but the movie allowed me to be there literally when she died. I didn’t have to get on a plane. But then when I was back on set, I just kept hearing these lines that I had written, and they took on a whole new meaning… lines that I had sort of written in a very theoretical way all of a sudden were hitting me in a, ‘God, I can’t believe how true this was, and I didn’t even know.'”

The autobiography that drove “Mouse” extended behind the scenes in even more literal ways. Christen Pitts, the choreographer behind the movie’s climactic ballet elegy sequence set to a cover of Cyndi Lauper’s “Time After Time,” was O’Sullivan’s high school dance teacher. “It feels like so many different chapters of my life are just compressing into the same space, and it feels like a culmination of my entire adult life and teenage years and echoes of the past existing,” O’Sullivan said.

Thompson and O’Sullivan have maintained their filmmaking footprint in and around Chicago — even as “Mouse” brought them to Arkansas — and they don’t feel especially tempted to make the leap to Hollywood, though there have been offers.

“I just write from a place of experience most of the time, and I don’t know, I’ve seen so many movies set in L.A. and New York, and I actually don’t identify with those towns,” O’Sullivan said. “I feel like enough people are doing that, and I like writing from a place of specificity … I’ve spent maybe a year in both places cumulatively. It doesn’t feel like a character that I personally need to explore. But having said that, if I spent more time there, it felt like a story was necessarily set there. I’d be open to it. I just don’t feel compelled to.”

“We really want to have a body of work,” Thompson said. “The people I admire the most are Steven Soderbergh and Sidney Lumet, directors who have dozens of films by the time they stop, and Soderbergh has not stopped, obviously.” He doesn’t know that a move to Los Angeles is possible given their artistic goals. “We’ve gone out on meetings, we’ve done pitches, we’ve considered projects from studios, and the timeline always felt kind of like it just hasn’t really worked out. ‘Mouse’ was so close to being that thing, and then the writers’ strike, and the SAG strike, we lost a cast member, and it just all fell away. So we just thought, ‘What if we just do what we did on ‘Ghostlight,’ but on steroids? If I can raise half a million dollars, I wonder if we can raise three.”

With the filmmakers now set up at Gersh talent agency, he added, “If we want to make a movie every 15 months, we probably can’t do that in the studio system. But I think we both like the idea of playing in a bigger sandbox and taking the intimacy, taking all the things we’ve learned, and working in a bigger sandbox. I don’t think that’s unattractive, but it’s just, for the way we work, this has made the most sense so far.”

Next up, Thompson directed a high-concept body-swap comedy starring the “Ghostlight” father-daughter (and real-life father-daughter) team of “Mouse” star Katherine Mallen Kupferer with Keith Kupferer. Plus, they’ve co-directed “The Steel Harp,” starring Lois Smith and O’Sullivan in a return to acting. Both are expected in 2027.

“We shoot on the same lenses as ‘Saint Frances,’ same aspect ratio as ‘Mouse,’ in a world that winks at a bigger sandbox,” Thompson said of the body swap movie. “It’s a total gamble. I’ve got no idea if it’s going to work… It seems to be quite funny according to my three-year-old.”

“Mouse” is now playing in New York and Los Angeles, with a wider expansion to follow in November.

#3539. Steam Officially Makes 8/10 Turn-Based RPG 100% Free Until November 12

A remarkable turn-based RPG is 100% free on Steam until November 12, and I highly encourage you to check out this game alone or with friends, as it supports multiplayer co-op. Free games are common on the gaming platform, and every so often, there’s a new free game on Steam that you can download and keep forever. Alternatively, there are also a few promotional periods where paid games become entirely free to keep forever if you can grab them in time, while others are offered for free for a short period. There’s never a shortage of what to play there.

Now, the platform is offering a paid game for free, but only until November 12. In a limited-time promotion, you can download and play For the King 2 for free on Steam. The offer ends on November 12, meaning that you’ll be unable to continue playing the turn-based RPG for free when the date arrives. Even so, during the period, you can play the base game’s content entirely for free, no strings attached. All you have to do is click on the Play Game button on its product page on Steam to start the download.

What I consider one of the greatest RPGs of the decade, For the King 2 is a turn-based adventure RPG with roguelike elements, where you go through various stages to defeat the tyrannical Queen. Released in 2023, this turn-based RPG uses procedurally generated maps, so every playthrough feels slightly different from the previous one. The title will have you explore an overworld that’s full of dangers, completing missions to get stronger, as well as dungeons along the way. When you enter combat, you adhere to a small grid-like map, and strategy plays a huge part.

Every character is expected to take on a different role. As such, while one character is mostly responsible for the damage output, another needs to take care of their companions. There are several different classes in For the King 2, and more are being added constantly. For example, just recently, the game received the Pugilist and the Gravedigger classes, as part of the Dust to Dust expansion. #3537. 5 Best Death-Game Books for ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ Fans, Ranked

Millions of readers have now taken a chance on Dungeon Crawler Carl, though many online profess that they've never read a "LitRPG" story before. The obscure subgenre is an odd quirk for many fans, with some diving into other titles and many wondering if they'll really like anything beyond DCC. However, on a simpler level Dungeon Crawler Carl sticks to a familiar format in the sci-fi/fantasy genre: the "death game." Stories about deadly competitions have been popular in speculative fiction for years, from tournaments and tests of strength to bloody trials and rites of passage. There's nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, but the books below are a great starting point for DCC fans looking for their next binge.

The LitRPG setting is brilliant for death game fiction because it allows the author to flesh out all the rules and mechanics in extreme detail. It becomes more than worldbuilding minutiae when the characters' lives depend on these rules, and Dungeon Crawler Carl has a lot of fun playing with the absurdity of it all. Still, many fans are weary of exploring more LitRPG without the overwhelming recommendations DCC already has behind it. For those that want another death game after DCC without with the LitRPG format, here are five books you might enjoy.

If you've picked up Dungeon Crawler Carl within the last year or two, chances are you did so knowing about it's meteoric rise in popularity. As long as you're catching up on popular ongoing series, you might as well give the works of Sarah J. Maas a try. Today, the author is best known for her series A Court of Thorns and Roses, but prior to that she wrote an eight-book series called Throne of Glass. The two series are loosely connected as they take place in the same universe — though in different dimensions.

Throne of Glass follows a young assassin named Celaena Sardothien, who is imprisoned and on the verge of death when the series begins. Celaena's only chance at freedom is competing in a series of contests to choose the "King's Champion." She goes up against other assassins and warriors in a series of extremely dangerous competitions before finally facing the survivors in one-on-one duels. As if that wasn't dangerous enough, someone is picking off the contestants one by one behind the scenes, apparently in an attempt to affect the outcome of the games.

Sticking with topical picks, Stephen King's 1982 novel The Running Man is about a death game that comes pretty close to Dungeon Crawler Carl in terms of bleak absurdity. The book is set in a near future where economic collapse has left many Americans in desperate poverty. In the midst of this, a reality show called The Running Man seems to offer a way out — but at great risk. Contestants must avoid teams of hitmen sent out by the producers to kill them. They win money based on how long they stay alive, but viewers can also win money by turning them in, making things incredibly difficult. When the story begins, no contestant has ever survived to win the grand prize, but their families do get $100 for every hour they managed to stay alive.

The Running Man was adapted into a film in 1987 starring Arnold Schwarzenegger, though it diverged wildly from King's novel. Another adaptation was released just last year. It starred Glen Powell and stuck much more closely to the story. Fans will have three versions of the story to contrast and compare, and each one evokes the same kind of righteous fury as Dungeon Crawler Carl.

Of course, The Hunger Games series is one of the most iconic death game stories in recent decades, and it deserves a place on this list. For those that have watched the movies but not read the books, there are some very interesting differences to explore on the page. On top of that, Suzanne Collins' more recent prequel novels are even more interesting as they step outside of Katniss' first-person perspective and reveal more of Collins' range as an author.

The Hunger Games is also set in a dystopian near-future U.S.A. which is in the grip of a ruthless totalitarian regime. After several attempts at revolution, the ruling class instituted an annual spectacle called The Hunger Games in which two teenagers from every district are sent as "tribute" to compete in a battle royale competition. The books keep their focus on these death games throughout the story, though they do veer into plenty of other interesting territory along the way.

Many fans of Dungeon Crawler Carl are reaching for Pierce Brown's Red Rising series as well, and the death game aspect is just one more reason to recommend it. The novels introduce us to a distant future where humanity has thoroughly colonized the entire solar system, yet most people live under the yoke of a brutal caste system which is maintained with genetic engineering, social engineering, and brute force. The story follows a young man named Darrow who is secretly elevated from the lowest caste — red — to the highest — gold — to try and sabotage the rulers from within.

Darrow then participates in a ritualistic death game in order to join the elite ranks of ruling golds where he may be able to affect the most change. He and dozens of other teenage candidates must survive for months in a brutally sculpted wilderness, warring with each other to survive and dominate. It's not the focus of the entire series, but it's a brilliant introduction to Brown's sci-fi setting which sticks with you throughout the remaining books. Red Rising is nearly finished now, with Brown working on the final volume as we speak. It has also been greenlit for a film adaptation, so now is a great time to get onboard.

Finally, The Poppy War trilogy by R.F. Kuang is a must-read for modern fantasy fans, including DCC fans. Like Red Rising, its death game element is just one chapter among many, but it stands out and defines the characters in all the fights that follow. The Poppy War is set in a fantasy world inspired by China and other East Asian cultures. Protagonist Rin makes it into the Nikara Empire military academy despite her impoverished background, and is determined to rise through the ranks at any cost. She is drawn to the obscure field of shamanism, using meditation and psychoactive drugs to harness magical powers. Through her work, her perspective on the empire begins to shift.

The Poppy War is often billed as "grimdark." Dungeon Crawler Carl fans may think they're prepared for that, but there is little levity or absurdity to balance out the heartbreak here. Still, this is one of the best fantasy trilogies to come out in the last decade, and it has launched Kuang into a stellar career. It should be at the top of the TBR for fantasy fans with a book hangover.

All the books mentioned above are available now in print, digital, and audiobook formats, as is Dungeon Crawler Carl. The DCC TV adaptation is in production now, and the ninth book is well underway. So far, neither has a release date.

#3536. Our Plea to the New DC Studios Head: No More Shared Universe!

Four years ago, DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran relaunched the comics brand with grand ambitions to build a Marvel Cinematic Universe of their own with a crop of characters they believed to be superior to what Marvel and Disney had. They controlled Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, Green Lantern, The Flash, and a whole bunch more they could mold as they saw fit, and they promised they would fix the flawed Marvel Studios system of greenlighting projects before a strong screenplay was in place. They announced a massive slate of 10 films and series right out of the gate and had other expectations that stars they cast today would appear in future DC films for the long haul. Above all, they were going to be careful with the brand. Related Stories DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn, Peter Safran Stepping Down as Co-CEOs, Marvel Vet Jeremy Latcham Named Chief Creative Officer James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next

“No one was minding the mint,” Gunn said back in January 2023 in a telling quote. “They were just giving away IP like they were party favors to any creators who smiled at them. What we are going to do is promise that everything from our first project going forward is going to be unified.”

The real world quickly caught up to Gunn and Safran. In a move beyond their control, ownership of DC Studios changed hands yet again from Warner Bros. Discovery to Skydance, and now just four years, three films, and a couple of TV shows into their tenure, they’re out. Taking the reins is Jeremy Latcham, not a household name the way Kevin Feige or some of his lieutenants have been, but an architect of the early stages of the MCU and a key, former executive at Marvel (he left for an independent label of his own in 2017). He has comic book chops, having produced “The Avengers,” the first MCU “Spider-Man,” and more.

Because the ball didn’t really get rolling at DC Studios in the short time Gunn and Safran were on board, and because Latcham still has a lingering slate that includes a second “Superman” movie that’s already in the can and a second “The Batman” movie in the works that isn’t even connected to the DCU anyway, as he begins to map out his own ambitions for the next era of DC movies and series, we have a simple plea: no more shared universes. Please. We beg you. Enough already.

Do not try and build the next MCU or even the next DC(E)U or whatever you want to call it. Just make some really good superhero movies with the characters and brands people love.

Books have been and will be written about the producing success story Kevin Feige managed with the MCU, and David Ellison, fanboy that he is, would surely love to have his own version of “The Avengers.” Who wouldn’t? We’ve seen other studios try and recreate the MCU formula with their own IP, like the Godzilla vs. Kong-iverse from WB and Legendary or the incredibly misguided plan for a Universal monster-verse that fizzled out with Tom Cruise’s “The Mummy.“

Truth be told, Marvel is trying to reconstruct its own formula ever since “Avengers: Endgame,” and it has been a mixed bag. Sure, there were a few billion-dollar hits in there like “Deadpool & Wolverine” and this year’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” and “Avengers: Doomsday” too figures to be huge, but other new characters and would-be franchises like “Eternals” or “Shang-Chi” have gone through fits and stops. Movies like a “Blade” reboot have never been able to get off the ground as Marvel tries to fit a square peg into a round hole. Marvel has been forced to recast and scramble its carefully laid plans amid the controversy around Jonathan Majors. And the sheer glut of TV shows over the last few years has created immense homework for people that has led the actual flagship movies to drop off precipitously at the box office.

Is that what DC Studios really wants? More of that drama and headache? It feels like we’re well beyond the era where audiences are willing to commit for every new episode of a yearslong cinematic saga. Surely whatever vision Gunn and Safran had was grand, especially if you’re a real fan of those characters and want to see them all come together as the Justice League yet again, but it doesn’t feel like today’s young audiences want to sign up for that.

Gunn and Safran actually immediately ran into this problem as they tried to bridge the gap between the old DCEU and the new DCU they were building. People knew “The Flash” and “Aquaman 2” weren’t going to be part of the future, even as Gunn and Safran paid lip service to the idea and played coy about having some of these actors reprising their roles in the new universe. (Remember when Henry Cavill thought for a minute he was playing Superman again?) The films underwhelmed at the box office as a result, and it created confusion among casual fans as the execs were forced to dance around the fanboys and the Snyder Army.

Audiences, though, have demonstrated that superhero movies still matter when they feature characters they care about. “Spider-Man” stayed away for about five years, and “Brand New Day” is now one of the highest-grossing movies of all time. We hadn’t had a proper, standalone “Superman” movie in years, and it proved to be a great launching pad for Gunn’s slate, earning $618.7 million worldwide. There’s still huge excitement for “The Batman: Part II” from Matt Reeves, and there’s never been any pretense that it’s connected to some more important lore or that Pattinson’s Bruce Wayne might show up in a theoretical “Wonder Woman” sequel a decade down the road. People just really like Batman.

So what do you do now if you’re Latcham and have to answer to Ellison and former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz? It would make sense to just demonstrate how you’re going to make the most of the IP that you have. Signaling to audiences (and shareholders) that your next Wonder Woman movie won’t come out until 2037 because you’re mapping out the shared universe for how to carefully introduce all these characters doesn’t sound like the best approach. Just hire smart writers, entrust visionary directors, and make some good movies. It worked with “The Batman.”

This, of course, does not mean don’t make your big “Justice League” team up movie or don’t build a new franchise out of “Teen Titans.” It just means that times and appetites have changed from the pre-Covid and even pre-streaming boom MCU era when “Guardians of the Galaxy” could be a hit (in part) because of how it teased the arrival of Thanos and the Infinity Stones. Audiences have become more discerning about what they define as an event film, and DC Studios can beat Marvel at its own game so long as DC stops trying to become Marvel.

#3535. The Bose Premium Smart Ultra Soundbar Is Now Cheaper Than It Was During Prime Day

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3534. Clive Cussler’s Dirk Pitt Returns Today In Brand-New Sequel

Clive Cussler's Dirk Pitt series has been a staple of action-adventure fiction for more than five decades, taking readers on countless high-stakes adventures involving everything from ancient shipwrecks and lost civilizations to deadly international conspiracies. Since the release of The Mediterranean Caper in 1973, the series has become one of the most recognizable names in the genre, with Pitt himself earning a reputation as one of fiction's most enduring adventurers.

Sadly, Cussler passed away in 2020, leaving behind an incredible literary legacy that included several bestselling franchises. Fortunately, his beloved Dirk Pitt series was already in good hands. His son, Dirk Cussler, had co-written eight novels with his father before his passing, eventually taking over as the series' primary author and continuing to deliver the same kind of action-packed adventures that made the original books so popular.

Now, more than six years after Clive Cussler's death, his most iconic character is officially returning for another adventure, with a brand-new Dirk Pitt thriller arriving today, November 10.

Clive Cussler's most famous adventurer is officially back, with Obsidian Sky available now. Published by G.P. Putnam's Sons, the 28th installment in the bestselling Dirk Pitt series promises another globe-spanning thriller, complete with ancient mysteries, dangerous technology, and "a potential cataclysmic event that threatens all of humanity."

The official description opens with an intriguing tease:

"A forgotten civilization. A lost Biblical artifact. A criminal enterprise lurking beneath the seas."

The story begins when Dirk Pitt, director of the National Underwater and Marine Agency (NUMA), rescues a group of archaeologists trapped inside a cavern following an earthquake. Their ordeal leads to the discovery of a mysterious 2,000-year-old silver scroll, written in a language even older than Phoenician. The artifact appears to contain clues to a priceless ancient treasure, but its discovery is apparently only the beginning of a much larger mystery.

In Obsidian Sky, Pitt and his longtime partner Al Giordino investigate the disappearance of a freighter in the Mediterranean Sea, eventually locating the wreck only to discover that its cargo has vanished. The two mysteries ultimately send Pitt on a dangerous international adventure involving what the publisher describes as "drugs, deceit, secret technology" and events with potentially catastrophic consequences.

Although the novel carries Clive Cussler's name, Obsidian Sky was written by his son, Dirk Cussler, who has continued the franchise following his father's death in 2020. The younger Cussler previously co-authored eight Dirk Pitt novels with his father before taking over the series, subsequently writing The Devil's Sea and The Corsican Shadow.

Interestingly, Dirk Cussler also has real-world experience with underwater exploration, having participated in his father's NUMA expeditions and continuing his legacy of searching for historic shipwrecks.

You can purchase Dirk Cussler's Obsidian Sky via Amazon here.

Obsidian Sky is available today in hardcover, ebook, and audiobook formats, with the hardcover edition running 496 pages and a suggested retail price of $34, while the audiobook is narrated by Scott Brick. For longtime readers, it's a great opportunity to reunite with one of adventure fiction's most enduring protagonists, with Dirk Cussler continuing the literary legacy his father established more than 50 years ago.

#3532. Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore Nailed ‘The Debut’ by Singing, Styling Her Hair Like Liza Minnelli, and Avoiding Playing ‘Some Suffering Mom’

“Hello, I’m Julie,” said a radiant Julianne Moore, holding out her hand as she popped out of the elevator at Middleburg, Virginia’s Salamander Resort. Her hair was red, her skin was white, her dress as yellow as gold. A few hours later after a rapturous Middleburg Film Festival reaction to “The Debut” (December 11), we talked in a hotel meeting room. The A24 crowdpleaser has been wowing audiences and critics since Telluride.

Jesse Eisenberg has done it again. His follow-up to “A Real Pain,” which won Kieran Culkin the Supporting Actor Oscar, could score Best Actress for Moore. The musical comedy has earned Moore raves on the festival circuit for her role as a sad suburban homemaker turned anxious aspiring actress in a New Jersey community theater. A sixth Oscar nomination is inevitable, and possibly a second Oscar win after “Still Alice” in 2015. It’s hard to believe she launched her career in 1988 as a regular on soap opera “As the World Turns.” Related Stories Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It? From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race

Moore is the current Best Actress frontrunner, even though she has won before. Sometimes nabbing an Oscar is a disadvantage in the Oscar race. But not if the performance is undeniable: Katharine Hepburn holds the record with four, while nipping at her heels are three-time winners Meryl Streep, Frances McDormand, Jack Nicholson, and Sean Penn.

Eisenberg wrote a rich character for Moore, knowing what the veteran actress could do with the childlike housewife Mona who, in order to learn how to act, must find herself. The director and actress had worked together on “When You Finish Saving the World” (2022). “[‘The Debut‘] is about this woman who has been chewed up but not spit out,” said Eisenberg, quoting Mona’s signature song. “It’s my point of view through somebody I consider a muse. I was writing something about myself as a seven-year-old in 1990, but I couldn’t picture anybody else except her doing it.”

It helped that Moore had told Eisenberg exactly what she was looking for. “I said I had just done ‘Dear Evan Hansen,’ and I loved singing, and I would love to have another opportunity,” she said. “I told him that I would love to do more comedy, and I didn’t want to play some suffering mom.”

Eisenberg put all of this in the screenplay, “but in the most surprising and inventive way,” she said. “He’s such a specific writer. He’s so incredibly empathetic. He has a compassionate worldview. He understands creativity. All of that stuff went into this wonderful and delightful story. It’s joyful and life-affirming too.”

Moore didn’t know she was playing a seven-year-old version of Eisenberg until he started telling that to the press. “Then he was like, ‘This is my experience of being a kid and going to community theater.’ But I could sense that there was a personal point of view in it. I very much felt with Mona that she was on a subjective journey, and that he was inside of that. With Mona, I always knew he was looking through her.”

“The Debut” is told from her point of view, as she tries to talk the overbearing local community theater director Jerry (Paul Giamatti) into hiring her, an untrained actress. He does it because he has no one else. But first, he must teach her how to act.

Mona dresses like a schoolgirl, with skirts, blouses, cardigan sweaters. “She’s so contained, and the way she learns is so literal,” said Moore, “the way a baby learns, like, you make a face at a baby, the baby makes a face back, but they don’t have intention behind it. But they’re learning things in an exterior way, and then they match it with feeling later on. So everything she’s doing is a childlike way of learning.”

Mona goes from an invisible nonentity in her own home to someone who demands attention. “She’s a kid who has found friends for the first time,” said Eisenberg. “She’s the girl who transferred to the right school at seven years old, and then the first rehearsal happens, and she is told she is terrible, and she has no idea why. And it’s the girl who transferred to the right school and gets an F on the very first test, and then the rest of the semester is panicking, and all she’s seeing is everybody else get A’s, and she still has the F, and she doesn’t know what to do. And then the teacher pulls her aside and says, ‘You either show up, or you are out on your ass.’ And something switches in her, and she makes the decision: ‘I am going to show up.’ And she begins to turn into a monster.”

The theater troupe embraces Mona as she unfolds like a flower. “We’ve been like those theater kids cracking corny jokes and finding community,” said Moore. “It’s all done with so much affection. Jesse looks at that world with not a hint of malice.”

Giamatti’s director relentlessly pushes the newbie through her paces until they have a powerful confrontation on the empty stage where he forces her to break down. Eisenberg reduced the actors’ anxiety by placing the eight-page showstopper in the middle of the shoot: not the beginning, and not the end. On the first day he went over to Moore’s apartment to talk about the movie. He said, “I really don’t want you to worry about that scene. I don’t want you to worry about memorizing that because I know that as an actor, I would I lose my mind. I would just be drilling it all the time, and I wouldn’t be able to concentrate. We’re going to have a teleprompter on that day. So don’t worry about it.”

So Moore worked on it normally, she said, “like I worked on everything else in the movie. So when we got to it, I knew it. I didn’t need a teleprompter. He knew instinctively as a director and an actor that what scares us sometimes is just a volume of language. He didn’t want to freeze me up. And having a partner like Paul who was so awake and aware and generous made it a pleasure. We were enjoying it when we did shoot it.”

Moore and Giamatti had never worked together before. She once introduced herself to him in a bookstore in Montauk. “He was very shy,” she said. “He is the greatest scene partner. I didn’t expect him to be so generous. He’s so funny, and he’s so dear. He’s present, incredibly modest, and as a partner, so available. Paul and I would work on it occasionally. When we were doing that scene, the rhythm was so important in it. You throw something, he hits it right back. It was our sense together of keeping it aloft, keeping it moving, keeping the river flowing. It felt electric with the two of us.”

The big blowout happens early in the story. “In a lot of movies, that kind of set piece would happen later,” said Moore. “Instead, it’s like a discovery place. It’s where she starts to begin to unlock herself emotionally, but she doesn’t learn from it. She comes in the next day, and starts to rehearse. And her belief is that acting is size, that it’s just huge, right? That’s when she starts yelling. She thinks it’s about being loud, which then allows her to go on the next journey with Jerry, where he says, ‘Let’s talk about feeling and reality and intention.’ So she’s slowly putting these pieces together. But that’s the first moment where she attaches something outside of herself to her own emotion.”

The whole shoot was fast, as Eisenberg didn’t have time to muck about and often shot just one take of a scene. “She and Paul Giamatti are so good on take one,” said Eisenberg. “It’s embarrassing. This is a small budget movie. The first two days of our schedule, we filmed in one day. The first two days, which were big ensemble musical numbers, we filmed in one day because we were prepared as a crew, but the actors were perfect on take one.”

Moore didn’t feel rushed. “It doesn’t feel, working with Jesse, like you’re moving too fast,” she said. “Working in independent film, you’re always moving quickly because you need to. You don’t have the time. You don’t have the money. So you want to move through things quickly. But I never felt rushed with him. I never I never felt like I was leaving something, that I didn’t get to complete something.”

The challenge for Moore, as it is for every actor shooting out of order, was making her character changes seamless. Eisenberg started with the theater scenes, then shot her family, and then jumped into Mona’s increasing weirdness. “The hardest thing always is making sure that you’ve pitched things correctly,” Moore said. “You want to make sure that you’ve managed to match it to another scene. So it was always hard to figure out. That’s our job.”

Eisenberg wanted Mona to move from looking quite childlike in the beginning, and swiftly move through her evolving transformations. Moore had fun with the costumes, figuring out the crazy wigs, makeup, and outfits in the second half. “Jesse had written that Mona electrocutes herself and destroys her hair, and that she was going to get her hair cut,” said Moore, “but he hadn’t written in a color change. We were messing around with it and trying to figure out what to do with hair and makeup and wardrobe and we had this idea that by having her dye her hair dark and chop it off, I wanted to homage the great ladies of musical theater, Liza Minnelli and Chita Rivera and Patti LuPone. It’s a wonderful Easter egg for that character.”

Making everything easier for Moore was actor-turned-director Eisenberg, who’d tell her when to ‘raise the stakes’ or ‘go hotter.’ “He’s maybe the most collaborative person I’ve ever worked with my entire life,” said Moore. “He listens to everyone. He asks people for opinions. He’ll ask people for notes, in a way that I would be like, ‘you don’t have to do that. This is your movie. It’s your creation.’ But he does collate opinion in a way. He’s fascinating in his generosity.”

Needless to say, singing her centerpiece song (“This City May Have Chewed Me Up (But It Hasn’t Spit Me Out”) was nervous-making, given that Moore was surrounded by Broadway super-belters like Tony winners Danny Burstein and Bonnie Tillman. “These people have the voices of angels,” said Moore. “When I did sing that song for the first time, and they’re all sitting there watching me, I think they did feel worried for me because they have so much ease. The song that she sings is so beautiful. In the singing of the song, she’s attaching her own emotional experience suddenly to the song. She understands the song in the moment she’s singing that. Somehow she wants more, and she knows that this is an avenue for her to find that. And so it’s a journey back to herself: finding that creativity and connection and community brings her to an essential sense of self.”

If degree of difficulty counts with Oscar voters, Moore may have that advantage.

#3531. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

#3530. Ole Miss Racist Video: ACLU of Mississippi Investigating Complaints

The fallout from the racist video involving University of Mississippi students is growing ... with the ACLU of Mississippi now reviewing complaints about the disturbing incident.

Candi Richardson, Director of Communications & Community Relations for the ACLU of Mississippi, tells TMZ ... "We have received complaints about this incident and are looking into them, as we do with all such complaints."

Richardson also pointed to federal civil rights protections that require schools to take action when racial harassment creates a hostile environment for students.

She noted schools could violate federal law if they are aware of racial harassment and fail to take appropriate steps to stop it.

Richardson also pointed to Ole Miss' own policies against racial discrimination, saying the incident could potentially violate those rules.

However, the ACLU has not determined whether any laws were violated.

As we previously reported, three white female students were captured on Ring camera walking past an apartment shared by three black students Friday.

Two of the women appeared to make monkey noises and gestures toward the apartment door, while the third walked by without participating.

One of the residents, Jakiyra Metcalf, posted the footage on TikTok and later claimed the women were her upstairs neighbors.

Ole Miss officials have condemned the behavior and confirmed the university is investigating the incident. The school says it has also reached out to the students targeted in the video to offer support.

#3529. Original Harry Potter Star Officially Confirms Franchise Return Ahead of HBO Series

The release of HBO's Harry Potter is just a few weeks away at this point, and it feels like the entire world is watching and waiting to rejoin the Wizarding World. However, there are a select few who have already been there, and when given the opportunity to head back to Hogwarts, it seems like they just couldn't say no.

Speaking exclusively with Collider's Steve Weintraub while promoting his upcoming movie Ebenezer, Rupert Grint revealed that his return as Ron Weasley in Broadway's Harry Potter and the Cursed Child will probably be the last time he plays the character. The actor is scheduled to begin his limited engagement at New York's Lyric Theatre on February 2, 2027. Grint explained that, after just over 15 years away from the role, it felt like the right time because, not only does he now have a family of his own, but he's also reached roughly the same age as Ron in the stage production. Grint told Collider:

"It's funny, kind of, it's interesting. Kind of going back, I think I spent so much time after finishing Potter moving away from it and doing other things which I really enjoy doing. But I think now it's a very different Ron in a very different context, and weirdly, it's lined up that I'm kind of the exact age of the character in that story. So it just felt like a good time, and I love New York and being on stage. It's been a while since I've done that, and it's a very important thing to me. It was my childhood, and I have a very strong connection to that character and that world. And I think I'm not going to get many other opportunities to play him again. It probably is my last, and I think it'll be fun."

Grint previously made his Broadway debut in It's Only a Play in 2014, but returning to the stage as a character he's known for most of his life presents an entirely different challenge, and he admitted that he couldn't resist the challenge, while confessing the nostalgia had been a delight. "Well, yeah. I mean, it's very nostalgic," said Grint. "Even for me, it's fun to kind of go back and get back into that world. It's been a while." Of course, Weintraub couldn't resist asking the question that just about every Harry Potter fan will be thinking: could Grint persuade Radcliffe and Watson to join him on Broadway for a reunion?

"It would be fun. I don't know. I mean, it's obviously different for everyone. It was an intense kind of time. When we finished, I really enjoyed stepping away and not really even thinking about it. Because it was such an intense... I mean, it was enjoyable, and they looked after us. But it was a big part of us. So yeah, maybe. I don't know. It'd be fun."

Before Grint returns to Hogwarts, audiences will get to see him in Ebenezer, a new adaptation of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol starring Johnny Depp (Pirates of the Caribbean) as Ebenezer Scrooge, and directed by Ti West. Grint plays Bob Cratchit, the father of Tiny Tim. The tale has been adapted many times for the screen. It's a thrilling ghost story set in Dickens’ London that follows one man’s supernatural journey to face his past, present, and future — and his fight for a second chance.

In addition to Grint, the film stars Andrea Riseborough (To Leslie) as the Ghost of Christmas Past, Sam Claflin (The Hunger Games) as Fred, Daisy Ridley (Star Wars: The Force Awakens) as Clara, Arthur Conti (Beetlejuice Beetlejuice) as Young Ebenezer, Ellie Bamber (Willow) as Belle, Tramell Tillman (Severance) as the Ghost of Christmas Present, and Ian McKellen (The Lord of the Rings) as Jacob Marley. The screenplay comes from Nathaniel Halpern, with Emma Watts producing. Ebenezer opens in theaters on November 13, 2026.

Rupert Grint begins his limited Broadway engagement as Ron Weasley in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child on February 2, 2027, with performances scheduled through May 30. #3528. King Ghidorah Is Ready for Its Close-Up: How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Cracked the Legendary Monster’s Next Evolution

“Godzilla Minus Zero” builds on the strong visual foundation — and/or the rubble of Tokyo’s Ginza district — that director Takashi Yamazaki pounded into his previous film, “Godzilla Minus One.” Like that first film, “Minus Zero” is in conversation with the big ideas and cultural/emotional resonances behind Toho’s giant monsters, and it’s attuned to the beloved visual details of the franchise, going all the way back to the original “Godzilla” and the Shōwa era.

But historically, for all kinds of budgetary and technological reasons, King Ghidorah is usually not ready for his close-up.

The amount of time that “Godzilla Minus Zero” spends with its three-headed mutant space dragon on the ground is a notable departure from how Ghidorah is most often depicted: in flight, or towering far above Godzilla. Even in closer shots in a CGI-rich film like “Godzilla: King of the Monsters,” when all three heads get ready to chomp up a puny human or 10, the emphasis is on Ghidorah’s scale. Three heads are more terrifying than one. Related Stories Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It? From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race

But “Godzilla Minus Zero” spends a lot of time with just one head, or focused on just one head, and its Ghidorah is as scary on the ground as it is in the air, and this is in part due to the particular design experience that director Yamazaki and his team brought to the world’s deadliest gold dragon. Yamazaki was tapped to design “Godzilla the Ride” at Seibuen Amusement Park (its full name is Godzilla the Ride: Giant Monsters Ultimate Battle) in 2021 and therefore had to figure out a version of Ghidorah that would work from the other side of a safety rail.

Yamazaki and animation studio Shirogumi worked on a monster concept that would feel, according to “Minus One” and “Minus Zero” producer Kazuaki Kishida, “as though the audience was under attack by Ghidorah itself. So it had to be very scary and very close-up,” Kishida told IndieWire. “[In the ride,] we see Ghidorah basically crawling on the ground with its neck, because it has a very long neck, and then really going after the audience. To bring King Ghidorah very close to humans and bring the eyeline closer was a huge core concept for this. So there was a lot of research that had gone into the ride that we were able to apply to ‘Godzilla Minus Zero.'”

The film uses Ghidorah’s eyeline to great effect. One of the most unnerving moments in its initial attack on Matsumoto City, as scientists Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka) and Akira Hagiwara (Ko Maehara) scramble to both document the new monster on the block and survive the utter destruction of whole city blocks, is a moment of getting really, uncomfortably close to Ghidorah’s eye.

That forced proximity to Ghidorah makes all the spectacular space-dragon stuff it can do even more effective, though these effects are also as grounded in the natural and the tangible as much as possible. For Ghidorah’s destructive beam, for instance, visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima did more research than even he thought he could do on how lightning visualizes itself.

“Everyone sort of recognized the string of light, that line of light. But if you look at lightning in slow motion, it leaves a line of something that lingers — this is apparently just water vaporizing instantly and turning into plasma,” Nojima told IndieWire. “I don’t fully know the science behind it, but there’s a visual effect that lightning leaves behind. So for Ghidorah’s destruction beam, I wanted to emphasize that element of it. I scatter particles around, kind of blur the imagery, and then let it linger longer than it normally would.”

Of course, whenever the destruction beam hits something, Nojima and the VFX team got to build the explosion. But it’s that visual sense of Ghidorah’s power lingering, and of getting too close to where Ghidorah can see you, that makes this version of the monster feel so dangerous.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now playing in theaters.

#3527. Exclusive Halo Excerpt Brings The Master Chief's First Meeting With Cortana To Life

Halo has always been far more than just a massive game franchise. While I was hooked with the games from the start—Halo literally led to my picking up the Xbox back in 2001—I was slow to realize there were tie-in novels. But Eric Nylund's excellent book The Fall of Reach was published in October that year, exploring the Master Chief's history and helping to flesh out his world. It became the foundation of a transmedia franchise that continues to this day. That book even (loosely) influenced the sadly-canceled Halo TV series.

Now, in celebration of Halo's 25th anniversary, Simon & Schuster is re-releasing The Fall of Reach in a full-cast audiodrama that reunites Steve Downes as the Master Chief and Jen Taylor as Dr. Halsey and Cortana. It's now available from retailers like Amazon, or directly from Simon & Schuster. ScreenRant is proud to reveal an exclusive excerpt, the first ever meeting between the Master Chief and Cortana, alongside an exclusive interview with Steve Downes himself.

Copyright © 2001 by Microsoft Corporation. Audio excerpt courtesy of Simon & Schuster Audio from the audiobook HALO: THE FALL OF REACH (Full-Cast Dramatized Adaptation) by Eric Nylund, read by Steve Downes, Jen Taylor, and Tim Dadabo, published by Simon & Schuster Audio, a Division of Simon & Schuster, Inc. Used with permission from Simon & Schuster, LLC.

ScreenRant: How has the role of the Master Chief evolved and changed for you?

To say it's been one helluva ride for 25 years would be an understatement. Playing the Chief has changed my life exponentially. One of the joys of being involved with this character is that over time, I've watched Spartan 117 evolve in the eyes of the fans. When we started in 2001, the role of the Master Chief was relatively one dimensional. Mostly he barked at Cortana and smashed aliens! The fans saw something deeper. Something aspirational and wanted more.

ScreenRant: Which is your favorite Halo story?

It has always been The Fall of Reach. I read it after recording "Combat Evolved" and in addition to being a great read, it was incredibly informative for me as an actor. It fleshed out the character in so many ways, and changed how I approached all future recording sessions for later games. I had such a deeper understanding of not only who the Chief was, but of the entire Halo universe.

ScreenRant: How different an experience was it recording for an audiobook compared to a game?

The word that comes to mind is liberating. I had recorded a chapter or two of other Halo books in the past that served as promotional vehicles. My first real chance to sink my teeth into recording the Chief for an audio book was for Kelly Gay's Halo: Edge of Dawn in 2025. That story was a continuation of Halo: Infinite;. It was great to expand that story. Not long after, when word came down about an enhanced audio version of The Fall of Reach, complete with original cast members, music and sound effects, I was over the moon. We had recently completed work on re-recording the first game, now called Campaign Evolved;. So in a way, doing The Fall of Reach completed the circle of the origin story of the Master Chief and Halo in general, with the hindsight of 25 years.

ScreenRant: What do you think The Fall of Reach adds to in terms of understanding the Master Chief?

How John became Spartan 117 is to me the most illuminating. My initial inspiration in finding a voice for the Master Chief was Clint Eastwood's Man with No Name protagonist in Sergi Leone's Spaghetti westerns "Fistfull of Dollars", "For a Few Dollars More", and "The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly;" But in those films, it was never made clear why Clint's character was the way he was. In The Fall of Reach, we begin to understand what shaped John. We learn at the very least that his story is more complicated than it appears at first blush.

ScreenRant: What was your favorite part of The Fall of Reach?

First of all, I love the overall story arc that paints the UNSC as not necessarily "straight shooters" metaphorically speaking. After all, the Spartan program was originally developed to put down rebellions led by fellow human beings. To subjugate, and if necessary, kill their own species. What were they rebelling against and why? That story takes a back seat once the Covenant arrives, but it already creates the beginning of a moral conflict in John, even as a teenager. I'm also fascinated by the story arc of Jacob Keyes.

ScreenRant: The Fall of Reach had a massive influence on the Halo TV show. What did you think of that adaptation, and what would you hope to see for any future revivals?

In my opinion, Reach should have been much more of an influence on the Paramount series. It was practically nonexistent in season one and only began to reveal itself somewhat in the second half of the second season. The show runners admitted that they wanted to develop a separate timeline for Halo, apart from the games and the books. Why? Couldn't find enough material?

I thought the acting and the visuals were great, but a real opportunity was missed to create a top flight log running TV series that would appeal to hard core fans as well as viewers who were not gamers.

You can buy Halo: The Fall of Reach now from retailers like Amazon, or directly from Simon & Schuster.

#3525. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Danny Boyle‘s Netflix thriller dramatizes the beginnings of Rupert Murdoch’s empire, following the future mogul when he was just a young Australian newspaper man. When he launched The Sun alongside former business partner Larry Lamb in 1969, the two men effectively created the modern tabloid and figured out that audiences were hungry for a lot more than just truth. Guy Pearce stars as Murdoch alongside Jack O’Connell as Lamb, with James Graham handling the writing duties on the adaption of his hit West End and Broadway play.

“Ink” was the opening film for the 2026 Venice International Film Festival, where critics praised its entertainment value while acknowledging that it treads some familiar territory.

“That ‘Ink’ begins as a story of Larry Lamb and Rupert Murdoch launching the tabloid newspaper The Sun in 1969 and ends with a montage including Trump and Elon Musk tells you all you need to know about Danny Boyle’s new film: This is a vividly directed if overcooked political parable about How We Got Here Now,” IndieWire’s Ryan Lattanzio wrote in his review. “If you’ve seen ‘Nightcrawler’ or ‘Network,’ there’s nothing new to take away about the if-it-bleeds-it-leads newsroom mentality, but Jack O’Connell (who also starred in Boyle’s ’28 Years Later’) is terrific as an editor obsessively addicted to winning — and willing to mow down lives in the process.”

The original “Ink” play premiered on the West End in 2017, with a Broadway run following in 2019. Boyle spent years trying to make a movie out of the material, and recalled the lengthy process of convincing actors to remain on board during an interview with IndieWire at the 2026 Telluride Film Festival.

“I begged Guy to hang on,” Boyle said. “I apologized to Guy because it wasn’t like I’d offered it to him, but I’d said ‘I want you,’ and bless him he hung in there for us.
