#3523. This New Chrome AI Feature Reads Your Gmail to Make Filling Out Web Forms Easier

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3521. ABC Is Failing ‘High Potential’ and ‘The Rookie’ Once Again

ABC's fall procedural lineup has just two weeks left until it airs its mid-season finales and goes on hiatus for the winter, but the premiere dates for the spring lineup have only just been announced. Like 9-1-1, 9-1-1: Nashville, Grey's Anatomy, and R.J. Decker, ABC's lineup of procedurals premiering their new seasons this January all concluded their most recent seasons last spring. Whereas fans of the aforementioned shows only had to wait for the length of the standard summer hiatus, though, fans of the second group of shows will have had to wait up to nine months by the time they return.

For a show like Will Trent, which has been on this timeline since its debut, this is to be expected. The Rookie and High Potential, on the other hand, initially got to air in both the fall and the spring, and have since been relegated to just the latter. For two of ABC's most popular shows, it's already disappointing that they only get to air for a few months of the year. Now, though, there are just under two months until these shows return the first full week of January, and it's frustrating that their return dates have not been announced until last week.

The Rookie has been on the spring release schedule for three seasons now, but High Potential has only just been moved to this lineup. It's a particularly jarring choice for High Potential, considering the series is only on its third season, and the show's second season had monumental records of success. Just as the series was really gaining momentum, it was put on break for nine months, leaving fans to speculate on their own about the fallout of the Season 2 finale's intense cliffhanger ending. Fans of The Rookie, meanwhile, may be used to this by now, but it is still frustrating to watch a beloved Network TV show only air for about a third of the year, then go on break for the rest of it.

The Rookie started as a show about a man starting over at forty-five and turned into a proper ensemble drama somewhere around season three. Here is which of them you are, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

You started late and you are not embarrassed about it. Nolan walks into the academy at forty-five surrounded by people half his age, and the show is honest that this is both his biggest disadvantage and the only reason he is any good at the job.

You are better at this than people expect and you intend to keep proving it. Chen goes from rookie to the best undercover officer in the division, which works because she is genuinely good at becoming somebody else and genuinely bad at pretending she does not care.

You are hard on people because you have decided that is what caring looks like. Bradford is introduced as the worst training officer in the building and slowly revealed as the one who takes the job most seriously, which are the same fact seen from two angles.

You said what you wanted and then you went and got it. Lopez wanted detective from the first episode, said so out loud, and got there by being better at the work than the people who were quieter about wanting it.

There are a lot of benefits to being a fan of a Network TV show, from getting to watch the episodes live alongside other fans to getting to speculate each week about what will happen next. The best part, though, is loving a show with a predictable release schedule. When series then start changing their release schedule to only air for half the time, it is incredibly disappointing to fans. It means potentially fewer episodes for the new season, as well as a much longer wait in between seasons, dampening some of the excitement and anticipation earned by the finales of the previous seasons.

In a perfect world, ABC would move High Potential and The Rookie back to its fall release schedule, but as it stands, the network just needs to do better by the procedurals in its spring lineup. Both of these shows excellently set up suspense ahead of their new seasons by ending their most recent ones with massive cliffhangers after two explosive episodes. For The Rookie, the fan-favorite pairing of Lucy Chen (Melissa O'Neil) and Tim Bradford (Eric Winter) finally got engaged in a beautiful beach proposal, only to both get abducted seconds later. High Potential, on the other hand, introduced another new twist in the ongoing mystery of what happened to Roman Sinquerra. After Captain Nick Wagner (Steve Howey) went to a meetup to get more information on this mystery, Morgan Gillory (Kaitlin Olson) found him shot and left for dead, leaving Wagner's fate up in the air over the hiatus.

When both of these series concluded their most recent seasons, fans were left champing at the bit to find out what happens next. While there are still devoted fans excited for these series to return, there has no doubt been a loss of momentum for both of these series after their unusually long break. Most fans will likely have to do a refresher on the events of the previous seasons to remember the main events ahead of their returns, and while that's become standard for shows on streaming now, this is still atypical of Network TV shows. ABC needs to do better with the shows in its spring lineup, and to stop moving shows to mid-season after they've previously been airing for the entire season.

High Potential returns to ABC on Tuesday, January 5, at 9:00 P.M. EST. The Rookie returns to ABC the following night, on Wednesday, January 6, at 9:00 P.M. EST.

#3520. Sydney Sweeney's Star Wars Meets Transformers Space Opera Is 1 Of The Biggest Netflix Events Of The Decade

Netflix may be about to see its biggest movie ever, thanks to Sydney Sweeney. Not even very long ago, the idea of streaming movies was something that often attracted scorn. They were mostly considered rarities and oddities, initially dumped on platforms because they couldn't find a theatrical home or because of logistical issues like the COVID pandemic. But since Netflix heralded the age of the mega streamer, major blockbusters arriving as originals on streaming have become a fairly standard event.

Netflix already has a track record for expensive blockbusters, thanks to the likes of Red Notice, The Grey Man, and the Russos' painfully underrated and overhated The Electric State. And while they weren't exactly universally loved, in any other year, those expensive tent poles would have been summer or winter blockbusters released in theaters first. Basically, what was once seen as a secondary option is now completely transformed.

Looking ahead to the streamers' slate in 2027 and beyond, there are already some very high-profile projects to come, including, of course, Greta Gerwig's hotly-anticipated Chronicles of Narnia reboot. Alongside that potential fantasy titan, one upcoming project could actually eclipse everything that Netflix has done in the past 10 years. At a so-far unconfirmed point next year, Legendary Entertainment and Netflix will release the first live-action adaptation of Mobile Suit Gundam, and it could change everything. In short, the upcoming Gundam movie is a declaration of intent to own the high-spectacle sci-fi space opera genre.

With rising star Sydney Sweeney leading the charge and a legendary IP as the foundation, the Gundam movie has everything it needs to be Netflix's biggest flagship property. It promises high-stakes action, intergalactic politics, and raw star power that has previously driven the likes of Transformers and Star Wars. If it's not one of the biggest streaming events of the decade, something will have gone dramatically wrong.

Sweeney spent the past few years masterminding one of the most impressive career rises in recent Hollywood history without moving away from her R-rated and dark thriller roots. After establishing herself in intense character dramas like Euphoria and The White Lotus on the small screen, she reinforced her reputation with similar choices in adult-oriented thrillers and genre movies. While her sidestep into comic book cinema with the frankly awful Madame Web failed critically and financially, Sweeney clearly hasn't let that studio setback derail her appetite for bigger-scale projects, as well as a slate of interesting genre movies and thrillers.

She's also making her first strides into the sci-fi genre, as well as Gundam. Her upcoming schedule also includes Edgar Wright's reimagining of Barbarella and Jon M. Chu's adaptation of Split Fiction, meaning she could, over the next couple of years, carve out a distinct footprint in sci-fi, just as she has in other genres.

Taking the lead in Netflix's live-action Gundam is the biggest and most ambitious project on her entire slate, and sharing the screen with giant mechanical suits and interplanetary warfare means her on-screen presence and charisma will be tested in very new ways. If those three movies land the way they promise to, Sweeney will come out the other side as one of the more interesting sci-fi stars of this generation. If her role in Gundam can successfully bridge the gap between human drama and massive world-building and mech wars, she will step into a whole new world of blockbuster potential.

Bringing such a deep franchise into live-action will require somebody capable of handling scale and scope, and who also understands the source material. That responsibility falls to Gundam director Jim Mickle, who previously worked on Netflix's excellent Sweet Tooth, which was a completely different prospect, but which nailed the emotional heart of the source material.

And he won't be at the top table, of course, Gundam will be co-produced by Legendary Pictures and Bandai Namco Filmworks, with veteran franchise producers Makoto Asanuma and Neohero Ogata also involved. Their inclusion means the franchise is in good hands, and the movie should respect the deep lore that fans have loved for decades.

Production has already kicked off in Queensland, Australia, where Sweeney is joined by an impressive ensemble cast led by co-star Noah Centineo and including Jason Isaacs, Michael Mando, Shiole Kutsuna, Nontananzi, and Ida Brook, among others. Character names are so far locked away in the vault, but we know that the story centers on an epic rivalry between pilots trapped in a brutal, decades-long space conflict. We also know, because this is Mobile Suit Gundam, that there will be giant mechs involved, which is a big selling point.

By focusing on the pilot rivalry, set against a backdrop of military tension and space battles, the movie is clearly aiming to capture the grit of the classic anime while also leveraging Netflix's ample purse for big visual effects. Quite how much we'll get to see of mech-on-mech violence in the final project remains to be seen, but it surely has to be a major part of the story.

When Netflix released the first original movie, Beasts of No Nation in 2007, the idea of them making such a huge sci-fi space opera may have seemed very odd, but the sheer commercial potential of Gundam simply cannot be overstated here. Created by Yoshiyuki Tomino and Hajime Yatate, Mobile Suit Gundam is one of the most profitable and influential media empires on the planet. In 2025, Bandai Namco financial reports revealed that Gundam had actually grown to outperform anime heavyweights like Dragon Ball and One Piece, and the fact that it's taken so long for a live-action adaptation from Hollywood is a bit of a head-scratcher.

The revenue model is driven by multi-platform expansions, and Gundam arrives on Netflix with an already proven audience who are desperate for more. Mobile Suit Gundam literally invented the real-robot anime subgenre, shifting away from superheroic machines and introducing a more grounded military hardware focus, with more complex political narratives that make parallels with Star Wars feel very irresistible.

In many ways, Gundam arrives as Netflix's answer to Star Wars, as well as, of course, as representing its rival to the massively successful Transformers movie franchise. The combination of grand intergalactic conflict and political intrigue with personal stakes means we could get the ideal marriage of the tragic opera of Star Wars and the high-energy metal-on-metal chaos of Transformers. The fact that Hollywood is still racing to provide enough content to satisfy both of those audiences on an almost yearly basis suggests that Gundam offering a fresh alternative could give Netflix reach even further than the established franchise's audience.

When you combine a record-breaking global IP with Sydney Sweeney's rising star, a great ensemble cast, and Netflix's global distribution power, the sky for Gundam really is the limit. The movie possesses everything it could possibly need to become the platform's biggest-ever release, and if the quality matches the potential, Netflix could have a massive new sci-fi universe on its hands to expand even further.

#3517. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

#3512. ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Officially Delivers Record-Breaking Box Office Debut

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

Two overseas titles secured spots on the top-five list of the domestic box office this weekend, with Godzilla Minus Zero claiming the number-one spot and Ramayana: Rise of a Legend finishing fifth. While the top-five list was bookended by the two international movies, three vastly different homegrown titles took the remaining three spots. Among them were two new releases, the animated offering The Cat in the Hat, and the period musical Drummer Boy.

Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the most expensive Indian film of all time, with a reported production budget of approximately $200 million. The movie is the first part of a planned duology, with the second installment currently slated for a 2028 release. A grand international publicity tour was mounted to promote the mythological epic, necessitated by its massive production cost. As a rule of thumb, a film this size needs to gross twice its reported budget to break even. Ramayana got off to a lukewarm start, with $55 million globally and around $12 million domestically this past weekend.

Godzilla Minus Zero, on the other hand, had built-in buzz thanks to the positive word-of-mouth earned by its predecessor, Godzilla Minus One. Released in 2023, the previous installment grossed more than $110 million worldwide against a reported budget of $10 million. The movie broke box-office records for international titles in North America, having grossed more than $55 million in its theatrical run. Godzilla Minus One rode a wave of positive buzz to win the Best Visual Effects Oscar, beating out mega-budget behemoths.

The 2023 film was set in post-war Japan, serving as an allegory for the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Many viewed it as a companion piece to Christopher Nolan's biographical thriller Oppenheimer, which was released the same year. Like Nolan's film, Godzilla Minus One was critically acclaimed. It now holds a near-perfect 99% score on Rotten Tomatoes.

Godzilla Minus Zero has also received positive reviews. The film is currently sitting at a "Certified Fresh" 90% critics score and a "Verified Hot" 96% audience score on the aggregator website, where the consensus reads, "Keeping its epic action rooted in human interest, Godzilla Minus Zero solidifies director Takashi Yamazaki's take on the King of Monsters as one of the mightiest yet by upping the ante without losing sight of its lovable characters." Buoyed by positive reviews, the film grossed nearly $32 million in its domestic debut, nearly tripling the $11 million opening-weekend haul of its predecessor.

This is also the biggest debut for an international live-action movie. Godzilla Minus Zero's global opening stood at $63 million against a reported budget of $15 million. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3511. Star Trek In 2027 Will Get Its Biggest Boost In A Decade Thanks To Skydance (No, Really)

Skydance merging Paramount+ and HBO Max will be good news for existing Star Trek content and potentially gives Gene Roddenberry's 60-year-old franchise its biggest boost in the decade since Star Trek: Discovery premiered. Now, it's understandable if Trekkers are skeptical. Read any room Star Trek fans occupy, and there's a general uneasiness, at the least, about Star Trek's future under Skydance.

After all, it was the looming purchase of Paramount Global by Skydance back in 2023 that sparked the gradual cancellation of every Star Trek TV series on Paramount+ executive produced by Alex Kurtzman. While other factors contributed as well to Star Trek's diminishment, such as the cost of Kurtzman's Star Trek shows relative to their streaming numbers, Star Trek's new owners and their still undefined new direction for the venerable franchise led to the slate being wiped clean of original Star Trek shows on Paramount+.

In the eyes of fans, Star Trek is "going away" or is "over" after 2027, when Star Trek: Starfleet Academy and Star Trek: Strange New Worlds premiere their final seasons, with no new Star Trek in production. The doomsaying also has to do with fans' distrust of Skydance CEO David Ellison's right-leaning politics, which Trekkers fear will overrule the progressive vision Gene Roddenberry's Star Trek is built upon.

Whatever happens to Star Trek in terms of creative after 2027, something good will come out of Skydance's plans for HBO Max and Paramount+.

Skydance will bundle Paramount+ and HBO Max in early 2027, offering consumers both streamers for one price. Ellison called the bundle “our first step towards unifying the two services," in a conference call to Wall Street. Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ will take time, Ellison admits, but the ultimate goal is for one streaming service to host franchises like Game of Thrones, DC, Harry Potter, Landman, Dutton Ranch... and Star Trek.

The future of Star Trek is of paramount concern to fans. Roddenberry Entertainment COO Trevor Roth speaks to what's next for the franchise.

Star Trek's greatest heights in terms of viewership and pop culture relevance were in the 1990s, when audiences could visit the final frontier on free TV in syndication or on UPN. For well over the last decade, Star Trek has been trapped behind streaming paywalls, although Pluto TV offers classic Star Trek series and occasional episodes of Paramount+'s Star Trek shows to stream for free. With Paramount+ and HBO Max bundled en route to full integration, Star Trek has a chance to grow its audience in ways it couldn't before.

New and classic Star Trek series being offered alongside HBO's most prestigious series like The Pitt, House of the Dragon, and The White Lotus also raises the franchise's profile. Despite the high quality of Alex Kurtzman's series in terms of production values and visual effects, and casting Oscar-caliber A-list stars like Holly Hunter, Paul Giamatti, and Michelle Yeoh, Star Trek is still seen as a niche sci-fi franchise that has trouble enticing general audiences.

Simply making Star Trek available to HBO Max's audience makes it easier and more enticing to sample the final frontier and fall in love with Star Trek's rich universe of unforgettable characters and thought-provoking stories. Being exposed to HBO Max's viewers is potentially the biggest boost existing Star Trek will get to create new fans.

Skydance considers Star Trek a crown jewel IP, although the studio's top focus seems to be relaunching the Star Trek movie franchise before creating more TV shows. It's also likely that a new executive producer will replace Alex Kurtzman to oversee Star Trek in line with Skydance's vision for the franchise. How fans will feel about Skydance's Star Trek remains to be seen. Still, many are bracing for the worst.

Looking Star Trek pre- and post-Skydance, even if audiences reject the next iteration of the final frontier, the greater availability of 1966-2027 Star Trek will allow viewers to flock to the old shows and movies as part of their subscription to whatever the combined HBO Max and Paramount+ streamer will be called.

Paramount+ and HBO Max merging is beneficial to the Star Trek TV shows and movies fans already know and love. If the audience for Star Trek can grow with Skydance's bundle becoming a unified streaming service, more people discovering Captain Kirk, Captain Picard, Mr. Spock, Captain Pike, Data, Saru, and Captain Burnham is a good thing.

Star Trek TV series and feature films (except Star Trek: Prodigy) are streaming on Paramount+

#3510. Report: Apple and Samsung outperform rivals as smartphone chip shipments tumble 21%

According to Counterpoint Research, Apple and Samsung were the only major smartphone chip vendors to gain market share in Q3 2026, as global shipments declined 21% year-over-year. Here are the details.

At this point, most 9to5Mac readers are probably familiar with the challenges that smartphone vendors have been facing due to rising memory costs, and how Apple has managed to weather the impact better than many of its competitors.

Over the past few months, many reports have noted that while most smartphone vendors raised prices more than once throughout the year, Apple held off on increasing iPhone prices until September, with the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series.

Those same reports have been showing the iPhone outperforming the broader market in smartphone, even as the industry experiences a sharp downturn.

That said, Counterpoint Research recently published a report (via MacMagazine) examining how rising memory costs and slowing smartphone demand have affected the global smartphone chip market.

According to the report, Apple remained in third place among smartphone chip vendors in the third quarter, with its market share increasing from 17% in Q3 2025 to 21%.

MediaTek still led the global smartphone SoC market with a 28% share (down 6 percentage points year-over-year), followed by Qualcomm with 22% (down from 25%).

After Apple, UNISOC ranked fourth with 13% (down from 14%), while Samsung remained in fifth with an 8% share, up from 6% in Q3 2025. Other manufacturers went from a 4% share to 8%.

Overall, the market saw a 21% decline year-over-year, though the report didn’t disclose how many chips were shipped during the quarter.

Commenting on the numbers, Counterpoint Research Senior Analyst Shivani Parashar said:

“We saw three notable flagship chipset launches in September 2026, based on TSMC’s 2nm process node: Apple’s A20 series, MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 series. These launches are expected to boost premium smartphone SoC shipments in Q4 2026, although volumes are still likely to remain below Q4 2025 levels.”

Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects global smartphone chip shipments to decline 20% year-over-year in 2026, followed by another 3% to 4% drop in 2027. The research firm also expects memory prices to continue rising next year.

During its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings call, Apple described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” warning that further increases would continue to put pressure on its profit margins in the coming quarters.

To read Counterpoint’s full report, follow this link.

#3504. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

#3502. Fable Meets Classic Disney In New Fantasy Action Adventure

There are plenty of games out there that slot effortlessly into our predetermined categories and genres, letting us know what to expect, while at the same time potentially impinging on the excitement it has to offer. Murals is not one of those games, defying many of the expectations that one might have for it, and bringing players something entirely new in the process.

If you really want a definition, Murals is an action-adventure set in a fairytale world where increasingly eccentric characters are having all kinds of peculiar problems. That said, it's hiding a lot more under the proverbial hood than descriptions and store pages might suggest, so we sat down with the minds (and hands) behind the game over at Dlala Studios, CEO Aj Grand-Scrutton and Art Director Lucy Kyriakidou, to get a better understanding of exactly what sets Murals apart so much.

"So the sales pitch here is that it’s a twisted isometric hack-and-slash action adventure. We were going through weird versions of fairytales as a nameless amnesiac hero, but for us it was really about making a fun and hopefully funny comedy action adventure where you get to smack creatures with hammers and swords and various weapons. It's our love of combat put into a game that, hopefully, is quite pick-up and play," Grand-Scrutton explains.

"The main motivation is that we’re pretty weird. I think our Battletoads is quite a weird Battletoads. One of the mini-games in that has you massaging an alien. I always say the best stories you can tell are the ones that feel natural to you, and I think we’re all just a little bit weird. Going back and giving our own interpretations of these things feels very Dlala."

At the same time, the painted style of the game is genuinely pretty breathtaking to jump into for the first time, and it's clear that plenty of passion has gone into the project. As Kyriakidou confirms, evoking that feeling in the player is all a result of leaning into the team's strengths, above all else.

"We basically wanted to make sure the art team had a lot of fun, so we decided to lean into what they're best at. We have great painters and amazing concept artists, so what we wanted to do is take those and make it our own. The same way we wanted to make the stories our own. We're like, ‘let's make this art style what we all enjoy and what we're best at.

"We took what we learned from previous games, obviously, about clarity, but this is a different genre, isometric, and it was not what we did for the last two games, at the very least. So, we did have a back and forth to make sure the team was playing the game and we were checking in. If anybody had issues seeing something then we would address that. We got to a point where we were like, ‘Okay, let's make some clear rules with what we're doing, like lighting the floors and having contrast. We still check from time to time to make sure that we do have that there. We do have people on the team with color blindness, so we want to make sure that people get the most out of the game without worrying about hitting a wall."

One of the most impressive things about Murals at this juncture is that the combat comes with a remarkable level of visual clarity. At any one time, there can be a lot of things going on, from missiles heading towards you to things falling from the sky, all while melee minions attack with enthusiasm.

In a hand-painted world, the easiest pitfall would have been for those sequences to become a bit of a mess, and difficult for even the most ocularly sound of us to define properly. As someone who is color-blind, it's even easier to be caught out by games that haven't done their diligence in this regard, but Murals' prowess in that area doesn't come about by accident.

"Combat has been a nightmare, both visually and from a gameplay perspective. We've iterated on everything, and every time we land on something, we’d then iterate on the next bit, and then it wouldn't work. Honestly, I don't think we're really truly locked in the combat experience until six or seven months ago," Grand-Scrutton says.

"At one point, we had amazing weapons, but we couldn't get the enemies feeling good and then vice versa. It really took Chris Jones, who was art producer on Battletoads. He really wanted to move into design, and so this was his first foray, but he hadn't been there for all the baggage we had, all the different iterations. So he took it on and then he pitched me and Grant, and he said, the thing about modern Doom is that each of the enemies only really does one thing, and the interest comes from the combinations, and what happens when the player is put against two pairs of enemies that he’s never faced in that combo before. It sounded weird but we let him play with it and that's what you see now. Although you wouldn't look at the game and think Doom is in it, it was probably the biggest influence for each enemy just doing one thing really well and then pairing them up. Combat was a nightmare, but, once again, we're still refining, we're still balancing."

As you might expect, it was just as difficult to get the game to where it is from an art perspective, as Kyriakidou explains further.

"The enemies have been something we just keep going back to. We designed and made sure that what they do is very clear and you know if you've seen one enemy, if one looks similar, you roughly know what they're going to do. But it was only a few days ago that the colors [were settled]. After some user testing AJ was on the call and he says, ‘oh, they actually said that the colors are very clear’, And I said ‘OK, everybody stop. Stop what you're doing. Please. We found it.’ All of our worlds are very unique, and they have their own moods, color palettes, and lighting, so finding consistency in the enemies so they stand out anywhere has been an absolute nightmare."

Murals also features an adorable player companion affectionately known as Loaf. Loaf is different from every other character in the game in that he is essentially a sketch, a doodle on the edge of a page. Loaf also comes with some amazing lines in both cutscenes, and while the player is actively playing the game, continuing the light tone that makes it so enjoyable in the first place. As a character, it also serves as the conduit through which the team can experiment vociferously, as Grand-Scrutton details.

"My lead writer, Kelsey, and I, we always say Loaf is basically the biggest self-insert. Lowe is the weird conversations that Kelsey and I have every day. That is what Loaf is. And Kelsey is the voice of Loaf, so even more so. I love Doodle Bob. I think Doodle Bob's a fantastic sponge. I think everyone's always scared to approach that, but he was literally the first on the call sheet for references. This is an airy-fairy creative director’s answer to this, but it is the truth. Everything in the world that pre-exists before what we're playing is 2D. The 3D characters are either the invasive force which is the distorted, and the hero to an extent, or it's the big boss fights later on, and they've been manipulated by the Creator.

"Loaf isn't either one of those things. Loaf was a sketch in your notebook that when the Creator used his magic to bring one of these murals to life, Loaf was this side effect that got caught up in it. So I didn't want Loaf to be pretty and have all the depth and dynamic lighting that everyone else had. I wanted Loaf to really feel like somebody had pulled him off of the page and thrown him into reality. What's really fun about that is that we have three categories: We have 3D characters, we have our 2D NPCs, and then Loaf is a cartoon character. A lot of the other 2D characters don't really follow cartoon rules. They have a bit of stretch and squish to them, but Loaf pops in with a balloon. His transformation animation in Rapunzel is one of my favorite animations in the whole game. Loaf can do whatever we want in that sense. That was really fun to me because he's just perfectly imperfect, and he's a proper little weirdo. He's a proper little weirdo."

As you progress through the game, you'll notice elements that play into the wider story of the game and its setting. In the preview levels we played through, Rapunzel's hair serves as a method of navigating up and down, essentially replacing the simple ladder in some sections. While there are other ways to do this that don't make a tangible difference to the gameplay loop, the methods Dlala have used add so much richness to the world, and it's a theme that continues later in the game.

"The game is split into sections and each section contains a bunch of murals. The first two levels you play, and that includes Rumpelstiltskin that comes just after, they're really about introducing you to this world, the mechanics etc. The further you get through the game, the bigger the world becomes," Grand-Scrutton says.

"If you ever get a chance to see the announce trailer, it's only in there for a split second, but in the Hansel and Gretel level, there are these big gingerbread head interactions where you're rotating platforms and kicking balls, and that was based on like Screwball Scramble and things like that. The mechanics within the levels come a lot more into play, but we never really used anything like puzzles, for instance, because we don't want to chuck them into the middle of the game and you get stuck because you're a combat player who doesn't want it. The more you move through, the more you'll get to interact with different parts of the world."

As Kyriakidou details further, absolutely none of those additions are going to stand out as unnatural, and all fit within the wider setting as a whole.

"They also always make sense within the world itself. That's why it never feels like it's just there to add things to do. It's more, ‘This world, what would it have? How would it change?’ It always feels like it's part of the environment, part of the story itself."

After spending a couple of hours with the game, it's abundantly clear that Murals has all the ingredients to potentially be in Game of the Year conversations when it drops in 2027. It's very tight mechanically, the world is engrossing, the jokes are funny, and Bob Mortimer is in it (which is never be a bad thing).

If it can carry the momentum it quickly builds up through to the end credits, then it will absolutely be one of the best examples of the genre in recent years. There are a lot of questions to answer between now and then, but Murals is clearly playing to win, and it has every chance of doing just that.

#3501. Resident Evil director Zach Cregger explains why the iPhone is vital to his work

There have been a number of high-profile movies technically shot on iPhone, but in most cases they are using the same professional cinematography kit they would use with other cameras, including lenses costing tens of thousands of dollars.

Resident Evil director Zach Cregger uses his own iPhone in a rather different way, taking an approach that could be useful to amateur and professional filmmakers alike …

There’s an ongoing debate about how meaningful it is to claim that a high-profile movie, ad, or keynote video was shot on iPhone. Naysayers argue that the quality is all down to the professional lenses, lighting rigs, and editing employed, while those on the other side of the fence point out that everything was captured by the iPhone sensor.

Cregger mostly sidesteps all of that, describing his own use of an iPhone for shot planning, creating photo boards that accurately represent the image that will be captured by each of the Pro lenses he intends to use.

We grew up with video games informing our visual sense just as much as movies and television did, and I feel like I’m able to make a movie that involves the gameplay. [Here] I have a wide angle lens, our protagonist is in the center of the frame as he’s moving, we’re following locked right behind him when he looks right and we swing, right. His attention is dictating where the camera goes, and I think that the effect of that is is a much more immersive horror experience where you’re feeling informed.

I’m a hyper prepper. I’ve got the iPhone that is, like, always on me. I’ll go to the location with my cinematographer and I’ll use Cadrage, an app that approximates different lenses, and I will basically plan out the sequence. I will know exactly what shot is going to cut to what shot, and I will print out these images and everyone will know we’re using this lens for these shots. This is what’s going to be in the frame, and there’s no guesswork.

He does, however, add that an iPhone is all that you need to make a movie, even if his own budgets give him access to rather more expensive kit.

Anybody can make a movie with what’s in your pocket right now.

At the other end of the scale, I use my iPhone in a similar way to him when planning my own amateur videos. I take still photos to create a photo board so that I have a visual reference for each of my planned shots. The videos themselves may be shot on my Blackmagic rig, my iPhone, or some mix of the two.

You can watch Cregger talk through his process for Apple TV here.

Resident Evil director Zach Cregger counts iPhone among his go-to filmmaking tools.Go inside his unique approach to crafting immersive horror experiences, and watch his latest movie now on the Apple TV app. https://t.co/oOpQL0mJde pic.twitter.com/RHWwlPjFID

#3500. ‘Sonic the Hedgehog’ Officially Returns With New Release

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

There was always one kid who got stuck playing Tails in Sonic the Hedgehog 2. If your friend had the first controller, you spent half of Emerald Hill trying to keep up and the other half waiting for Sonic to stop long enough for you to catch up. Still, when Sega introduced Miles “Tails” Prower in the 1992 Genesis game, handing somebody that second controller meant they could actually join you for the ride.

Thirty years later, the movie sequel with the same name gave the two their own big-screen team-up. Colleen O’Shaughnessey carried her role as Tails from the games into the movies, where the fox joined Ben Schwartz’s Sonic in taking on Dr. Robotnik. For fans who met the pair on the Genesis, though, a couple of red shoes and two wildly different patches of terrain are enough to place them.

Collider can exclusively share details on Dark Horse and Sega’s new classic Sonic and Tails vinyl figures, which pull the pair straight out of the 1992 game. Previously teased at San Diego Comic-Con, the figures kick off Dark Horse’s official Sonic the Hedgehog collectible line. Bigshot Toyworks sculpted the figures, with J.W. Productions handling prototyping and paint.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

Sonic stands 8 inches tall, with one of his red shoes kicked back and a cloud of dust trailing him as he tears across a Chemical Plant Zone base. If you spent your childhood dreading the part of Chemical Plant where the pink liquid starts rising, there’s something funny about seeing Sonic look this unbothered. He’s already halfway out of there.

Tails gets a piece of Emerald Hill Zone, the opening stage of the game that introduced him. His figure stands 7 inches tall and catches him on foot just before takeoff, with both tails raised behind him and his red-and-white shoes still on the ground. Put the two side by side and it looks like Sonic has already taken off for the next level while Tails is about to take the shortcut.

The Sonic and Tails figures retail for $59.99 each. Dark Horse is offering $10 off when you pre-order them together through Dark Horse Direct, bringing the pair to $109.98 before tax and shipping. Both figures are expected to ship in Q3 2027, while supplies last. Stay tuned to Collider for updates.

#3498. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3496. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

#3495. Nintendo Switch games running natively on Apple TV using Claude Code port

A Redditor has just released an open-source project allowing Switch and Switch 2 games to run natively on Apple TV.

So far, both Super Mario Odyssey and Animal Crossing: New Horizons are running, with work ongoing on The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom …

We’ve seen people using Claude Code to do some pretty wild things, like reverse engineering Adobe’s pro apps in order to create open-source versions of them. The latest example is a Redditor who’s created an open-source project called TVport to recompile Nintendo games from the Switch and Switch 2 to Apple TV.

Redditor FloatingFalafel shared the work on GitHub. They’ve so far ported three games to Apple TV, with one of them still a work in progress.

I have been working on a fork of nxnative that recompiles your OG Switch and Switch 2 dumps for AppleTV. Currently, this only works on a game-by-game basis. Most games run essentially the same on the switch, but some load textures into memory differently and need to be diagnosed and fixed before the game will run properly. My hope is to find outliers during this beta so more fixes can be added into the program, making it a seamless experience […]

Super Mario Odyssey – Runs at 60FPS, very slight stutters on occasion, and some audio issues around waterfalls specifically.

Animal Crossing: Horizon – Runs at 30FPS, zero issues so far on my plays.

Zelda: TOTK – Still being worked on, runs at 30FPS, gets thermal throttled. I have a work around for the thermal throttle. I have a render scale selection set at 75% and I am working on adding MetalFX upscaling.

They note you’ll need the 4th-gen Apple TV with its 8GB RAM in order to support some games, though these ones run on the 3rd-gen box.

Another Redditor is working on porting Nintendo 64 games to Apple TV using an app called Nativecade. How long any of these types of projects will survive is anyone’s guess.

#3493. James Gunn’s 10-Year DCU Plan Gets New Update After Shock Studio Exit

Credit: Jeffrey Mayer/MediaPunch/INSTARimages

The DC Universe franchise is ending its year with a big, unexpected bang.

2026 saw the Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merger come to fruition, as the two Hollywood titans became Skydance, which would include DC Studios as part of their empire. Despite it being initially reported that James Gunn and Peter Safran were staying in their co-CEO positions, Skydance fully announced on November 9 that the duo will officially exit their roles, with Jeremy Latcham set to take over, starting on December 1. While audience members and industry figures alike are having different reactions, more details on the shake-up are now emerging in a massive report.

Puck is reporting that they are being told that there are already plans "afoot to dismantle much of what Gunn and Safran had plotted out beyond next summer’s Gunn-directed Man of Tomorrow, the currently shooting The Batman: Part II," as well as an untitled "in-the-works HBO series." Per the outlet, "DC goes back into reboot mode… again," but no official statements have been given as of yet.

The Hollywood Reporter broke down in detail what seemingly went down behind the scenes between DC Studios' Gunn and Safran, and Paramount's David Ellison, Ynon Kreiz, along with Skydance Motion Picture Group's Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg. According to the trade's sources, the DC heads learned their fate on Friday, November 6, when Ellison and Kreiz visited their office at the Warner Bros. lot to inform them in person.

Despite Gunn and Safran staying with DC Studios, as confirmed on October 2, the two executives were informed that Latcham would be taking over for the two of them. The new DC boss, whose film-producing history goes back to the early days of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, is no stranger to the Superman filmmaker, after executive producing 2014's Guardians of the Galaxy. Per THR, the changing of the DC guard has been "in the works since early fall and had been precipitated by a reachout to Latcham" by Greenstein. Prior to the announcement on Monday, November 9, Gunn and Latcham had not been in contact about the massive shake-up, but reportedly were planning to have a phone call yesterday afternoon, at the time of this story's publication.

Sources claimed that there were "several points of tension between DC’s Gunn and Safran and Skydance’s Greenstein and Goldberg." The DC partners were previously reporting directly to former WBD CEO David Zaslav, instead of Warner Bros. Pictures' Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, as "their contracts stipulated they would maintain that kind of direct reporting structure in the event of a change of leadership, in this case Ellison." However, this led to a "chafing with Greenstein and Goldberg, who are trying to consolidate all production of motion pictures under them."

Since the launch of DC Studios in 2022, followed by a slate of movies and TV shows being unveiled in 2023, Gunn and Safran had gotten used to having "strong control over every aspect of the rollout of DC products," per one insider telling THR. But with the merger leading to a different setup, the publication stated that "they were not about to get layered in the reporting structure," from what they were being informed.

The points of tension don't stop there, with THR going on to mention that the DC Studios co-CEOs were not "forthcoming or very slow in sharing plans, slate details, and footage," with the Skydance film bosses. This was seemingly a major element in what got Latcham the gig, as he will report directly to Goldberg and Greenstein. Another insider, who gave a more "blunt assessment," added that Ellison allegedly was never looking to have DC report directly to him "in the first place," while not having time for "studio politics, such as any posturing between division heads."

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Finances were also a factor that played into the decision, as Superman's $618 million gross, while being profitable, "did not net out, or have the kind of pop culture impact, in the way that kind of movie should have, the Skydance regime’s thinking went." While Supergirl was a commercial failure, the R-rated Clayface, which has made over $103 million worldwide on a $40 million budget, has emerged as a modest success, along with a strong critical reception.

The outlet added that sources describe Latcham as a "down the middle shooter" with the goal of making financial hits for the general audience and getting them to theaters. Multiple sources also added that if Gunn is seen as the filmmaker to "deliver f-bombs and lesser known characters," then the new DC Studios CEO, who is expected to divide his time between L.A. and his home back in Texas, is "the guy to deliver what’s more in line with Ellison’s more meat and potatoes tastes." As for how this will affect upcoming DC movies, he is predicted to be a "very hands on producer" who enjoys spending time on sets. THR adds that Gunn and Safran, who are returning to more creative roles, will still have "direct links to the studio," but just less control.

Following Gunn's comments yesterday, people close to him have noted that he's "somewhat relieved to go fully back to the creative side of the business," a sentiment that he addressed in his separate statement from the Skydance announcement. While he is in post-production on the Man of Tomorrow movie, 2027 won't be the end of his DC adventures, as he is also an executive producer on HBO Max's The People Vs. Gorilla Grodd, and is also currently penning a new mystery project in the franchise. The director stated the following about his future on social media:

Oh, boy. What a four years. Thanks to all of you who have supported me and Peter in our time as the heads of DC Studios.

When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri, I used to write and draw my own comics with a mix of DC Comics characters and my own characters. Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream come true. I didn't know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn't pass up the unique opportunity. I'm glad I took the job.

There have been so many highs along the way - releasing Superman and Clayface, making Peacemaker, reading the scripts to The People Vs, the entire process of Man of Tomorrow, which thus far has been the best filmmaking experience of my life, and numerous other moments. The highest of the highs have been all the talented and wonderful people l've worked with and grown to love: the DC Studios crew, our talented collaborators, our casts and crews, and the boisterous and hilarious fans. And the best part of all has been working with Peter Safran, the smartest and most competent person I know. You've been the best partner a person could ask for, and, more so, a truly good friend.

But what only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I'm always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and l've stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years (Jenn, I love you and I'm sorry and you don't need to feel guilty for being the happiest of all people that I'm no longer doing this job). And the thing my ADHD hyperfocus has had the most difficulty with has been dividing my time between projects I'm incredibly passionate about and the ones I'm not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head. So, yes, I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I'm also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking.

That's not to say Peter and I are immediately done with DC or superheroes. We have Man of Tomorrow out this summer. And we've just been engaged on another DC project which I'm writing, and we'll see where it goes after that. And, of course, the characters we set up will live on.

Thank you so very, very much for embracing the characters and stories we've put on screen.

The last note about the future of DC Studios comes with concern from a source that THR describes as having "knowledge of DC’s inner workings." There is "a real concern" about how many times viewers can or will be willing to invest in versions of these characters and the actors who get cast as them. While the DCU may not be ending in the near future, time will tell what the outcome becomes, especially as Latcham takes over for Gunn and Safran as the next CEO.

#3492. The Newest 4K Amazon Fire TV Stick Is Nearly 60% Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade. And because this streaming stick measures just 3.6 inches and draws power directly from your TV's USB port using the included cable, it can sit out of sight behind your screen without taking up another wall outlet.

Despite its small size, it supports 4K streaming over Wi-Fi 6, along with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG for improved contrast and color on compatible televisions. What you don't get is Dolby Vision or Dolby Atmos audio. If either is important to your home theater setup, the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus, currently $39.99, is worth considering for the extra $15. Otherwise, there's little to complain about when it comes to performance, with PCMag reporting that apps respond almost instantly and 4K streams load quickly with almost no blurry, low-resolution moments.

The redesigned Alexa voice remote is another improvement, with a more comfortable shape, an easier-to-find home button, and dedicated shortcuts for major streaming services. You can also use Alexa to search for shows, launch apps, or control compatible smart home devices. The software experience is less impressive, with advertisements and recommendations dominating the home screen, leaving relatively little room for your actual apps. There's also no support for Apple AirPlay or Google Cast, so sharing content directly from your phone isn't particularly convenient. Still, if you're comfortable with Amazon's interface and don't need the missing Dolby formats, the Fire TV Stick 4K delivers responsive streaming and a useful remote for just $25.
